lessons.title: What Peripherals and Interfacing Are
lessons.content:
Imagine a brilliant chef locked inside a kitchen with no doors and no windows. The chef can cook anything, but nobody can hand in vegetables, and nobody can carry out the food. All that skill is useless. A CPU with no peripherals is exactly that chef. It can add billions of numbers every second, but without a keyboard, a screen, a disk or a network card, it cannot get any work in and cannot show any result out. This course is about the doors and windows of the computer: the devices around the CPU and the clever connections that let them talk to it.

What a peripheral is: A peripheral is any device that is connected to the core of the computer (the CPU and main memory) to put information in, take information out, store it, or carry it somewhere else. The word comes from periphery, which means the outer edge. Your keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, speaker, webcam, hard disk, pen drive and Wi-Fi card are all peripherals. Some live outside the box, like the printer. Some live inside, like the SSD or the network card. Location does not matter. What matters is that they sit around the CPU and memory, not inside them.

The four kinds of peripherals: Input devices bring information in: keyboard, mouse, touch screen, scanner, microphone, camera, fingerprint reader. Output devices send information out to people or machines: monitor, printer, speaker, LED, motor. Storage devices keep information when the power is off: hard disk, SSD, pen drive, memory card, DVD. Communication devices move information between computers: network card, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, modem. Some devices are two kinds at once. A touch screen is input and output. A pen drive is storage, but you can also think of it as a way to carry files between computers.

What interfacing means: Interfacing is the job of connecting a peripheral to the computer so that both sides understand each other and nothing gets damaged. An interface is the meeting point. It includes the physical connector and wires, the electrical signals, the timing rules, and the software rules about what each message means. Think of a translator standing between two people who speak different languages, who also makes sure neither person talks too fast for the other. The interface is that translator.

Why interfacing is needed at all: You might ask why we cannot just wire the keyboard straight onto the CPU pins. The answer is that the CPU and the device disagree on almost everything. Engineers usually list four big mismatches. Every interface you will meet in this course exists to fix one or more of them.

Mismatch 1, speed: A modern CPU runs at about 3 GHz, meaning around 3 billion clock ticks per second. A fast typist presses maybe 8 keys per second. A printer may take several seconds per page. A hard disk needs a few milliseconds just to move its arm. If the CPU sat and waited for each device, it would waste almost all its time. On the other side, a fast device like a network card can receive data faster than a careless program can collect it, so data can be lost. The interface needs buffers (small waiting rooms for data) and signals that say I am ready and I am busy.

Mismatch 2, voltage and power: Inside a modern chip, logic signals may be 3.3 volts or even lower. Some older parts use 5 volts. An old RS-232 serial port uses plus and minus voltages up to about 12 volts. A motor may need 12 volts and a lot of current. If you connect these directly, you can burn the chip. So the interface includes level shifters, transistors, relays and protection parts to change voltages safely.

Mismatch 3, data format: The CPU likes data in parallel groups of bits, like 32 or 64 bits at a time. A USB cable sends bits one after another in a single stream (serial). A keyboard sends a small code for each key, not the letter itself. A microphone produces a smooth changing voltage (analog), not numbers. So the interface must convert: parallel to serial and back, key codes to characters, analog to digital and back.

Mismatch 4, timing and synchronisation: The CPU must know exactly when data is valid. Is the byte on the wires right now the new one or the old one? Has the printer finished the last line? Two sides need agreed signals, like a strobe that says data is ready now and an acknowledge that says got it. This back-and-forth is called handshaking, and you will see it in many lessons.

The three layers of every connection: Every working peripheral has three parts working together. First, the device itself, for example the actual keyboard with its keys. Second, the controller, a small circuit (often a tiny chip with its own logic) that sits between the device and the computer's bus. The controller has a few registers, little storage boxes, that the CPU can read and write. Third, the driver, a piece of software in the operating system that knows exactly which registers to touch and in what order. The CPU never talks to the raw device. It talks to the controller through registers, guided by the driver.

Ports and connectors: The word port has two meanings, and students mix them up. A physical port is the socket you plug into, like a USB port or an HDMI port. An I/O port in the programming sense is an address that the CPU uses to reach a controller register, like port 60h for the old PC keyboard controller. Both are called ports because both are doors. Just remember: one is a hole in the case, the other is a number in a program.

Standards make it all work: Why can a mouse made in China work on a laptop made in Taiwan running software written in the USA? Because everyone follows published standards. USB, HDMI, SATA, PCI Express, Bluetooth and Ethernet are all standards written by industry groups. A standard fixes the connector shape, the voltages, the timing and the message format. If two products both follow the standard, they work together without the makers ever meeting. Standards are the hidden heroes of this course.

Plug and play: In old computers, adding a new card meant setting tiny switches (jumpers) by hand to choose its address and interrupt number, and if two cards chose the same numbers, the computer crashed. Modern interfaces are plug and play. When you plug in a device, it tells the computer who it is (a maker number and a product number), and the operating system picks free resources and loads the right driver automatically. Hot plugging goes one step further: you can plug and unplug while the computer is on, as with USB. Not every interface supports hot plugging. You should never pull a graphics card out of a running PC.

Speeds you should keep in your head: It helps to know rough sizes. A keyboard sends a few bytes per second. A mouse sends a few hundred small reports per second. A fast USB 3 pen drive moves a few hundred megabytes per second. A good NVMe SSD moves several gigabytes per second. Main memory moves tens of gigabytes per second. Each step is roughly ten to a thousand times faster than the one before, so one single way of connecting things could never suit them all. That is why so many different interfaces exist.

A quick history: Early computers in the 1950s and 1960s used punched cards, paper tape and big printers, each with its own special wiring. In 1981 the IBM PC came with expansion slots (the ISA bus) and standard ports, so other companies could build add-on cards. Serial ports, the parallel printer port and PS/2 keyboard ports were common through the 1990s. In 1996 USB arrived to replace that zoo of different ports with one universal plug. Today almost everything uses fast serial links: USB, SATA, PCI Express, HDMI and DisplayPort.

Real-life example 1, a bKash payment at a shop: You show your phone's QR code at a shop in Mirpur. The shopkeeper's scanner (input peripheral) shines light and its camera sensor turns the pattern into numbers. Those go through a USB cable (interface) as if typed on a keyboard. The shop computer's CPU checks the amount, sends a request through the network card (communication peripheral) to the server, gets the reply, and then the small thermal printer (output peripheral) prints a receipt. In a few seconds, at least four peripherals and three different interfaces did their jobs, and you never thought about any of them.

Real-life example 2, a weather station in a school: A science club in Rajshahi builds a small weather station. A temperature sensor gives a voltage that rises with heat. A tiny analog-to-digital converter turns that voltage into a number. A microcontroller reads the number, shows it on a small LCD screen, and sends it over Wi-Fi to a phone. Here, interfacing means choosing the right resistor so the LCD's backlight does not burn, making sure the 5 volt sensor does not damage a 3.3 volt chip, and writing code that reads the sensor at the right time. That is exactly the kind of thinking this course teaches.

What this course covers: First we learn the general rules: how the CPU addresses devices, the three ways to move data (polling, interrupts and DMA), and buses like PCI Express. Then we study the famous connections: serial and parallel ports, USB, and the chip-to-chip buses SPI and I2C. Next come the devices themselves: keyboards, mice, touch screens, displays, printers, scanners, hard disks and SSDs. Finally we go to the electronics edge: converting analog to digital, reading sensors, driving motors with a microcontroller, and power and networking.

How this links to earlier courses: In Microprocessors and Assembly you met chips like the 8255 parallel port chip and the 8259 interrupt controller, and you learned address decoding with the 8086. We will not repeat those details. Here we zoom out to the whole modern computer and its real devices. From Digital Logic you need binary, gates and flip-flops. From Electronic Devices you need the idea of a transistor as a switch and Ohm's law (V = I x R), which we will use many times.

Common mistakes and exam questions: A common mistake is thinking the CPU talks directly to a device. It always talks through a controller and its registers. Another mistake is mixing up physical ports and I/O port addresses. Students also forget that storage and communication devices are peripherals too, not only keyboard and screen. Exams often ask: define peripheral and interface, classify a list of devices into input, output, storage and communication, and explain why an interface is needed using the speed, voltage, format and timing mismatches.

Recap: A peripheral is any device around the CPU and memory that brings data in, sends it out, stores it or moves it. Interfacing connects the two sides safely by fixing four mismatches: speed, voltage, data format and timing. Every peripheral works through a device, a controller with registers, and a driver. Standards like USB and HDMI let products from different companies work together. Next lesson, we look closely at how the CPU actually finds and talks to those controller registers.
key_points: A peripheral is any device around the CPU and main memory that inputs, outputs, stores or communicates data.
Peripherals fall into four groups: input, output, storage and communication; some devices belong to more than one.
An interface is the meeting point: connector, electrical signals, timing rules and message meaning.
Interfaces exist to fix four mismatches between CPU and device: speed, voltage, data format and timing.
Every working peripheral has three layers: the device, a controller with registers, and a software driver.
A physical port is a socket; an I/O port is an address the CPU uses to reach a controller register.
Published standards like USB, HDMI and PCI Express let devices from different makers work together.
lessons.tip: For every device in this course, ask the same four questions: how fast is it, what voltage does it use, what format is its data, and how does it say it is ready? The answers tell you what the interface must do.
lessons.task: Walk around your home and list 10 devices connected to a computer or phone (including inside ones like the battery charger or SIM). Put each into input, output, storage or communication, and for each write which of the four mismatches seems biggest.

quiz.q: Which of these is a storage peripheral?
quiz.explain: An SSD keeps data when power is off, so it is a storage device. The microphone is input, the monitor is output, Wi-Fi is communication.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four main mismatches an interface fixes?
quiz.explain: The four mismatches are speed, voltage, data format and timing. The colour of the case has nothing to do with interfacing.

quiz.q: The CPU normally talks to a peripheral through:
options: A controller's registers, guided by a driver
quiz.explain: The CPU reads and writes the controller's registers; the driver software knows which registers to use and in what order.

quiz.q: What is handshaking?
options: Signals like ready and acknowledge that keep two sides in step
Shaking the mouse to wake the PC
quiz.explain: Handshaking is the exchange of signals such as strobe (data ready) and acknowledge (got it) so both sides agree on timing.

quiz.q: Why can a mouse from one company work with a laptop from another company?
options: Both follow a published standard such as USB
quiz.explain: Standards fix the connector, voltages, timing and message format, so any two products that follow them work together.

lessons.title: The I/O System: Addresses, Controllers and Drivers
lessons.content:
Think of a big apartment building in Dhanmondi. Every flat has a number, like 4B or 7A. When the courier comes with a parcel, he does not need to know who lives inside or what they do. He only needs the flat number. The CPU treats devices in the same way. It does not know what a printer or a disk really is. It only knows addresses. Behind each address sits a small register belonging to some controller, and writing or reading that register is how the CPU sends orders and gets news. This lesson is about that addressing system and the software layers on top of it.

The I/O system in one picture: Picture the CPU at the top. Below it is a bus, a shared set of wires (or fast links) that carries addresses, data and control signals. Main memory hangs off this bus. So do many device controllers: one for the keyboard, one for the disk, one for the network, one for USB, and so on. Each controller connects to its real device on the other side. On top of all this, inside the operating system, sit the device drivers. When a program wants to print, it asks the operating system, the operating system asks the printer driver, and the driver touches the controller registers. That chain is the I/O system.

What a device controller is: A device controller (also called an adapter or interface card) is the electronics that understands one type of device. A disk controller knows how to move disk heads and read sectors. A USB host controller knows the USB rules. A network controller knows how to send and receive Ethernet frames. The controller does the low-level, fast, fiddly work so the CPU does not have to. Many controllers today are tiny computers themselves, with their own processor and firmware (software stored in the chip).

The three classic registers: Almost every controller exposes at least three kinds of register to the CPU. The data register holds the byte or word being moved, either coming in from the device or going out to it. The status register holds flags that describe the device right now, such as busy, ready, error or data available. The control register (sometimes called the command register) receives orders from the CPU, such as start, stop, reset, enable interrupts, or choose a speed. Real controllers often have many more registers, but these three ideas cover most of them.

A tiny example with a pretend printer: Suppose a simple printer controller has a status register at address 0x379 and a data register at 0x378, and bit 7 of status means ready. To print the letter A, the CPU first reads 0x379 and checks bit 7. If it is 0, the printer is busy, so the CPU checks again. When bit 7 becomes 1, the CPU writes 65 (the ASCII code of A) into 0x378, then sets a strobe bit in the control register to say take it now. These addresses are in fact the traditional ones for the first PC parallel port, but the important thing is the pattern: check status, move data, give a command.

How the CPU reaches a register, two styles: There are two ways to give device registers addresses. In port-mapped I/O (also called isolated I/O), devices live in a separate small address space, and the CPU uses special instructions to reach them. On x86 these are IN and OUT, and the I/O space has 65,536 port addresses. In memory-mapped I/O, device registers get addresses inside the normal memory address space, so the CPU uses ordinary load and store instructions to touch them. You met the hardware details of both in the Microprocessors course. Here we just compare them as a system designer.

Comparing the two styles: Port-mapped I/O keeps device addresses from eating into memory space, which mattered when memory space was small, and makes I/O instructions easy to spot in code. Memory-mapped I/O is simpler for programmers because every normal instruction can work on a device register, and it is the only option on processors without IN and OUT, such as ARM and RISC-V. Modern PCs use both. Old devices like the legacy keyboard controller still sit on I/O ports, while a graphics card or an NVMe SSD exposes large regions of memory-mapped registers. Your phone, which runs on ARM, uses memory-mapped I/O for everything.

A catch with memory-mapped I/O: Normal memory can be cached, but a device register must not be. If the CPU kept a cached copy of a status register, it might keep seeing busy forever even after the device became ready. So the operating system marks device regions as uncached. Programmers writing low-level C code also mark such variables as volatile, which tells the compiler: do not assume this value stays the same, read it fresh every time. Forgetting this is a classic bug in embedded programming.

Address decoding in one breath: Something must notice that the CPU has put a particular address on the bus and wake up the right controller. That job is done by address decoding logic, which compares address lines with a pattern and enables one chip. You already practised this with decoder chips like the 74LS138. In modern PCs the chipset and the PCI Express system do this automatically, as we will see in lesson 5.

Device drivers: A device driver is the software that knows the secrets of one controller. It knows which register does what, what order of steps starts a transfer, and how to handle errors. Drivers are usually written by the device maker and run inside the operating system with high privilege. A buggy driver can crash the whole computer, which is why Windows blue screens are very often caused by drivers, not by Windows itself. When you install a new printer and Windows says installing device software, it is loading the driver.

Why we need a driver layer: Imagine every app had to know the registers of every printer ever made. Microsoft Word would need code for thousands of printers. Instead, the operating system defines a common interface, such as print this page or read 4 KB from block 1000, and each driver translates that common request into the exact register pokes for its own hardware. This idea is called device independence. The app speaks one language, the driver translates.

The layers of I/O software: From top to bottom, a typical operating system has these layers. First, the user program, which calls something like write or print. Second, device-independent operating system software, which handles naming files and devices, checking permissions, buffering and caching. Third, the device driver for the specific hardware. Fourth, the interrupt handler, a small piece of the driver that runs when the device signals it is done. Fifth, the hardware itself: controller and device. Requests go down this ladder, and results come back up.

Block devices and character devices: Operating systems sort devices into two big families. A block device stores data in fixed-size blocks (often 512 bytes or 4096 bytes), and you can jump to any block, like a hard disk, SSD or pen drive. A character device sends or receives a stream of bytes one after another with no jumping around, like a keyboard, mouse, serial port or printer. Network cards are often treated as a third family, because they deal in packets. On Linux you can see this in the /dev folder, where each device file is marked as block or character.

Buffering: Because devices and programs run at different speeds, the operating system keeps buffers, areas of memory where data waits. When you type, key codes pile up in a keyboard buffer until your program reads them. When you copy a file to a pen drive, Windows may say done before the data is really written, because it is still sitting in a buffer. That is why you should use Safely Remove or Eject before pulling the drive, so the buffer is flushed to the device.

What happens when you press a key, end to end: You press the letter K. Inside the keyboard, a tiny microcontroller spots which key closed and makes a code for it. It sends that code over USB. The USB host controller in the PC receives it and stores it in memory, then raises an interrupt. The CPU pauses what it was doing and runs the USB driver's interrupt handler. The driver passes the code up to the keyboard driver, which turns it into the character k, considering whether Shift was held. The operating system puts the k into the input queue of the window you are typing in. The app reads it and draws it on screen, which sends new pixels through the graphics driver to the display. All of that happens in a few milliseconds.

Real-life example 1, a post office counter: Think of the GPO in Dhaka. Customers (programs) do not walk into the sorting room. They go to a counter (system call), fill a standard form (common interface), and a clerk who knows the local rules for each district (driver) handles the details. The sorting room has trays marked incoming, outgoing and problem (data, control and status registers). If tomorrow a new courier company joins, only the clerk's rulebook changes, not the customers. That is exactly how drivers protect programs from hardware changes.

Real-life example 2, a printer at a photocopy shop near a university: The shop owner buys a new printer model. The old computer cannot print until he installs the driver from the maker's website. After that, Word, PDF readers and browsers can all print, without any of them being updated. If he plugs in a printer whose driver is broken, it may print garbage, or the computer may freeze. One small piece of software sits between every app and the hardware.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think the status register is written by the CPU; normally the CPU reads it and the device sets it. Another mistake is thinking memory-mapped I/O uses real RAM chips; it does not, the addresses just point to device registers instead. Students also confuse a driver with firmware: firmware runs inside the device, the driver runs on the main CPU. Exams ask you to draw the layers of I/O software, compare port-mapped and memory-mapped I/O, name the three controller registers, and explain block versus character devices.

Recap: The CPU reaches devices through controller registers, mainly data, status and control. Those registers get addresses either in a separate I/O space (port-mapped) or inside memory space (memory-mapped). Drivers hide each controller's details behind a common operating system interface, giving device independence. Devices are grouped as block or character, and buffers smooth out speed differences. Next lesson, we compare the three ways of actually moving data: polling, interrupts and DMA.
key_points: A device controller is the electronics that understands one device and exposes registers to the CPU.
The three classic controller registers are data, status and control (command).
Port-mapped I/O uses a separate address space and IN/OUT instructions; memory-mapped I/O puts device registers in the memory address space.
Device registers must not be cached, and low-level code marks them volatile so they are read fresh every time.
A device driver translates common operating system requests into exact register operations for one piece of hardware.
I/O software layers: user program, device-independent OS code, driver, interrupt handler, hardware.
Block devices allow random access to fixed-size blocks; character devices are byte streams.
lessons.tip: Whenever you read a device datasheet, first find the register map and mark which registers are status, data and control. Everything else in the datasheet becomes easier after that.
lessons.task: On a Windows PC, open Device Manager and expand five categories. For one device, open Properties and look at the Driver tab (provider, date, version) and the Resources tab if shown. On Linux or a Mac terminal, run ls -l /dev and find one line starting with b (block) and one with c (character).

quiz.q: Which controller register usually tells the CPU whether the device is busy or ready?
quiz.explain: The status register holds flags such as busy, ready and error that describe the device right now.

quiz.q: In memory-mapped I/O, the CPU reaches device registers using:
quiz.explain: Device registers get addresses in normal memory space, so any normal memory instruction can access them.

quiz.q: Why must device registers not be cached?
options: Registers are too big for the cache
A cached copy could hide the device's real, changing value
quiz.explain: A status bit can change at any moment; a cached copy might keep showing an old value like busy forever.

quiz.q: Which is a character device?
quiz.explain: A keyboard produces a stream of bytes with no random access; disks and pen drives are block devices.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of the driver layer?
options: Programs use one common interface while drivers handle hardware details
It removes the need for controllers
quiz.explain: Device independence: apps speak one language to the OS, and each driver translates it for its own hardware.

lessons.title: Moving Data: Polling, Interrupts and DMA
lessons.content:
Imagine you have ordered a pizza and you are waiting for the delivery rider. You have three choices. You could keep running to the gate every minute to check if he has arrived. You could do your homework and let the doorbell tell you when he comes. Or you could ask the guard downstairs to take the pizza, pay from money you left with him, and only tell you once it is all done. Those three choices are exactly the three ways a computer moves data between the CPU and a device: polling, interrupts and DMA.

The basic problem: A device has some data ready, or needs some data. The CPU is busy running programs. Somebody has to notice that the device is ready, and somebody has to carry the bytes between the device's data register and main memory. The three methods differ in who notices and who carries. Choosing the right one is about not wasting the CPU's time while still not losing any data.

Method 1, programmed I/O with polling: In programmed I/O, the CPU does everything itself by running instructions. Polling means the CPU repeatedly reads the device's status register to ask are you ready yet. When the ready bit is set, the CPU reads or writes the data register, then goes back to asking. In pseudo-code: while (status.ready == 0) { do nothing }; data = DATA_REG. The waiting loop is called a busy-wait loop, because the CPU is busy doing nothing useful.

When polling is fine: Polling is simple, needs no extra hardware, and has very low delay when the device becomes ready, because the CPU is already looking. If the device is fast and almost always ready, or if the CPU has nothing else to do, polling is a good choice. Tiny microcontrollers in toys often poll their buttons in a loop. Very fast network cards in big servers sometimes switch to polling under heavy load, because there is always data waiting.

When polling is bad: If the device is slow, the CPU wastes huge numbers of cycles asking a question whose answer is mostly no. A person types maybe 5 to 10 keys per second. A CPU polling the keyboard millions of times per second gets no millions of times. It is like running to the gate every few seconds for an hour while the pizza is still being baked.

Method 2, interrupt-driven I/O: Here the device itself raises a signal on an interrupt line when it needs attention. The CPU carries on with other work. When the interrupt arrives, the CPU finishes its current instruction, saves where it was (the program counter and flags) and jumps to a small piece of code called the interrupt service routine (ISR), which is part of the driver. The ISR reads or writes the data register, tells the device it has been served, and returns. The CPU then picks up its old work exactly where it left off.

What interrupts cost: Interrupts are not free. Saving the state, jumping to the handler, running it and returning may take a few hundred to a few thousand CPU cycles, depending on the system. For a keyboard that interrupts 10 times per second, that cost is nothing. But if a device interrupts for every single byte at high speed, the overhead becomes huge. The details of interrupt vectors and the 8259 controller were covered in the Microprocessors course; modern PCs use newer controllers (APIC) and message-signalled interrupts on PCI Express, but the idea is the same.

Method 3, Direct Memory Access (DMA): For big transfers, like reading a 1 MB block from a disk, even one interrupt per byte is too many. DMA solves this. A special circuit called a DMA controller (or, in modern systems, the device itself acting as a bus master) moves data directly between the device and main memory without the CPU touching each byte. The CPU only sets up the job: it tells the DMA engine the memory address, the number of bytes and the direction. Then the CPU goes back to work. When the whole block is done, the DMA engine raises one interrupt to say finished.

DMA step by step: First, the driver writes the start address in memory, say 0x20000, the count, say 8192 bytes, and the direction, device to memory, into the DMA registers. Second, it tells the device to start. Third, whenever the device has data, the DMA engine asks for the bus, gets it, and writes the data to the next memory address, increasing the address and decreasing the count. Fourth, when the count reaches zero, it interrupts the CPU. The CPU's work was a few register writes at the start and one interrupt at the end, instead of 8192 separate actions.

Sharing the bus during DMA: The memory bus can only carry one transfer at a time, so the DMA engine and the CPU must share. In burst mode, the DMA engine takes the bus and moves a whole block at once while the CPU waits for the bus. In cycle stealing mode, it takes the bus for one transfer at a time, stealing a cycle here and there, so the CPU slows only a little. In transparent mode, it uses the bus only when the CPU is not using it. Modern CPUs have caches, so the CPU can often keep working from cache while DMA uses memory.

A catch with DMA, cache coherence: If the DMA engine writes new data into memory but the CPU's cache still holds an old copy of those addresses, the CPU might read stale data. Systems handle this either by hardware that keeps caches in sync with DMA (common in PCs) or by the driver telling the cache to flush or invalidate those lines before and after the transfer (common in small embedded chips). This is a favourite topic for tricky bugs.

Comparing with numbers: Suppose a 2 GHz CPU must handle a device sending 8 MB per second. With interrupt-driven I/O moving 4 bytes per interrupt and 400 cycles per interrupt, we need 8,000,000 / 4 = 2,000,000 interrupts per second, costing 2,000,000 x 400 = 800,000,000 cycles. That is 800 million out of 2 billion cycles, or 40 percent of the CPU, just for this one device. With DMA moving 8 KB blocks, we need about 8,000,000 / 8,192, roughly 1,000 blocks per second. If each block costs 1,500 cycles of setup and one interrupt, that is 1,500,000 cycles per second, about 0.075 percent of the CPU. DMA wins by a huge margin for bulk data.

Now the same for a keyboard: A keyboard makes about 10 events per second. With interrupts at 400 cycles each, that is 4,000 cycles per second, practically zero. With polling at 1,000 checks per second, each costing 100 cycles, that is 100,000 cycles, still tiny but wasted. Setting up DMA for single key presses would be silly. So the rule of thumb is: polling for very simple or always-ready cases, interrupts for small, unpredictable events, DMA for big blocks.

Mixing the methods in real systems: Real drivers often combine methods. A network card may use DMA to drop each packet into memory and then raise an interrupt. Under very heavy traffic that would mean tens of thousands of interrupts per second, so many cards use interrupt coalescing: they wait a tiny moment and raise one interrupt for a whole bunch of packets. Linux goes further: when traffic is heavy, the driver switches off the card's interrupts and polls it for a while, then switches interrupts back on when traffic calms down. So the best answer is often not one method, but switching between them as the load changes.

Interrupt priority in one line: When two devices interrupt at the same moment, the system must choose who goes first. Devices that lose data quickly, like a network card or a timer, usually get higher priority than slow ones like a printer. You studied priority and masking in detail in the Microprocessors course.

Handshaking: Whatever method we use, the two sides must agree on when data is valid. In a simple parallel handshake, the sender puts data on the wires, then pulls a strobe line to say data is ready. The receiver reads the data and pulls an acknowledge line to say got it. The sender then removes the strobe and can send the next byte. This two-signal dance is the heart of the old Centronics printer port and many chip interfaces. It means a fast sender cannot overrun a slow receiver.

Synchronous and asynchronous transfer: In synchronous transfer, both sides share a clock signal, and data is valid on a particular clock edge. This is fast and simple to time, and it is used by memory buses, SPI and I2C. In asynchronous transfer, there is no shared clock, and the sides use handshake signals or agreed timing to stay in step. A UART serial link is asynchronous: both sides agree on a speed like 9600 bits per second and use start and stop bits, as we will see in lesson 6.

Real-life example 1, a bank counter in Motijheel: Polling is the customer who keeps asking the cashier is my cheque ready, is my cheque ready. Interrupts are the token system: you sit down, and the display beeps your number when it is your turn. DMA is when the company's accounts officer gives a full list of 200 salary transfers to the bank, and the bank's system moves all the money and sends one confirmation at the end. The officer is free to do other work meanwhile.

Real-life example 2, watching a video on your phone: When you stream a cricket match on Toffee or YouTube, the Wi-Fi chip receives packets and uses DMA to write them straight into memory. The video decoder reads from memory, and the display controller uses DMA to pull each frame from memory to the screen 60 times a second. Your touch on the screen to pause arrives as an interrupt. Meanwhile, a tiny chip checking the battery temperature might simply be polled every few seconds. All three methods are working together in your pocket.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think DMA means the CPU is not involved at all; it still sets up the transfer and handles the final interrupt. Another mistake is thinking interrupts are always better than polling; for very fast, always-ready devices polling can be cheaper. Some forget that DMA competes with the CPU for the memory bus. Exams ask you to compare the three methods in a table, calculate CPU overhead percentages like the example above, describe DMA steps and modes, and draw a strobe and acknowledge handshake timing diagram.

Recap: Polling means the CPU keeps checking a status register; it is simple but wastes time on slow devices. Interrupt-driven I/O lets the device signal the CPU only when needed, which suits small, unpredictable events. DMA lets a controller move whole blocks to or from memory with only a setup and a final interrupt, which suits bulk data. Handshaking keeps sender and receiver in step, with or without a shared clock. Next lesson, we look at the buses that carry all this traffic.
key_points: Polling: the CPU repeatedly reads a status register until the device is ready; simple but wasteful for slow devices.
Interrupt-driven I/O: the device signals the CPU, which runs an interrupt service routine and then resumes its work.
DMA: a controller moves a whole block between device and memory; the CPU only sets it up and handles one final interrupt.
DMA modes include burst, cycle stealing and transparent, depending on how the bus is shared with the CPU.
Overhead maths: events per second x cycles per event / CPU clock gives the fraction of CPU used.
Handshaking uses strobe (data ready) and acknowledge (data taken) so a fast sender cannot overrun a slow receiver.
Synchronous transfer shares a clock; asynchronous transfer uses handshakes or agreed timing with no shared clock.
lessons.tip: Practise the overhead calculation until it is automatic: work out events per second, multiply by cycles per event, divide by clock rate. Exams love it and it builds real intuition.
lessons.task: A 1 GHz CPU handles a device sending 2 MB per second. Calculate the CPU percentage used if (a) each interrupt moves 2 bytes and costs 500 cycles, and (b) DMA moves 4 KB blocks costing 2,000 cycles per block. Then write one sentence on which you would choose.

quiz.q: In polling, the CPU:
options: Waits for the device to send an interrupt
Repeatedly reads the device's status register
Lets a DMA controller move data
quiz.explain: Polling means the CPU keeps checking the status register itself until the ready bit is set.

quiz.q: Which method is best for copying a large file from disk to memory?
quiz.explain: DMA moves the whole block without the CPU touching each byte, then interrupts once at the end.

quiz.q: A device causes 1,000,000 interrupts per second, each costing 500 cycles, on a 1 GHz CPU. What fraction of the CPU is used?
quiz.explain: 1,000,000 x 500 = 500,000,000 cycles per second, which is half of 1,000,000,000.

quiz.q: In cycle stealing DMA mode:
options: The DMA engine never uses the bus
The CPU is stopped until the whole file is moved
The DMA engine takes the bus for one transfer at a time
Data goes through the CPU registers
quiz.explain: Cycle stealing grabs the bus briefly for single transfers, slowing the CPU only a little.

quiz.q: In a strobe and acknowledge handshake, the acknowledge signal means:
options: The receiver has taken the data
quiz.explain: The sender pulls strobe to say data is ready; the receiver answers with acknowledge to say it got it.

lessons.title: Buses and System Interconnect
lessons.content:
Think of the roads of Dhaka. Some are narrow lanes where only one rickshaw fits. Some are wide highways with many lanes. Some carry traffic only one way. At busy crossings, a traffic police officer decides who goes first. A computer has roads too. They are called buses, and they carry addresses, data and control signals between the CPU, memory and devices. How wide those roads are, how fast the traffic moves and who gets to go first decide how quickly the whole computer can work.

What a bus is: A bus is a shared communication path that connects several parts of a computer. In the classic picture, it is a set of parallel wires, each wire carrying one bit. Any device connected to the bus can see what is on it, but only one device should drive (put signals on) the bus at a time, otherwise their signals fight. The word bus comes from the Latin omnibus, meaning for all, because it is shared by everyone, just like a city bus.

The three groups of lines: A classic bus has three groups of lines. Address lines say where: which memory location or device register is being used. Data lines carry the actual value being read or written. Control lines say what and when: read or write, memory or I/O, clock, interrupt requests, bus request and grant, reset, and so on. You studied how the 8086 used these in the Microprocessors course. Here we care about the system-level questions: how much data can a bus carry, and how do many devices share it?

Bus width: Bus width is the number of data lines, which is how many bits move in one transfer. An 8-bit bus moves 1 byte per transfer. A 64-bit bus moves 8 bytes. A wider bus is like a road with more lanes. The address bus width decides how much memory can be reached: with n address lines, 2 to the power n locations. For example, 20 address lines reach 2^20 = 1,048,576 locations, which is 1 MB if each holds one byte.

Bus clock and transfers per clock: A synchronous bus has a clock, and transfers happen on clock edges. If a bus does one transfer per clock tick, the clock rate is the transfer rate. Some buses do two transfers per tick, one on the rising edge and one on the falling edge. That is called double data rate, which is where the DDR in DDR4 memory comes from. Speeds are often written in MT/s, mega transfers per second, instead of MHz, to avoid confusion.

Bandwidth calculation: Bandwidth is how many bytes per second a bus can carry at best. The simple formula is: bandwidth = (width in bytes) x (transfers per second). Example 1: a 32-bit bus at 33 MHz with one transfer per clock gives 4 bytes x 33,000,000 = 132,000,000 bytes per second, about 133 MB/s. Example 2: DDR4-3200 memory on a 64-bit channel does 3,200 million transfers per second, so 8 bytes x 3,200,000,000 = 25.6 GB/s per channel. Remember that this is the peak. Real buses lose some time to addresses, waiting and turnarounds, so real throughput is lower.

One read on a simple bus, step by step: First, the master puts the address on the address lines. Second, it sets the control lines to say this is a memory read. Third, the addressed slave recognises its address, finds the value and puts it on the data lines. Fourth, the slave signals that the data is valid (or the master simply waits a fixed number of clock ticks). Fifth, the master copies the data and releases the bus. If the slave is slow, it can hold a wait or not-ready signal, and the master adds extra clock ticks called wait states. A write works the same way, except the master puts the data on the lines too.

Latency versus bandwidth: Bandwidth is how much water flows through a pipe each second. Latency is how long the first drop takes to arrive after you open the tap. A bus can have great bandwidth but high latency, or the other way around. For moving a big video file, bandwidth matters most. For a mouse click or a small memory read, latency matters most. Engineers always ask about both.

Multiplexed buses: To save pins, some buses use the same wires for address and data at different times. First the address is put on the wires and latched (held) by a special signal, then the same wires carry the data. The 8086 did this with its AD lines, and the old PCI bus did it too. It saves wires and pins, but each transfer takes an extra step, so it is a little slower.

Bus masters and slaves: A bus master is a device that can start a transfer by putting an address and a command on the bus. A bus slave (also called a target) only responds when addressed. The CPU is the main master. A DMA controller, a disk controller or a network card that does DMA can also be masters. Memory is always a slave. When more than one master exists, they need a fair way to take turns.

Bus arbitration: Arbitration is deciding which master gets the bus next. In centralised arbitration, one arbiter circuit receives request lines from all masters and gives a grant to one. In daisy chain arbitration, the grant signal passes from device to device in a line, and the first device that wants the bus keeps the grant. This is simple but unfair: devices near the front of the chain always win, and a far device may starve. In parallel (independent request) arbitration, each master has its own request and grant lines to the arbiter, which can use fixed priority or round-robin to be fair. In distributed arbitration, there is no single arbiter; the devices themselves compare priorities on shared lines.

A tiny arbitration example: Three masters A, B and C share a bus with a fixed priority A over B over C. At one moment B and C both request. A is quiet. The arbiter grants B. B does its transfer and releases the bus. C still waits, and now A also requests. The arbiter grants A, because it has the highest priority. C waits again. If A and B keep requesting, C could wait forever. That is called starvation, and round-robin arbitration fixes it by rotating who is first.

Why one bus is not enough: If the CPU, memory, graphics, disk and keyboard all shared one bus, the slow keyboard and the very fast memory would share the same road. The bus would have to run at a speed all devices can handle, and every transfer would block everyone else. Also, long buses with many devices have more electrical load, so they cannot run very fast. The solution is a bus hierarchy: several buses at different speeds, connected by bridges.

The classic hierarchy: In PCs from the mid 1990s to about 2008, the CPU connected to a chip called the northbridge through the front-side bus. The northbridge handled the fast things: main memory and the graphics slot (AGP, later PCI Express). Below it, the southbridge handled the slower things: PCI slots, USB, disk ports (IDE, SATA), audio, and the old keyboard and mouse ports. A bridge is a chip that passes traffic from one bus to another, translating speeds and protocols, like a toll plaza between a highway and a city road.

The modern layout: Later the memory controller and the main PCI Express lanes moved inside the CPU chip itself, to cut latency. Intel did this around 2008 to 2009, and AMD even earlier with Athlon 64. The northbridge disappeared as a separate chip. Today the CPU talks directly to memory and to the graphics card. A single chip often called the Platform Controller Hub (PCH) on Intel, or simply the chipset, handles USB, SATA, extra PCI Express lanes, audio and networking, connected to the CPU by one fast link. In laptops and phones, almost everything is on one chip, called a system on chip (SoC).

From parallel buses to serial links: Old buses were wide and parallel: many wires, all switching together. At high speeds, parallel wires cause problems: signals on different wires arrive at slightly different times (skew), and wires disturb each other (crosstalk). So modern interconnects use point-to-point serial links: a few pairs of wires, each running extremely fast, connecting just two devices. PCI Express, SATA and USB are all built this way. The word bus is still used out of habit, even when the thing is really a set of private links.

ISA, the first PC expansion bus: The original IBM PC in 1981 had an 8-bit expansion bus running at 4.77 MHz, later called ISA (Industry Standard Architecture). The IBM PC/AT in 1984 widened it to 16 bits at about 8 MHz. ISA cards needed jumpers to set addresses and interrupts by hand, and conflicts were common. It was slow, but it was open and simple, so thousands of companies built cards for it. It was replaced by PCI in the 1990s, which is the topic of the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka flyover: Before the flyovers, all traffic, from rickshaws to buses to private cars, shared the same crossings, and one slow vehicle blocked everyone. A flyover is like a bus hierarchy: fast through traffic goes on the upper road, local slow traffic stays below, and ramps (bridges) connect the two. Each road can run at the speed that suits its traffic. That is exactly why computers split fast memory traffic from slow USB traffic.

Real-life example 2, a school microphone system: In a school assembly in Sylhet, many teachers want to speak, but there is only one microphone. The headmaster decides who speaks next. If he always picks the senior teacher first, a junior teacher may never get a turn: that is fixed priority and starvation. If he goes around the stage in order, everyone gets a chance: that is round-robin. The microphone is the bus, the teachers are bus masters, and the headmaster is the arbiter.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up bandwidth and latency, or forget to convert bits to bytes in the bandwidth formula. Another mistake is thinking the address bus width decides data speed; it decides how much memory can be addressed. Students also think the northbridge still exists in every PC; in modern PCs its jobs moved into the CPU. Exams ask you to calculate bandwidth from width and clock, to compare daisy chain and parallel arbitration, to explain why a bus hierarchy is needed, and to draw the classic northbridge and southbridge diagram.

Recap: A bus is a shared path with address, data and control lines. Width and transfers per second give bandwidth; latency is the delay before data starts. Masters start transfers and arbitration decides which master goes next, using daisy chain, parallel or distributed schemes. Because devices run at very different speeds, computers use a hierarchy of buses joined by bridges, and modern systems have moved to fast point-to-point serial links. Next lesson, we study the most important of those links: PCI and PCI Express.
key_points: A bus is a shared path with address, data and control lines; only one device may drive it at a time.
Bandwidth = width in bytes x transfers per second; DDR does two transfers per clock.
Latency is the delay before data starts; bandwidth is how much flows per second once it starts.
Bus masters start transfers, slaves respond; arbitration (daisy chain, parallel, distributed) decides who goes next.
Daisy chain is simple but can starve far devices; round-robin arbitration is fair.
A bus hierarchy with bridges separates fast traffic (memory, graphics) from slow traffic (USB, audio).
Modern PCs put the memory controller and main PCIe lanes in the CPU; a chipset (PCH) handles slower I/O.
lessons.tip: When you see any speed number for a bus, write it as width x transfers per second and convert bits to bytes yourself. It catches most exam traps.
lessons.task: Find the specification of your own computer or phone (search the model name). Note the RAM type and speed, for example DDR4-3200 or LPDDR5. Calculate the peak bandwidth of one 64-bit channel using width x transfers per second.

quiz.q: A 64-bit bus does 100 million transfers per second. What is its peak bandwidth?
quiz.explain: 64 bits is 8 bytes; 8 x 100,000,000 = 800,000,000 bytes per second, which is 800 MB/s.

quiz.q: What does DDR mean in DDR memory?
options: Data is moved on both rising and falling clock edges
Two memory chips on one stick
Data is stored twice for safety
quiz.explain: Double data rate means two transfers per clock tick, one on each edge.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of daisy chain arbitration?
options: It always picks the last device
Devices far down the chain can starve
quiz.explain: The grant passes down the line and the first requesting device keeps it, so far devices may never win.

quiz.q: Why do computers use a hierarchy of buses?
options: So fast and slow devices do not have to share one slow road
quiz.explain: Separating fast memory and graphics traffic from slow I/O lets each bus run at the right speed.

quiz.q: In modern PCs, where did the northbridge's memory controller go?
options: It was removed and memory is not used
quiz.explain: The memory controller and main PCIe lanes moved into the CPU to reduce latency; the separate northbridge disappeared.

lessons.title: PCI and PCI Express
lessons.content:
Imagine a market where all shops share one long counter. Only one shopkeeper can serve at a time, and everyone else waits. That is how the old PCI bus worked. Now imagine every shop gets its own private lane straight to the customer, and a busy shop can get two, four or sixteen lanes. That is PCI Express. Almost every fast thing inside a modern PC, the graphics card, the NVMe SSD, the Wi-Fi card, the network card, talks to the CPU through PCI Express. This lesson explains how it got here and how it works.

The problem PCI solved: In the early 1990s, PCs used the ISA bus, which was slow (about 8 MB/s in practice), and cards needed hand-set jumpers for addresses and interrupts. Graphics with windows and pictures, and network cards, needed much more speed. Intel introduced PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) in 1992, and it became the standard expansion bus for PCs through the late 1990s and 2000s. It was also used in many non-PC machines.

PCI basics: Classic PCI is a parallel, shared, synchronous bus. It has 32 data and address lines, multiplexed: the same lines carry the address first and then the data. It runs at 33 MHz. So the peak bandwidth is 4 bytes x 33 million = about 133 MB/s, shared by all the cards on the bus. Later versions offered 64-bit width and 66 MHz, raising the peak to about 533 MB/s, but those were mostly used in servers.

Bus mastering and bursts: Any PCI card can become a bus master and perform DMA on its own, after winning arbitration from a central arbiter in the chipset. PCI also supports burst transfers: after sending one address, a master can send many data words one after another, each going to the next address. This makes long transfers much more efficient than sending an address before every word.

Plug and play through configuration space: PCI's biggest gift was automatic setup. Every PCI device has a small block of registers called configuration space, 256 bytes in classic PCI. At the start are fixed fields: a Vendor ID (who made it, for example 8086 hex is Intel), a Device ID (which product), a Class Code (what kind of device, such as network or display), and Base Address Registers (BARs). At startup, the BIOS or operating system scans every possible slot, reads these IDs, finds out how much address space each device needs through its BARs, assigns non-overlapping addresses and an interrupt, and loads the right driver. No more jumpers.

How devices are named: Each PCI function is identified by three numbers: bus, device and function, written like 00:1f.3. There can be up to 256 buses, 32 devices per bus and 8 functions per device. A single card can have several functions, for example a card with both a network port and a USB controller. On Linux, the command lspci lists every device this way, and on Windows, Device Manager shows similar location information.

Why PCI ran out of road: Being shared, PCI split its 133 MB/s among all cards. A single fast network card or graphics card could use it all. Making a wide parallel bus run faster was hard because of skew and crosstalk between the many wires, and because all cards on the bus had to run at the speed of the slowest. Graphics got a temporary private road called AGP in 1997, but a complete new design was needed.

PCI Express arrives: PCI Express (PCIe) was released in 2003. Despite the similar name, its wires are completely different. Instead of one shared parallel bus, PCIe uses point-to-point serial links. Each device has its own private link to a switch or to the root complex (the part of the CPU or chipset where PCIe starts). But in software, PCIe looks almost exactly like PCI: same configuration space idea (extended to 4 KB), same IDs, same BARs. So old operating systems and drivers could support it with little change. This trick of new hardware with the old software model is a big reason PCIe succeeded.

Lanes: The basic unit of PCIe is a lane. One lane has two differential pairs of wires: one pair to send and one pair to receive, so data flows both ways at the same time (full duplex). A link can bundle 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 lanes, written x1, x2, x4, x8 and x16 and read as by one, by four, by sixteen. Bytes are spread across lanes, like dealing playing cards to several players, so an x16 link is about 16 times faster than x1.

Differential signalling: Each signal in a lane uses two wires carrying opposite voltages. The receiver looks only at the difference between them. If outside noise pushes both wires up by the same amount, the difference does not change, so the noise is cancelled. This is why PCIe, USB, SATA and HDMI can run at billions of bits per second over thin copper.

Embedded clock and encoding: PCIe does not send a separate clock wire. The receiver recovers the timing from the data itself, from the moments when bits change. That only works if there are enough changes, so the data is encoded first. PCIe 1.0 and 2.0 use 8b/10b encoding: every 8 bits of data become 10 bits on the wire, so 20 percent is overhead. PCIe 3.0 to 5.0 use 128b/130b encoding: 128 bits become 130, only about 1.5 percent overhead.

Generations and speeds: PCIe 1.0 runs 2.5 GT/s per lane; after 8b/10b that is 250 MB/s per lane in each direction. PCIe 2.0 doubles to 5 GT/s, 500 MB/s. PCIe 3.0 runs 8 GT/s with 128b/130b, about 985 MB/s, close to 1 GB/s per lane. PCIe 4.0 doubles to about 2 GB/s per lane, and PCIe 5.0 to about 4 GB/s per lane. PCIe 6.0 doubles again using a new signalling method that sends 2 bits per symbol. Each generation roughly doubles the speed of the one before.

Worked example: What is the bandwidth of a PCIe 4.0 x16 graphics slot? Each lane gives about 2 GB/s per direction (16 GT/s x 128/130 / 8 bits per byte = about 1.97 GB/s). Multiply by 16 lanes: about 31.5 GB/s each way. Now an NVMe SSD on PCIe 3.0 x4: about 0.985 x 4 = about 3.9 GB/s, which is why such SSDs advertise read speeds around 3,500 MB/s. The numbers on the box match the maths.

Packets and layers: PCIe sends everything as packets, like a small network inside the PC. The transaction layer builds packets called TLPs (transaction layer packets) for memory reads, memory writes, configuration accesses and messages. The data link layer adds a sequence number and an error check (CRC) and resends any packet that arrives damaged. The physical layer does the encoding and the electrical signalling. Even interrupts are sent as small memory-write messages, called MSI (message signalled interrupts), instead of separate wires.

The PCIe tree: PCIe devices form a tree. At the root is the root complex, built into the CPU or chipset. Its ports connect either directly to endpoints (the actual devices, like an SSD) or to switches. A switch is like a multi-plug for PCIe: one link goes up towards the root, and several links go down to devices. Packets travel up and down this tree, and the switch forwards each packet to the right branch using its address, much like a network switch does with Ethernet frames. Two devices can even send packets to each other through a switch without going through main memory.

Link training: When the computer starts, each PCIe link goes through a short automatic process called link training. The two ends send special patterns to each other, agree on how many lanes actually work, find the highest generation both support, and tune their receivers for the cable or board traces between them. If one lane is damaged, the link can still come up with fewer lanes, for example x8 instead of x16, so the device works but more slowly. Tools on Linux and Windows can show the negotiated width and speed, which is a handy check when a card seems slow.

Slots and compatibility: Physical slots come in x1, x4, x8 and x16 sizes. A smaller card fits and works in a bigger slot. Many motherboards have an x16-sized slot that is wired with only 4 lanes, so read the manual. Generations are backward and forward compatible: a PCIe 3.0 card works in a 4.0 slot and the reverse, at the speed of the slower side. M.2 slots on laptops are another physical shape, and the NVMe ones carry PCIe lanes, usually x4.

What goes where: The graphics card normally takes the x16 slot connected directly to the CPU. NVMe SSDs take x4 links. Wi-Fi cards, extra network ports and sound cards usually need only x1. Thunderbolt and USB4 can even carry PCIe traffic through a cable, which is how some laptops use external graphics boxes. In servers, PCIe connects high-speed network cards and AI accelerators.

Real-life example 1, a gaming PC from Multiplan Center: A student in Dhaka builds a PC for gaming and video editing. The salesman puts the graphics card in the top x16 slot, which is wired to the CPU. The fast NVMe SSD goes into the M.2 slot, also wired to the CPU. A Wi-Fi card goes into a small x1 slot that comes from the chipset. When the student opens a game, textures move from the SSD over PCIe into memory, then from memory over PCIe into the graphics card's memory. Every frame on screen depends on those lanes.

Real-life example 2, a bank's data centre: A bank's server in a data centre in Dhaka handles thousands of mobile banking requests. It uses a 25 or 100 gigabit network card in a PCIe slot, and many NVMe SSDs, each on its own lanes. Because each device has a private link rather than sharing one bus, the network card does not slow down the disks, and they can all transfer at the same time.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think PCIe is just a faster PCI bus; it is a completely different physical design, serial and point-to-point, that keeps PCI's software model. Another mistake is forgetting the encoding overhead when calculating bandwidth, or forgetting that the figure is per direction. Students also mix up the physical slot size with the number of wired lanes. Exams ask you to compare PCI and PCIe in a table, calculate bandwidth for a given generation and lane count, explain configuration space and plug and play, and explain why serial links replaced parallel buses.

Recap: PCI (1992) was a shared, 32-bit, 33 MHz parallel bus with about 133 MB/s and brought plug and play through configuration space. PCI Express (2003) keeps the same software model but uses private serial lanes with differential signalling and embedded clocks. Links can be x1 to x16, and each generation roughly doubles the per-lane speed. Next lesson, we look at serial and parallel communication in general, starting from the simple UART.
key_points: PCI (1992) is a shared parallel bus: 32-bit, 33 MHz, about 133 MB/s peak, shared by all cards.
Configuration space holds Vendor ID, Device ID, class code and BARs, so the OS can set up devices automatically.
PCI Express uses point-to-point serial lanes; each lane has one send pair and one receive pair (full duplex).
Links bundle x1, x2, x4, x8 or x16 lanes; bandwidth scales with lane count.
Differential signalling cancels noise; the clock is recovered from the data using 8b/10b or 128b/130b encoding.
Per-lane speed roughly doubles each generation: about 250 MB/s (1.0), 500 MB/s (2.0), 1 GB/s (3.0), 2 GB/s (4.0), 4 GB/s (5.0) per direction.
PCIe keeps PCI's software model, so drivers and operating systems carried over easily.
lessons.tip: Memorise one anchor: PCIe 3.0 is about 1 GB/s per lane per direction. Double for each newer generation and halve for each older one, then multiply by the lane count.
lessons.task: On Linux, run lspci (or on Windows open Device Manager, View, Devices by connection). List three PCI or PCIe devices and their bus:device.function numbers. Then calculate the bandwidth of a PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD.

quiz.q: What is the peak bandwidth of classic 32-bit, 33 MHz PCI?
quiz.explain: 4 bytes x 33 million transfers per second is about 133 MB/s, shared by all cards.

quiz.q: What does one PCIe lane contain?
options: One send differential pair and one receive differential pair
A single wire with no ground
quiz.explain: A lane has two differential pairs, one each way, so it is full duplex.

quiz.q: Roughly what is the bandwidth of a PCIe 3.0 x4 link in one direction?
quiz.explain: PCIe 3.0 gives about 0.985 GB/s per lane; x4 is about 3.9 GB/s.

quiz.q: Which PCI configuration field tells the operating system who made the device?
quiz.explain: The Vendor ID identifies the maker, for example 8086 hex for Intel; the Device ID identifies the product.

quiz.q: Why did PCIe 3.0 move from 8b/10b to 128b/130b encoding?
options: To cut encoding overhead from 20 percent to about 1.5 percent
To remove the need for a receiver
quiz.explain: 8b/10b wastes 2 of every 10 bits; 128b/130b wastes only 2 of every 130.

lessons.title: Serial vs Parallel Communication and the UART
lessons.content:
Imagine you need to move 8 friends from Farmgate to Gulshan. You could hire 8 rickshaws and send them side by side, or put everyone on one bus in single file. Side by side sounds faster. But in real traffic, the 8 rickshaws get separated, some arrive late, and you must wait at Gulshan for the slowest one before you can start the party. The single bus arrives all together. Computer engineers learned the same lesson with wires: sending bits side by side (parallel) sounds faster, but sending them one after another (serial) very quickly often wins. This lesson explains why, and then takes apart the simplest serial link of all, the UART.

Parallel communication: In parallel communication, several bits travel at the same moment, each on its own wire. An 8-bit parallel link has 8 data wires plus ground and some control wires, and it moves one whole byte per transfer. The old printer port worked like this, and so did old disk cables (IDE) and the PCI bus. Inside a chip, over very short distances, parallel buses are still everywhere, because there the wires are tiny and short.

Serial communication: In serial communication, bits travel one after another over a single data line (or one differential pair). To send a byte, the sender sends bit 0, then bit 1, and so on up to bit 7. It needs far fewer wires. USB, SATA, PCI Express, Ethernet, HDMI and the UART are all serial.

Why serial won for long and fast links: Three problems hurt parallel links as speeds rise. First, skew: tiny differences in wire length and electrical behaviour make bits that left together arrive at slightly different times. At low speed nobody notices, but when each bit lasts less than a nanosecond, a little skew mixes up bits from different bytes. Second, crosstalk: wires next to each other disturb each other, like voices leaking through a thin wall. More wires means more noise. Third, cost and size: more wires need more pins, wider connectors and thicker cables. A serial link has none of the skew problem between data wires, and with differential signalling and clever encoding it can run at billions of bits per second.

Bit rate and baud rate: Bit rate is the number of bits sent per second, measured in bits per second (bps). Baud rate is the number of symbols (signal changes or signal states) sent per second. If each symbol carries exactly one bit, as in a simple UART, then bit rate equals baud rate, and people use the words interchangeably. But a modem or a modern link may send symbols that carry 2 or more bits each. For example, if each symbol can be one of 4 voltage levels, it carries 2 bits, so 1,000 baud gives 2,000 bits per second. So bit rate = baud rate x bits per symbol.

Simplex, half duplex and full duplex: These words describe the direction of traffic. Simplex means data goes only one way, ever, like a radio or TV broadcast. Half duplex means data can go both ways but not at the same time, like a walkie-talkie where you say over before the other side talks. Full duplex means both directions work at the same time, like a phone call. A UART with separate send and receive wires is full duplex. A single-wire link that takes turns is half duplex.

Synchronous and asynchronous serial: In synchronous serial, the receiver knows exactly when to read each bit because a clock is shared. Either there is a separate clock wire (as in SPI and I2C), or the clock is hidden inside the data and recovered by the receiver (as in PCI Express and USB). In asynchronous serial, there is no clock wire, and bytes can start at any moment with gaps between them. The two sides simply agree in advance on the speed and the frame format, and use a start bit to line up at the beginning of each byte. The UART is the classic asynchronous serial device.

What a UART is: UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter. It is a small hardware block that takes a byte from the CPU and shifts it out one bit at a time on a transmit line (TX), and on the receive line (RX) it collects incoming bits and assembles them back into bytes. Inside, it has shift registers, a baud rate generator that divides a clock to produce the bit timing, and small FIFO buffers. Nearly every microcontroller has one or more UARTs, and they are the simplest way for two chips, or a chip and a computer, to talk.

The UART frame: When nothing is being sent, the line sits at logic 1, called idle or mark. To send a byte, the UART first sends a start bit, which is a 0. This falling edge from 1 to 0 tells the receiver a byte is coming and lets it line up its timing. Then come the data bits, usually 8, sent least significant bit first. Then an optional parity bit. Finally one or two stop bits, which are 1, returning the line to idle and giving a gap before the next start bit.

The 8N1 shorthand: Settings are written in short form like 9600 8N1. That means 9600 bits per second, 8 data bits, No parity, 1 stop bit. Other forms are 7E1 (7 data bits, even parity, 1 stop bit) and 8O2 (8 data bits, odd parity, 2 stop bits). Both sides must use the same settings, or the received bytes will be garbage. If you ever see strange symbols in a serial monitor, the first suspect is a wrong baud rate.

Worked frame for the letter A: The letter A has ASCII code 65, which is 0100 0001 in binary. Sent least significant bit first, the data bits are 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. With 8E1 (even parity), there are two 1s in the data, which is already even, so the parity bit is 0. The whole frame on the wire is: idle 1, start 0, data 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 0, parity 0, stop 1, then idle 1 again. With 8N1, simply leave out the parity bit.

Parity in one minute: Parity is a very simple error check. With even parity, the sender sets the parity bit so the total number of 1s in data plus parity is even. With odd parity, the total is made odd. The receiver counts the 1s again. If the count is wrong, at least one bit flipped, and the UART reports a parity error. Parity catches any single-bit error, but if two bits flip, the count looks right and the error is missed. Stronger links use better checks such as CRC.

Timing maths: At 9600 bps each bit lasts 1 / 9600 seconds, about 104 microseconds. With 8N1 each byte uses 10 bits on the wire (1 start + 8 data + 1 stop). So the maximum is 9600 / 10 = 960 bytes per second. At 115200 bps, a common faster setting, each bit is about 8.7 microseconds and the maximum is 11,520 bytes per second. Notice that 20 percent of the bits are framing overhead in 8N1, since only 8 of every 10 bits are data.

How the receiver samples: The receiver does not have the sender's clock, so it uses its own, usually 16 times faster than the bit rate. When it sees the falling edge of the start bit, it waits about 8 of its fast ticks to reach the middle of the start bit and checks it is still 0, to reject short noise spikes. Then it waits 16 ticks at a time and samples each data bit near its middle. Sampling in the middle gives the most room for small differences between the two clocks. Because it re-lines up on every start bit, small clock errors do not build up across many bytes, only across the 10 or 11 bits of one frame. That is why the two clocks only need to agree to within a few percent.

UART errors: A framing error means the receiver expected a stop bit of 1 but saw 0, usually because of a wrong baud rate or noise. A parity error means the parity check failed. An overrun error means a new byte arrived before the CPU read the previous one, so data was lost; FIFO buffers and interrupts help prevent this. A break condition is when the line is held at 0 for longer than a whole frame, sometimes used as a special signal.

The UART is not the cable: Students often mix up the UART with RS-232 or USB. The UART only decides the frame format and timing, at logic levels like 0 and 3.3 volts. RS-232 is one standard for the voltage levels and connector used to carry those frames over a cable, which is the next lesson. And a USB-to-serial adapter is a small chip that pretends to be a UART on one side and a USB device on the other.

Real-life example 1, a GPS module on a delivery bike: Many low-cost GPS modules talk to a microcontroller over UART, often at 9600 8N1 by default. Every second, the module sends text lines (in a format called NMEA) containing latitude, longitude and time. A food delivery bike's tracker in Dhaka can read those lines, pick out the position, and send it to the server over mobile data. If the developer sets the wrong baud rate, all he sees is junk characters until he fixes it.

Real-life example 2, fixing a router at an ISP: Technicians at an internet provider sometimes open a broken home router and connect three wires, TX, RX and ground, to small pads on its board, using a USB-to-UART adapter. On the laptop, a terminal program at 115200 8N1 shows the router's boot messages, and the technician can see exactly where it fails. The serial console is one of the oldest and still one of the most useful debugging tools in electronics.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget that data bits are sent least significant bit first, or forget the start and stop bits when calculating bytes per second. Many say baud rate always equals bit rate, which is only true when each symbol carries one bit. Connecting TX to TX instead of TX to RX is the classic wiring mistake. Exams ask you to draw the frame for a given character and format, calculate parity, find transfer time for a message, compare serial and parallel, and explain simplex, half duplex and full duplex with examples.

Recap: Parallel sends many bits at once on many wires; serial sends one after another on one line, and wins at high speed because it avoids skew and crosstalk and needs fewer wires. Bit rate equals baud rate only when each symbol carries one bit. A UART frame is start bit 0, data bits LSB first, optional parity, and stop bit 1, with the line idle at 1. With 8N1, every byte costs 10 bits. Next lesson we carry these frames over cables with RS-232 and meet other legacy ports.
key_points: Parallel sends several bits at once on separate wires; serial sends bits one after another on one line or pair.
Serial wins for fast, long links because it avoids skew and crosstalk and needs fewer pins.
Bit rate = baud rate x bits per symbol; they are equal only when each symbol carries one bit.
Simplex is one way, half duplex is both ways in turns, full duplex is both ways at once.
A UART frame: idle 1, start bit 0, data bits LSB first, optional parity, stop bit 1.
With 8N1 each byte takes 10 bits, so 9600 bps gives at most 960 bytes per second.
UART errors: framing (bad stop bit), parity, overrun (data not read in time).
lessons.tip: Whenever a serial link shows junk, check in this order: same baud rate, same 8N1 style settings, TX crossed to RX, and a shared ground. These four fix most problems.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the 8E1 UART frame for the letter C (ASCII 67) bit by bit, with the parity bit worked out. Then calculate how many seconds it takes to send a 1,000 byte message at 9600 8N1.

quiz.q: Why does parallel communication struggle at very high speeds?
options: Skew and crosstalk between many wires
quiz.explain: Bits on different wires arrive at slightly different times (skew) and wires disturb each other (crosstalk).

quiz.q: In a UART frame, the start bit is:
quiz.explain: The idle line is 1, so a 0 start bit creates a falling edge that tells the receiver a byte is starting.

quiz.q: How many bytes per second can 9600 8N1 carry at most?
quiz.explain: Each byte uses 10 bits (start + 8 data + stop), so 9600 / 10 = 960 bytes per second.

quiz.q: A walkie-talkie, where only one person talks at a time, is an example of:
quiz.explain: Data can go both ways but not at the same time, which is half duplex.

quiz.q: If each symbol carries 2 bits and the link runs at 2400 baud, the bit rate is:
quiz.explain: Bit rate = baud rate x bits per symbol = 2400 x 2 = 4800 bps.

lessons.title: RS-232 and Legacy Ports
lessons.content:
Go to any old computer shop in Elephant Road or Nilkhet and look at the back of a desktop from the late 1990s. You will see a strange row of sockets: a small D-shaped one with 9 pins, a long D-shaped one with 25 holes, two round purple and green sockets, and maybe a 15-hole game port. Today a laptop may have only USB-C. Yet those old ports are not dead. Factory machines, bank card terminals, medical equipment and network switches still use them. Learning them also teaches the basic ideas that every newer port is built on.

Why we still learn legacy ports: First, they are simple enough to understand fully, wire by wire. Second, many industrial and embedded systems last 20 or 30 years, and engineers in Bangladesh's garment factories, power stations and telecom companies still meet RS-232 and RS-485 every week. Third, almost every microcontroller still has a UART, and the UART's natural partner is the RS-232 family. Fourth, exams love them.

RS-232 in one line: RS-232 is a standard, first published in 1960 and updated many times, that defines the voltage levels, timing signals, pin meanings and connectors for sending serial data between two devices. It carries exactly the UART frames you learned in the last lesson: start bit, data bits, optional parity, stop bits. The UART decides the frame; RS-232 decides how that frame travels on a cable.

RS-232 voltage levels: This is the part that surprises students. RS-232 does not use 0 and 5 volts. A logic 1 (called mark) is any voltage between minus 3 and minus 15 volts. A logic 0 (called space) is any voltage between plus 3 and plus 15 volts. The zone between minus 3 and plus 3 volts is undefined. So RS-232 is inverted compared with normal logic, where 1 is high. The big swing from negative to positive made old cables resistant to noise over several metres.

Why you must not connect RS-232 directly to a microcontroller: A microcontroller pin expects 0 to 3.3 volts or 0 to 5 volts. Feeding it minus 12 or plus 12 volts can destroy it. And the microcontroller's 3.3 volt output is too small and the wrong polarity for an RS-232 receiver. So we need a level shifter in between, a chip that converts both ways.

The MAX232 level shifter: The classic chip for this is the MAX232 and its many copies. Its clever trick is that it runs from a single 5 volt supply but makes the positive and negative voltages it needs using charge pumps, small circuits with a few external capacitors that pump charge to double and invert the supply. Inside are two drivers (logic to RS-232) and two receivers (RS-232 to logic), and they also do the inversion. Versions like the MAX3232 work from 3.3 volts.

DTE and DCE: RS-232 was designed to connect a terminal or computer, called DTE (Data Terminal Equipment), to a modem, called DCE (Data Circuit-terminating Equipment, often read as Data Communications Equipment).
