The names of the pins are from the DTE's point of view. So the DTE sends on TxD and receives on RxD, while the DCE receives on TxD and sends on RxD. This is why a straight cable works between a PC and a modem.

The DB-9 connector: The original standard used a 25-pin connector, but PCs settled on a 9-pin one (the DE-9, usually called DB-9). On a PC (DTE) the pins are: 1 DCD (carrier detect), 2 RxD (receive data), 3 TxD (transmit data), 4 DTR (data terminal ready), 5 signal ground, 6 DSR (data set ready), 7 RTS (request to send), 8 CTS (clear to send), 9 RI (ring indicator). For a simple link, only three wires are really needed: TxD, RxD and ground.

Flow control: What happens if the sender is faster than the receiver can handle? The receiver's buffer fills up and bytes are lost. Flow control stops this. In hardware flow control, the RTS and CTS lines are used: a side that is ready to receive keeps its line active, and when its buffer is nearly full it drops the line, telling the other side to pause. In software flow control, called XON/XOFF, the receiver sends a special byte, XOFF (code 19, Ctrl-S), to say stop, and XON (code 17, Ctrl-Q) to say continue. Software flow control needs no extra wires but cannot be used when the data itself might contain those byte values.

The null modem: What if you want to connect two PCs directly, both DTE? Each one sends on pin 3 and receives on pin 2, so a straight cable would connect transmit to transmit. A null modem cable crosses the wires: TxD of one goes to RxD of the other, and the handshake lines (RTS to CTS, DTR to DSR) are crossed too. The name means a modem that is not there. It is the same idea as crossing TX and RX when connecting two UARTs.

Speed and distance: RS-232 is slow by modern standards. Common speeds are 9600 and 115200 bits per second. The standard was designed for cables of about 15 metres (50 feet) at its rated speed, and longer cables work only at lower speeds. Because it uses a single wire per signal measured against ground, it is affected by noise and ground differences between buildings.

USB-to-serial adapters and COM ports: Most laptops today have no serial port, so people use a small USB-to-serial adapter. Inside is a chip that appears to the computer as a USB device, but on the other side produces UART frames, either at logic level (for connecting to a microcontroller board) or at RS-232 levels (for a DB-9 plug). Windows shows it as a virtual COM port such as COM3 or COM7, and Linux as something like /dev/ttyUSB0. Programs that were written decades ago for real serial ports work with it unchanged, because the operating system hides the difference. Always check whether an adapter gives logic level or RS-232 level output before connecting it.

RS-485, the factory cousin: For longer distances and many devices, industry uses RS-485. It sends each signal as a differential pair (two wires with opposite voltages), so noise is cancelled, as in PCI Express. It can reach about 1,200 metres at lower speeds and allows many devices on the same pair, typically up to 32 standard loads, taking turns (half duplex). Energy meters, factory controllers and building systems often talk over RS-485 using a protocol called Modbus. In a garment factory in Gazipur, the machines on the floor may well report to the control room this way.

The Centronics parallel port: Before USB, printers connected through a parallel port, based on a design by the Centronics company. On a PC it used a 25-pin female D connector. It had 8 data lines carrying one byte at a time, plus control and status lines: Strobe (computer says data is valid), Busy (printer says wait), Acknowledge (printer says got it), Paper Out, Select and Error. The first port, LPT1, usually used I/O addresses 378 hex for data, 379 hex for status and 37A hex for control, the same ones from our earlier printer example.

The parallel port handshake: To print a character, the PC checks that Busy is low, puts the byte on the 8 data lines, pulses Strobe low for at least a microsecond, and waits. The printer sets Busy while it takes the byte, then pulses Acknowledge and clears Busy when ready for the next. This is the strobe and acknowledge handshake from lesson 3, in real hardware. Later the IEEE 1284 standard (1994) added faster two-way modes called EPP and ECP, used by scanners and external drives. Parallel cables were limited to a few metres.

Why hobbyists loved the parallel port: Because each of its data pins could be set high or low directly by writing a byte to an I/O address, the parallel port was a cheap way for students to switch LEDs, relays and motors from a PC program. Many university labs in the 2000s used it for interfacing experiments. Today a microcontroller board over USB does the same job more safely.

The PS/2 ports: The round 6-pin mini-DIN sockets, purple for keyboard and green for mouse, came with IBM's PS/2 computers in 1987. PS/2 is a synchronous serial link: the device (keyboard or mouse) generates a clock on one wire and sends data on another. Each frame has 11 bits: a start bit 0, 8 data bits least significant bit first, an odd parity bit and a stop bit 1. The host can also send commands, for example to turn on the Caps Lock light. PS/2 was not designed for hot plugging, so plugging it in while the PC is on is not officially supported. Some gaming keyboards still offer PS/2 because each key press reaches the computer as soon as it happens, without waiting for USB polling.

Real-life example 1, a supershop billing counter: At a supershop in Chattogram, the old weighing scale at the vegetable counter sends the weight to the billing PC over an RS-232 cable at 9600 bits per second. The new PC has no serial port, so the technician uses a USB-to-serial adapter. Windows shows it as COM3, the billing software is set to COM3 at 9600 8N1, and the weight appears on the bill automatically. When it stops working, the first things he checks are the COM port number and the baud rate.

Real-life example 2, configuring a network switch: An engineer at a telecom company in Dhaka sets up a new managed switch. Before it has an IP address, the only way in is the console port, which is RS-232 (sometimes on an RJ-45 shaped socket or USB). She connects a console cable, opens a terminal at the speed in the manual, often 9600 8N1, and types commands to configure it. Even in modern networking, RS-232 is the emergency door.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think RS-232 uses 0 and 5 volts; it uses negative for 1 and positive for 0. They connect RS-232 straight to a microcontroller and destroy it. They mix up straight and null modem cables. Exams ask: give RS-232 voltage levels, name the DB-9 pins, explain hardware versus software flow control, draw a null modem connection, explain why the MAX232 is needed, compare RS-232 and RS-485, and describe the Centronics handshake.

Recap: RS-232 carries UART frames on a cable using inverted, bipolar voltages (1 is minus 3 to minus 15 volts, 0 is plus 3 to plus 15 volts), so a level shifter like the MAX232 is needed for logic chips. DB-9 pins include TxD on 3, RxD on 2 and ground on 5 at the PC end. RTS/CTS or XON/XOFF provide flow control, and a null modem crosses the lines to link two computers. RS-485 uses differential pairs for long, multi-device links. The Centronics port sent bytes in parallel with Strobe, Busy and Acknowledge, and PS/2 sent keyboard and mouse data with a device-driven clock. Next lesson, we meet the port that replaced them all: USB.
key_points: RS-232 defines voltages, pins and connectors for carrying UART frames on a cable.
RS-232 logic 1 is minus 3 to minus 15 volts and logic 0 is plus 3 to plus 15 volts, inverted compared with normal logic.
A level shifter such as the MAX232 (using charge pumps) is needed between RS-232 and a microcontroller.
On a PC's DB-9: pin 2 RxD, pin 3 TxD, pin 5 ground, pins 7 and 8 RTS and CTS.
Flow control can be hardware (RTS/CTS) or software (XON/XOFF bytes).
A null modem cable crosses TxD/RxD and handshake lines to connect two DTEs directly.
RS-485 uses differential pairs for long distances and many devices; the Centronics port sent bytes in parallel with Strobe, Busy and Acknowledge.
lessons.tip: Draw the DB-9 connector once from memory with all 9 pin names, then draw a null modem beside it. That one sketch answers most RS-232 exam questions.
lessons.task: Search for a photo of the back panel of an old desktop motherboard (for example from around the year 2000). Label every port you can find: serial, parallel, PS/2 keyboard and mouse, USB, VGA, audio. Then write which modern port replaced each one.

quiz.q: In RS-232, a logic 1 (mark) is represented by:
options: A voltage between minus 3 and minus 15 volts
A voltage between plus 3 and plus 15 volts
quiz.explain: RS-232 is inverted: mark (1) is negative, space (0) is positive.

quiz.q: Why is a MAX232 chip used?
options: To convert between logic levels and RS-232 voltage levels
quiz.explain: It shifts and inverts levels both ways and makes the needed plus and minus voltages from a single supply.

quiz.q: On a PC's DB-9 serial connector, which pin is signal ground?
quiz.explain: Pin 5 is signal ground; pin 2 is RxD and pin 3 is TxD.

quiz.q: What does a null modem cable do?
options: Adds a modem in the middle
Crosses transmit and receive (and handshake lines) to link two computers
quiz.explain: Two DTEs both transmit on the same pin, so the null modem crosses TxD to RxD and the handshake pairs.

quiz.q: Which standard is best for connecting many devices over hundreds of metres in a factory?
quiz.explain: RS-485 uses differential pairs, reaching about 1,200 metres and supporting many devices on one pair.

lessons.title: USB Part 1: Topology, Connectors, Speeds and Power
lessons.content:
Think about the charger drawer in your home. Ten years ago it was full of different cables: a round pin for the old Nokia, a wide flat plug for one phone, a special cable for the camera, another for the MP3 player. Today most of them are USB, and more and more are the same USB-C plug that charges a phone, a laptop, earbuds and even a power bank. USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, and it truly became universal. In this lesson we see how it is organised, what the plugs and speeds are, and how it carries power. Next lesson we look at how it actually talks.

The mess before USB: In the early 1990s a PC had a serial port for the modem, a parallel port for the printer, a PS/2 port for the keyboard, another for the mouse, a game port for the joystick, and expansion cards for anything else. Each had its own connector, its own driver style, and usually you had to switch off the PC before plugging in. Setting addresses and interrupts caused endless problems. A group of companies, including Intel, Microsoft, Compaq, IBM and others, designed USB to replace all of that with one simple, hot-pluggable, self-configuring port.

USB goals: The designers wanted one connector type for many devices, plug and play with no jumpers, hot plugging while the computer is on, power delivered through the same cable for small devices, enough speed for keyboards, mice, printers and storage, and low cost so it could go into every PC. USB 1.0 came out in 1996, and USB 1.1 in 1998 fixed early problems. The first iMac in 1998 used only USB, which pushed many makers to adopt it.

Host and devices: USB is host-centred. There is one host, usually the computer, which controls everything. Devices never talk to each other directly and never speak unless the host asks. The host has a host controller (hardware) and a USB driver stack (software). Every transfer is started by the host, which keeps things simple and avoids collisions on the wires.

The tiered star topology: USB devices are connected as a tree, called a tiered star. At the top is the root hub, built into the host controller, which provides the ports on your computer. Into those ports you can plug devices or more hubs, and each hub provides more ports. The standard allows up to 127 devices per host controller, because each device gets a 7-bit address (1 to 127; address 0 is reserved for a newly plugged device that has not been given an address yet). Hubs count as devices too. There are also limits on depth: at most 5 external hubs in a chain between the host and a device.

What a hub does: A hub is like a multi-plug with brains. It repeats traffic from the host down to its ports and from devices back up, detects when a device is plugged or unplugged and reports it to the host, and controls power to each port. A bus-powered hub takes its power from the upstream port and must share it among its devices, so it may not be able to run a hard disk. A self-powered hub has its own adapter and can give full power to every port.

The USB versions and speeds: USB 1.x defined Low Speed at 1.5 megabits per second (for keyboards and mice) and Full Speed at 12 megabits per second. USB 2.0 in 2000 added High Speed at 480 megabits per second, which made USB flash drives and external disks practical. USB 3.0 in 2008 added SuperSpeed at 5 gigabits per second, using extra wires. Later versions added 10 gigabits per second, then 20 gigabits per second using two lanes in a USB-C cable. USB4, from 2019, is built on Thunderbolt technology and runs at 20 or 40 gigabits per second, with a newer version going to 80.

The naming mess: USB names are famously confusing. The 5 gigabit speed was first called USB 3.0, then renamed USB 3.1 Gen 1, then USB 3.2 Gen 1. The 10 gigabit speed is USB 3.1 Gen 2 or USB 3.2 Gen 2. The 20 gigabit speed is USB 3.2 Gen 2x2. The industry now encourages simply writing the speed, like USB 5Gbps or USB 10Gbps, on packaging. When buying, always look for the actual speed number, not just the version.

Bits versus bytes in practice: USB speeds are in bits per second. To get bytes, divide by 8, and then expect less because of protocol overhead. 480 megabits per second is 60 megabytes per second in theory, but a USB 2.0 flash drive usually reaches only about 30 to 40 megabytes per second in real use. A USB 3 5 gigabit port can reach a few hundred megabytes per second. So a 4 GB movie takes over a minute and a half on USB 2.0 at 40 MB/s, but well under half a minute on a good USB 3 drive at 300 MB/s.

Inside a USB 2.0 cable: A USB 2.0 cable has just four wires. VBUS carries plus 5 volts power (usually a red wire). GND is ground (black). D plus and D minus are the data pair (usually green and white), a twisted differential pair carrying data in both directions, but only one direction at a time, so USB 2.0 is half duplex. USB 3 cables add two more differential pairs, one to send and one to receive, so SuperSpeed is full duplex. A USB-C cable has even more wires.

Connector types: Type-A is the familiar flat rectangle on computers and chargers. Type-B is the square-ish plug on printers. Mini-B was common on cameras and old phones around 2005 to 2010. Micro-B was the standard Android phone plug for many years. USB 3 versions of A and B have extra pins; a USB 3 Type-A port often has a blue plastic insert. Type-C, introduced in 2014, is small, oval and reversible, with 24 pins. It can carry USB 2, USB 3, USB4, high power, and even video, depending on what the devices and cable support. The European Union now requires USB-C charging ports on new phones sold there.

Connector is not speed: A USB-C plug does not mean fast. A cheap USB-C cable might only carry USB 2.0 at 480 megabits per second, while another carries 40 gigabits per second and 240 watts. The connector is the shape; the speed depends on the wires inside the cable and the chips on both ends. This confuses buyers all the time.

Power over USB: Every USB port supplies 5 volts. A USB 2.0 port must give at least 500 milliamps to a configured device, which is 2.5 watts. A USB 3 port gives 900 milliamps, 4.5 watts. A device must not take more than 100 milliamps until the host has configured it. The Battery Charging specification allows dedicated charging ports to give up to 1.5 amps. USB-C ports can advertise 1.5 amps or 3 amps at 5 volts through resistors on special pins.

USB Power Delivery: For laptops and fast charging, USB Power Delivery (USB PD) lets the charger and the device negotiate a higher voltage. They talk over a special pin in the USB-C cable and agree on, for example, 9 volts, 15 volts or 20 volts. At 20 volts and 5 amps, that is 100 watts, enough for most laptops. A newer version raised this to 48 volts at 5 amps, 240 watts. Higher voltage means the same power with less current, so the thin cable does not overheat. Cables rated for 5 amps contain a tiny chip, called an e-marker, that tells the charger what they can safely carry.

Power calculation example: A phone charging at 9 volts and 2 amps receives 9 x 2 = 18 watts. A laptop at 20 volts and 3.25 amps gets 65 watts. A bus-powered hub on a USB 2.0 port has only 500 milliamps to share. If you plug in a 300 milliamp keyboard and a 500 milliamp external drive, the total is 800, which is more than it can give, so the drive may not start. That is why portable hard disks sometimes have a Y cable with two USB plugs.

Hot plugging and safety: USB connectors are designed so that the power and ground pins are longer than the data pins. When you plug in, power and ground connect first, and the data pins connect a moment later. When you unplug, the data pins disconnect first. This protects the electronics. However, for storage devices you should still eject first, because the operating system may have data waiting in its buffer, as we saw in lesson 2.

USB On-The-Go: Normally a phone is a USB device when connected to a PC. But with USB On-The-Go (OTG), a phone can act as a host, so you can plug a pen drive, a keyboard or even a mouse into it with an OTG adapter. With USB-C, the roles are worked out automatically when the cable is connected, and either side can be host or device, and either can supply power.

Real-life example 1, a mobile repair shop in Gulistan: A customer says his phone charges very slowly. The repairman checks: the charger can do fast charging with USB PD up to 20 watts, but the customer is using a cheap thin cable. With a USB meter (a small gadget that shows voltage and current), he sees only 5 volts and 0.5 amps, 2.5 watts. He swaps in a proper cable, the phone and charger negotiate 9 volts at about 2 amps, and the meter shows about 18 watts. The plug shape was the same; the cable inside was not.

Real-life example 2, a university computer lab: A lab in Khulna has 40 PCs, and students keep plugging in pen drives, keyboards and phones. USB's tree structure, automatic addressing and drivers mean nobody has to configure anything. When a student plugs a 2.5 inch external hard disk into the front panel through a cheap unpowered hub, it keeps clicking and disconnecting. The lab assistant explains: the hub cannot supply enough current, so the disk must go directly into a rear port or a powered hub.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse megabits and megabytes, think USB-C always means high speed, believe devices can talk to each other directly without the host, and forget address 0 is reserved for new devices. Exams ask: list USB speeds by version, draw the tiered star topology, explain why the limit is 127 devices, name the four wires of a USB 2.0 cable, calculate power from volts and amps, and explain USB Power Delivery.

Recap: USB replaced many different ports with one hot-pluggable, self-configuring, host-controlled bus. Devices form a tiered star tree with hubs, up to 127 per host controller. Speeds grew from 1.5 and 12 megabits per second to 480 megabits, then 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 gigabits per second. USB carries 5 volts power, and with USB-C and Power Delivery it can negotiate up to 100 or 240 watts. The connector shape tells you nothing certain about speed. Next lesson, we look at how USB actually talks: enumeration, descriptors, classes and transfer types.
key_points: USB is host-centred: the host starts every transfer, and devices never talk directly to each other.
Devices form a tiered star tree through hubs, up to 127 devices per host controller (7-bit address, 0 reserved).
Speeds: 1.5 Mbps (Low), 12 Mbps (Full), 480 Mbps (High, USB 2.0), then 5, 10, 20 Gbps, and 40/80 Gbps with USB4.
A USB 2.0 cable has four wires: VBUS (5 V), GND, D+ and D-; USB 3 adds separate send and receive pairs.
Type-C is reversible and versatile, but the connector shape does not guarantee speed or power.
Basic USB power is 5 V at 500 mA (USB 2.0) or 900 mA (USB 3); USB Power Delivery negotiates higher voltages up to 100 W or 240 W.
Power and ground pins are longer so they connect first, making hot plugging safe.
lessons.tip: Make a small table with three columns: version name, speed in bits per second, and realistic bytes per second. Filling it in yourself once fixes the naming mess in your head.
lessons.task: Collect three USB cables or chargers at home. Read the labels on the chargers (output volts and amps) and calculate the watts for each. If any says PD or shows several voltages like 5V/9V/12V, note the highest power it can give.

quiz.q: Why can a single USB host controller support at most 127 devices?
options: Each device gets a 7-bit address and address 0 is reserved
quiz.explain: 7 bits give 128 addresses (0 to 127); 0 is used for a newly attached device, leaving 127.

quiz.q: What is the High Speed rate of USB 2.0?
quiz.explain: USB 2.0 High Speed runs at 480 megabits per second.

quiz.q: Which wires are in a USB 2.0 cable?
quiz.explain: Power (VBUS, 5 V), ground, and the D+/D- differential data pair.

quiz.q: A USB PD charger supplies 20 volts at 5 amps. What power is that?
quiz.explain: Power = volts x amps = 20 x 5 = 100 watts.

quiz.q: Which statement about USB-C is true?
options: USB-C is a connector shape; speed and power depend on the cable and devices
USB-C only works with Apple devices
quiz.explain: A USB-C cable may be USB 2.0 only or support 40 Gbps and 240 W; the shape alone does not tell you.

lessons.title: USB Part 2: Enumeration, Descriptors, Classes and Transfers
lessons.content:
Imagine a new student joins your class in the middle of the year. The teacher does not ignore her. First the teacher notices someone new at the door. Then she gives the student a roll number. Then she asks questions: what is your name, which school did you come from, which subjects do you take, do you need a seat near the front? Based on the answers, she places the student in the right group. USB does exactly this every time you plug in a device. The process is called enumeration, and it is why a pen drive just works without you installing anything.

How the host notices a new device: Remember the D plus and D minus data wires. On the host side, both wires are gently pulled down to 0 volts by resistors. A device has a pull-up resistor (1.5 kilohms) on one of the data lines. A Full Speed device pulls up D plus; a Low Speed device pulls up D minus. When you plug it in, that line rises, and the hub sees the change. From which line went high, the hub even knows the device's basic speed. A High Speed device first appears as Full Speed and then performs a special chirp exchange during reset to agree on 480 megabits per second.

Signals on the wire: USB 2.0 sends bits using a differential pair, so noise is cancelled. It uses an encoding called NRZI (non-return to zero inverted): a 0 bit is sent as a change in the line state, and a 1 bit as no change. A long run of 1s would mean no changes, and the receiver could lose its timing. So USB uses bit stuffing: after six 1s in a row, the sender inserts an extra 0, which forces a change. The receiver removes it again. You do not need to remember the details, but it shows the same idea as PCI Express: keep enough transitions so the clock can be recovered from the data.

Enumeration step by step: Step 1, the hub detects the new device and reports to the host on its next check. Step 2, the host tells the hub to reset that port, which puts the device into a known default state. Step 3, the device now answers at address 0, the special address for new devices, on endpoint 0, the control endpoint every device must have. Step 4, the host asks for the first part of the device descriptor to learn the maximum packet size for endpoint 0. Step 5, the host sends SET_ADDRESS, giving the device a unique number from 1 to 127. Step 6, using the new address, the host reads the full device descriptor, then the configuration descriptor along with all interface and endpoint descriptors, and maybe string descriptors with the product name. Step 7, the host chooses and loads a driver. Step 8, the host sends SET_CONFIGURATION, and the device is ready to use. All this usually takes well under a second.

Why one device at address 0 at a time: Only one new device may be at address 0 at a moment, otherwise two devices would answer together. The host handles new devices one by one, giving each a fresh address before moving on. This is why the enumeration steps are done in order and why the reset step matters.

Descriptors, the device's ID card: A descriptor is a small, standard-format block of data that the device sends to describe itself. The device descriptor says which USB version it follows, its class, the maximum packet size for endpoint 0, its Vendor ID (VID), its Product ID (PID), and how many configurations it has. The configuration descriptor says how much power it needs (up to 500 milliamps on USB 2.0) and how many interfaces it has. Each interface descriptor describes one function, with its class. Each endpoint descriptor describes one data channel. String descriptors hold readable text like the maker's name and the product name.

VID and PID: The Vendor ID is a 16-bit number given to a company by the USB Implementers Forum, the body that manages USB. The Product ID is a 16-bit number the company chooses for each product. Together they let the operating system pick a specific driver. On Windows, Device Manager shows them as something like VID_046D and PID_C52B; on Linux, the lsusb command shows them as 046d:c52b. If you search those numbers online, you can often find out exactly what a mystery device is.

Device classes: If every product needed its own driver, plugging in a new keyboard would need a download. Instead, USB defines classes, standard behaviours that the operating system supports with built-in class drivers. HID (Human Interface Device, class 03 hex) covers keyboards, mice, game controllers and barcode scanners. Mass Storage (08 hex) covers pen drives, card readers and external disks. Audio (01 hex) covers USB headsets and microphones. CDC (Communications Device Class, 02 hex) covers USB-to-serial devices and some modems. Printer (07 hex), Hub (09 hex) and Video (0E hex, for webcams) are others. A device that follows a class standard works with no extra driver.

Composite devices: One device can have several interfaces, each with its own class. A USB headset may have an Audio interface for sound and a HID interface for its volume buttons. A phone may show a Mass Storage or media transfer interface and also a debugging interface. The operating system loads one driver per interface, so a single plug can bring several functions.

Endpoints and pipes: An endpoint is a numbered buffer inside the device, the place where data enters or leaves. Each device can have endpoint numbers 0 to 15, and each number can have an IN and an OUT direction. Directions are named from the host's view: IN means device to host, OUT means host to device. Endpoint 0 is special and two-way: it is the control endpoint used for enumeration and commands. A pipe is the logical connection between host software and one endpoint.

Packets: USB communication is made of packets. Token packets (IN, OUT, SETUP) come from the host and say who and what: which address, which endpoint, which direction. Data packets carry the bytes, alternating between DATA0 and DATA1 so the receiver can detect a repeated packet. Handshake packets report the result: ACK means received correctly, NAK means not ready yet, try again later, and STALL means error or unsupported request. Token packets use a small 5-bit CRC check, and data packets use a 16-bit CRC.

Frames and timing: The host divides time into frames. At Full Speed each frame is 1 millisecond, and at High Speed it is divided into 8 microframes of 125 microseconds. Every frame starts with a Start of Frame packet. The host schedules transfers inside frames, reserving time for devices that need guaranteed timing and filling the rest with bulk data.

The four transfer types: USB has four types of transfer, and each endpoint uses one. Control transfers are used for setup and commands, such as enumeration requests; they have a setup stage, an optional data stage and a status stage, and are always error checked. Bulk transfers move large amounts of data with full error checking and retries, but with no guaranteed timing; they use whatever bandwidth is left. Pen drives and printers use bulk. Interrupt transfers are small and have a guaranteed maximum delay; keyboards and mice use them. Isochronous transfers get guaranteed bandwidth and fixed timing but no retries; if a packet is damaged it is simply lost. Audio and webcams use isochronous, because a late sound sample is useless anyway.

Interrupt transfers are actually polled: This surprises students. USB devices cannot interrupt the host on their own. An interrupt endpoint is one that the host promises to poll at a fixed interval given in its endpoint descriptor. If the device has nothing new, it answers NAK. A typical mouse is polled every 8 milliseconds (125 times per second), and gaming mice ask for 1 millisecond (1,000 times per second), so the movement reaches the computer faster. The USB host controller then raises a real interrupt to the CPU when data arrives.

Worked example: plugging in a pen drive: You plug a pen drive into a laptop. The hub sees D plus go high and reports a new Full or High Speed device. The host resets it, reads its descriptor at address 0, gives it address 5, and reads its configuration. The interface descriptor says class 08 hex, Mass Storage, with one bulk IN and one bulk OUT endpoint. Windows loads its built-in mass storage driver, which sends SCSI-style commands over the bulk endpoints to read the drive's file system. A drive letter appears. You never installed anything because the pen drive followed the class standard.

Real-life example 1, a barcode scanner at a pharmacy: A pharmacy chain in Dhaka buys barcode scanners. They plug into any computer and immediately type the product code into whatever box has the cursor, like a keyboard. That works because the scanner reports itself as a HID keyboard, class 03 hex. Windows uses its keyboard class driver, and the shop's billing software needs no special support. The scanner's interrupt endpoint is polled regularly, and each scanned code arrives as a quick burst of key presses.

Real-life example 2, a USB sound card for online classes: A teacher in Barishal uses a USB headset for online classes. It enumerates as a composite device: an Audio interface with isochronous endpoints for the microphone and speakers, and a HID interface for the mute and volume buttons. When the internet is slow, her voice may break up, but the headset itself never pauses to resend old audio, because isochronous transfers choose steady timing over retries.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think USB devices can interrupt the host directly; interrupt transfers are polled. They mix up IN and OUT directions, which are always from the host's view. They think every device needs a vendor driver, forgetting class drivers. Exams ask: list the enumeration steps, name the descriptors and what each holds, compare the four transfer types with an example device for each, explain VID and PID, and explain why the keyboard uses interrupt transfers while a webcam uses isochronous.

Recap: When a device is plugged in, a pull-up resistor tells the hub, and the host enumerates it: reset, talk at address 0, read descriptors, assign an address, load a driver and set the configuration. Descriptors give VID, PID, class, power and endpoints. Standard classes like HID and Mass Storage work with built-in drivers. Endpoints are channels named from the host's view, and transfers are control, bulk, interrupt (polled with guaranteed delay) or isochronous (guaranteed timing, no retries). Next lesson, we go inside the circuit board to the small chip-to-chip buses SPI and I2C.
key_points: A device signals its presence and speed with a pull-up resistor on D+ (Full Speed) or D- (Low Speed).
Enumeration: detect, reset, read descriptor at address 0, SET_ADDRESS, read all descriptors, load driver, SET_CONFIGURATION.
Descriptors (device, configuration, interface, endpoint, string) hold VID, PID, class, power and endpoint details.
Class drivers (HID, Mass Storage, Audio, CDC, Video) let standard devices work without installing vendor drivers.
Endpoints are numbered channels 0 to 15; IN means device to host, OUT means host to device; endpoint 0 is control.
Four transfer types: control (setup), bulk (big, reliable, no timing guarantee), interrupt (small, polled at fixed interval), isochronous (fixed timing, no retries).
USB interrupt transfers are actually host polling; a typical mouse is polled every 8 ms, gaming mice every 1 ms.
lessons.tip: Learn the four transfer types by one device each: pen drive (bulk), mouse (interrupt), headset (isochronous), and plugging in anything (control). Then reason from the device to the transfer type in any question.
lessons.task: Plug a USB device into a computer. On Windows, open Device Manager, find it, and in Properties, Details, Hardware Ids, note its VID and PID. On Linux or a Mac, run lsusb (Linux) or check System Information, USB (Mac). Search the VID online to find the maker.

quiz.q: During enumeration, what address does a newly attached device answer on before it is given its own?
quiz.explain: Address 0 is reserved for a new device until the host sends SET_ADDRESS.

quiz.q: Which transfer type does a USB webcam or headset microphone usually use for its stream?
quiz.explain: Isochronous gives guaranteed timing and bandwidth without retries, which suits live audio and video.

quiz.q: In USB, the direction IN means:
quiz.explain: USB directions are named from the host's point of view; IN is data coming into the host.

quiz.q: Why does a new USB keyboard work without installing a driver?
options: Keyboards need no driver at all
It follows the HID class, which has a built-in class driver
quiz.explain: HID is a standard class, and operating systems ship a class driver for it.

quiz.q: How do USB interrupt endpoints really work?
options: The device pulls a dedicated interrupt wire
The device sends data whenever it wants
The host polls them at a fixed interval set in the endpoint descriptor
quiz.explain: USB is host-controlled; an interrupt endpoint is polled regularly, giving a guaranteed maximum delay.

lessons.title: SPI, I2C and 1-Wire: Chip-to-Chip Buses
lessons.content:
Open up a smartwatch, a drone or even a modern rice cooker, and you will find a small main chip surrounded by helpers: a temperature sensor, a clock chip that keeps time, a tiny memory chip, a screen controller, a motion sensor. These chips sit a few centimetres apart on the same board and need to chat all day. They do not use USB or PCI Express; those are too big and complex for such short, simple conversations. Instead, they use small, cheap serial buses with just two to four wires. The two most famous are SPI and I2C, with 1-Wire as a cute little cousin.

Why on-board buses exist: A microcontroller has a limited number of pins. If every sensor needed 8 data lines, you would run out quickly. On-board serial buses connect many chips using very few pins, with simple rules that small chips can follow. They run at modest speeds (from about 100 kilobits per second to tens of megabits per second), which is plenty for reading a sensor or writing to a small screen.

SPI in one line: SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface), introduced by Motorola, is a fast, simple, synchronous, full duplex bus with one master and one or more slaves, using four signals. The master provides the clock, and data moves in both directions on every clock tick.

The four SPI wires: SCLK is the serial clock, always driven by the master. MOSI (master out, slave in) carries data from master to slave. MISO (master in, slave out) carries data from slave to master. SS or CS (slave select or chip select) tells one slave you are the one I am talking to; it is usually active low, meaning the slave is selected when the line is pulled to 0. Newer documents may use the names COPI and CIPO (controller and peripheral) for MOSI and MISO, but they mean the same thing.

How SPI moves data: Inside both master and slave is an 8-bit shift register. On each clock pulse, the master shifts one bit out on MOSI and the slave shifts one bit out on MISO at the same moment. After 8 clocks, the two registers have swapped contents. So every SPI transfer is really an exchange. If the master only wants to read, it sends dummy bytes (often 0xFF) to keep the clock running. If it only wants to write, it simply ignores what comes back.

Multiple SPI slaves: Since SPI has no addresses, each slave usually gets its own chip select line from the master. With 3 slaves, you need 3 CS pins, plus the shared SCLK, MOSI and MISO, so 6 wires in total. Only the selected slave drives MISO; the others keep their MISO output disconnected (high impedance). Some chips also support a daisy chain, where the MISO of one goes to the MOSI of the next, so data passes through all of them like a long shift register.

SPI modes: Two settings decide clock timing. CPOL (clock polarity) says whether the clock idles low (0) or high (1). CPHA (clock phase) says whether data is sampled on the first or second clock edge. Together they make four modes, 0 to 3. Mode 0 (CPOL 0, CPHA 0) is the most common. The master must use the same mode as the slave's datasheet says, or the bits will be shifted wrongly. This is the number one SPI bug.

SPI strengths and weaknesses: SPI is fast (often tens of megahertz), full duplex, and very simple to implement. It has no fixed byte format, so it is flexible. But it needs one extra pin per slave, has no built-in acknowledgement (the master does not know if a slave even exists), has no error checking, and is meant only for short distances on one board. SD cards can work in SPI mode, and SPI is widely used for flash memory chips, small displays, and analog-to-digital converters.

I2C in one line: I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit, said I-squared-C or I-two-C), created by Philips in 1982, is a two-wire, half duplex, synchronous bus with addresses, so many chips can share just two lines. It is slower than SPI but uses far fewer pins.

The two I2C wires and pull-ups: SDA is serial data and SCL is serial clock. Both lines are open-drain: a chip can only pull a line down to 0 or let go of it. It can never push it up to 1. A pull-up resistor on each line (often a few kilohms, like 4.7 kilohms) pulls it to 1 when nobody is pulling down. This clever design means two chips can never fight with one pushing 1 and the other pushing 0, because if anyone pulls down, the line is 0. It is a wired-AND.

I2C speeds: Standard mode runs at 100 kilobits per second, Fast mode at 400 kilobits per second, Fast-mode Plus at 1 megabit per second, and High-speed mode at 3.4 megabits per second. Most sensors support at least 100 and 400.

I2C addresses: Each slave has an address, usually 7 bits. The master starts every message by sending the address of the chip it wants, so all chips listen but only the matching one answers. The 7 bits give 128 addresses, though a few are reserved for special uses. Many chips let you change the last one or two address bits with pins, so you can have two of the same sensor on one bus. A 10-bit address mode also exists but is less common.

Start, stop and data rules: Normally SDA may change only while SCL is low, and must stay steady while SCL is high, because that is when the bit is read. There are two special exceptions. A START condition is SDA going from 1 to 0 while SCL is high. A STOP condition is SDA going from 0 to 1 while SCL is high. These two events frame every message, like saying excuse me at the start and thank you at the end.

The address byte and ACK: After START, the master sends 8 bits: the 7-bit address followed by one R/W bit, 0 for write and 1 for read. Then comes a ninth clock pulse, the acknowledge bit. The master lets go of SDA, and the addressed slave pulls SDA low to say ACK, I am here. If nobody pulls it low, SDA stays high: a NACK, which means no device with that address answered. Every byte on I2C is followed by such an ACK or NACK from the receiver. For example, a chip at address 0x68 gets the write byte 0xD0 (0x68 shifted left by one, plus 0) and the read byte 0xD1.

Worked I2C transaction, reading a temperature: Suppose a temperature sensor sits at address 0x48 and its temperature value is in register 0. The master sends START, then 0x90 (address 0x48 with write bit 0), and the sensor ACKs. The master sends 0x00, the register number, and the sensor ACKs. Now the master sends a repeated START (a new START without a STOP), then 0x91 (address with read bit 1), and the sensor ACKs. The sensor now sends the first data byte; the master ACKs to ask for more. The sensor sends the second byte; the master sends NACK to say that is enough. Finally the master sends STOP. Two bytes of temperature have been read using just two wires.

Clock stretching and multi-master: A slow slave can hold SCL low for a while to make the master wait; this is called clock stretching. I2C also allows more than one master. If two masters start at once, they both watch SDA while sending. A master that sends 1 but sees 0 knows another master is sending, so it stops. The winner never even notices. This is arbitration by the wired-AND, with no extra wires at all.

I2C inside your PC: Your desktop also uses a variant called SMBus. Each RAM stick has a small memory chip that stores its speed and timing information, and the motherboard reads it over SMBus at startup to set up the memory correctly. Temperature and fan chips on the motherboard often sit on SMBus too.

1-Wire: The 1-Wire bus, designed by Dallas Semiconductor (now part of Analog Devices), uses just one data line plus ground. Devices can even draw their power from the data line itself while it is high, called parasitic power. Each device has a unique 64-bit ID burned in at the factory, so the master can find and talk to each one on the same wire. It is slow, but perfect for things like the popular DS18B20 temperature sensor, where you might hang several sensors on one long cable through a poultry farm or a cold storage room.

Comparing the three: SPI uses 4 wires plus one CS per extra slave, is full duplex, very fast, has no addresses and no ACK. I2C uses 2 wires for many devices, is half duplex, slower, has addresses and an ACK after every byte, and needs pull-up resistors. 1-Wire uses one wire plus ground, is the slowest, and identifies each device by a unique 64-bit ID. Choose SPI for speed (displays, flash, fast ADCs), I2C for many slow sensors with few pins, and 1-Wire for long, simple sensor chains.

Real-life example 1, a smart weather box for farmers: An agri-tech startup in Rangpur builds a small box for farmers. The microcontroller talks to a temperature and humidity sensor and a real-time clock chip over I2C, using just two pins for both. It stores readings in a flash memory chip over SPI because flash writes are big and need speed. A small colour screen is also on SPI with its own chip select. Each morning, farmers see last night's lowest temperature to plan irrigation.

Real-life example 2, a cold storage monitor: A potato cold storage in Munshiganj must stay cool. A technician runs one long cable through the rooms, with ten DS18B20 sensors clipped on it using 1-Wire. The controller reads each sensor's unique ID once, then asks each one for its temperature in turn. If any room warms up, an alarm sends an SMS to the manager.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the pull-up resistors on I2C is the most common beginner mistake; nothing works without them. Using the wrong SPI mode gives garbage data. Students also forget that the I2C address byte includes the R/W bit, so a 7-bit address 0x48 becomes 0x90 or 0x91 on the wire. Exams ask you to draw SPI connections for multiple slaves, explain the four SPI modes, draw START and STOP conditions, write out the bytes of an I2C read or write, and compare SPI, I2C and 1-Wire in a table.

Recap: SPI uses SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a chip select per slave; it is full duplex and fast, and every transfer is a shift register exchange. I2C uses SDA and SCL with pull-ups, 7-bit addresses, START and STOP conditions, and an ACK after each byte. 1-Wire uses a single wire with unique 64-bit device IDs. Next lesson, we look at the most familiar input device of all, the keyboard, and how it knows which key you pressed.
key_points: SPI uses SCLK, MOSI, MISO and one active-low chip select per slave; it is synchronous, full duplex and fast.
Every SPI transfer is a shift register exchange; four modes come from CPOL and CPHA, and the mode must match the slave.
I2C uses two open-drain lines, SDA and SCL, with pull-up resistors; many devices share them using 7-bit addresses.
I2C START is SDA falling while SCL is high; STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high.
The I2C address byte is the 7-bit address plus an R/W bit; the receiver ACKs every byte by pulling SDA low on the 9th clock.
I2C speeds: 100 kbit/s standard, 400 kbit/s fast, 1 Mbit/s fast-mode plus, 3.4 Mbit/s high speed.
1-Wire uses one data line plus ground and unique 64-bit device IDs, ideal for long sensor chains.
lessons.tip: When working with any new chip, first check its datasheet for three things: which bus (SPI or I2C), the I2C address or SPI mode, and the register map. Write them on a sticky note before writing code.
lessons.task: On paper, write the full byte sequence (with START, ACK, NACK, repeated START and STOP) to read 2 bytes from register 0x3B of a chip at I2C address 0x68. Then draw how you would connect one master to three SPI slaves, labelling every wire.

quiz.q: How many wires does a basic SPI link with one slave use for signals?
quiz.explain: SCLK, MOSI, MISO and CS (plus ground).

quiz.q: Why does an I2C bus need pull-up resistors?
options: Chips can only pull lines low, so resistors pull them high when released
To make the bus faster than SPI
quiz.explain: SDA and SCL are open-drain; without pull-ups the lines would never return to 1.

quiz.q: A chip has 7-bit I2C address 0x48. What byte does the master send to start a read?
quiz.explain: Shift the address left by one and add R/W = 1: 0x48 x 2 + 1 = 0x91.

quiz.q: An I2C START condition is:
options: SCL going low while SDA is high
SDA going from 1 to 0 while SCL is high
SDA going from 0 to 1 while SCL is high
quiz.explain: START is SDA falling while SCL is high; STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high.

quiz.q: Which bus identifies each device by a unique 64-bit factory ID on a single data wire?
quiz.explain: 1-Wire devices like the DS18B20 each have a unique 64-bit ROM ID.

lessons.title: The Keyboard: Matrix Scanning, Debouncing and Scan Codes
lessons.content:
Press the letter A on your keyboard. It feels instant and simple. But inside, a tiny computer is checking more than a hundred keys many times every second, ignoring the electrical shaking of the switch, working out exactly which key moved, turning it into a code, and sending that code to the PC, where software decides whether it should become a, A, or the Bangla letter আ. This lesson follows that journey, and every step is a neat little interfacing trick.

What is inside a keyboard: Under each key is a switch. When you press, two contacts touch and complete a circuit; when you release, they separate. A typical full-size keyboard has 104 or more keys. Along with the switches there is a small microcontroller, often called the keyboard controller or encoder, plus the cable or wireless chip that talks to the computer. The microcontroller's job is to answer one question many times per second: which switches are closed right now?

Why not one wire per key: The obvious design gives each key its own wire to the microcontroller. With 104 keys that would need 104 input pins plus ground, which is far too many for a cheap chip. So keyboards use a much smarter layout called a key matrix.

The key matrix: Arrange the switches in a grid of rows and columns. Each switch connects one row wire to one column wire. With 8 rows and 16 columns you get 8 x 16 = 128 crossing points, enough for 128 keys, using only 8 + 16 = 24 pins instead of 128. In general, r rows and c columns handle r x c keys using r + c pins. Real keyboards do not look like a neat grid on the PCB, but electrically they are.

Scanning the matrix: The microcontroller drives the rows one at a time. Say the column inputs have pull-up resistors, so they read 1 when nothing is pressed. The controller pulls row 0 low and leaves the others high (or floating). Then it reads all 16 columns. Any column that reads 0 must be connected to row 0 through a pressed key. So if column 5 reads 0, the key at row 0, column 5 is down. Then it releases row 0, pulls row 1 low, reads the columns again, and so on through all 8 rows. Then it starts over. A full scan takes well under a millisecond, so the keyboard can scan hundreds or thousands of times per second.

A scanning example: Suppose A is at row 2, column 1, and S is at row 2, column 2. You press both. When row 2 is pulled low, columns 1 and 2 both read 0, so the controller knows A and S are down. When other rows are pulled low, those columns read 1, so nothing else is reported. The controller compares this scan with the previous one: newly closed keys become press events, and newly opened keys become release events.

Switch bounce: Mechanical contacts do not close cleanly. When they touch, they bounce apart and together several times in a few milliseconds, like a ball dropped on the floor. To a fast microcontroller, one press can look like five quick presses. Without care, typing a once would print aaaaa.

Debouncing in hardware: One fix is a small resistor and capacitor (an RC filter) on each input, which smooths the fast bounces into a slow, steady change, often followed by a Schmitt trigger, a gate that switches cleanly only when the voltage clearly crosses its thresholds. This works well for a few buttons but is expensive for a hundred keys.

Debouncing in software: Keyboards usually debounce in their firmware. A simple method: when a key's state changes, do not report it immediately. Wait about 5 milliseconds and check again, and only accept the change if it is still the same. Another method keeps a short history for each key, such as the last 8 scans, and only accepts a change when all 8 agree. In pseudo-code: history = (history << 1) | current_bit; if history == 0xFF then key is down; if history == 0x00 then key is up. Bounce typically settles within a few milliseconds, so this costs almost no noticeable delay.

Ghosting: Matrices have a sneaky problem. Imagine you hold three keys that form three corners of a rectangle in the grid: row 1 column 1, row 1 column 2, and row 2 column 1. When the controller pulls row 2 low, current can flow from row 2 through key (2,1) to column 1, back up through key (1,1) to row 1, across through key (1,2) to column 2. So column 2 also reads 0 on row 2, and the controller thinks key (2,2) is pressed too, even though it is not. This phantom key is called a ghost.

Fixing ghosting: The clean fix is a small diode in series with each switch, which lets current flow only one way, from column to row, and blocks the sneaky backwards path. Gaming and mechanical keyboards often have a diode on every key. Cheaper keyboards skip diodes and instead block: when the firmware sees a pattern that could create a ghost, it simply ignores the extra key. That is why on some cheap keyboards, certain three-key combinations do not work. Designers place common combinations, like Ctrl, Shift and a letter, so they do not clash.

Key rollover: Rollover is how many keys can be held at once and still all be reported correctly. 2-key rollover means any two keys work. 6-key rollover is common with USB keyboards in their basic mode. N-key rollover (NKRO) means every key can be pressed at once and all are detected, which needs a diode per key. Fast typists and gamers care about this.

Scan codes: The keyboard does not send letters. It sends scan codes, numbers that identify a key position. When a key goes down, the keyboard sends a make code; when it comes up, a break code. In the old PC XT set (scan code set 1), A has make code 1E hex and break code 9E hex, which is the make code plus 80 hex. Most PS/2 keyboards use scan code set 2, where A is 1C hex for make and F0 1C for break. The PC's keyboard controller traditionally translated set 2 into set 1 for older software.

USB keyboards and HID reports: A USB keyboard is a HID device. Instead of make and break codes, it sends a small report whenever something changes. In the simple boot format, the report is 8 bytes: the first byte has one bit for each modifier key (left and right Ctrl, Shift, Alt and the Windows or Command key), the second byte is reserved, and the remaining 6 bytes list up to 6 keys currently held, using HID usage IDs (A is 04 hex). That is where 6-key rollover comes from. Keyboards can use other report formats to support NKRO.

From position to character: A scan code or usage ID says which physical key was pressed, not which letter it means. The operating system uses a keyboard layout (keymap) to turn the key plus the current Shift and Caps Lock state into a character. This is why the same key can produce q on an English layout, a on a French layout, or a Bangla letter when you switch to a Bangla layout such as Bijoy or Avro phonetic. The hardware does not change at all; only the software mapping does.

The lights on the keyboard: Caps Lock, Num Lock and Scroll Lock lights are not switched by the keyboard itself in a modern PC. When you press Caps Lock, the keyboard just reports the key. The operating system flips its own Caps Lock state and then sends a command back to the keyboard to turn the light on or off. This is why the light can sometimes be out of step with the real state after a crash. It is also a nice example of two-way communication on a device we usually think of as input only.

Auto-repeat: Hold down a key and, after a short delay, it repeats. This is called typematic repeat. There is a delay before the first repeat (often around half a second) and then a repeat rate (often 10 to 30 per second). PS/2 keyboards generate repeats themselves; with USB keyboards, the operating system usually creates the repeats from the fact that the key is still held. You can change both settings in your operating system.

Types of key switches: Membrane keyboards, the cheapest, use three thin plastic sheets with printed conductive traces; pressing a rubber dome pushes the top sheet to touch the bottom one. Laptop scissor-switch keys add a small scissor mechanism for a stable, short press. Mechanical keyboards have a separate spring-loaded switch under each key, with a defined feel and long life, often rated for tens of millions of presses. Some keyboards use capacitive or optical sensing with no metal contacts at all. All of them still end up in a matrix or similar scan.

Real-life example 1, typing Bangla in a newspaper office: A typist at a newspaper in Kawran Bazar types Bangla all day using the Bijoy layout on an ordinary English-labelled keyboard. When she presses the key labelled J, the keyboard sends exactly the same scan code as it would for English. The layout software in the computer maps it to a Bangla letter instead. If the computer crashes and restarts in English, the same keys print English letters. The keyboard never knew it was typing Bangla.

Real-life example 2, a cheap keyboard in a gaming cafe: In a gaming zone in Uttara, players complain that when they hold W and A to move diagonally and press Space to jump, sometimes the jump does not happen. The owner tests the keyboard with an online key-test page and finds that this three-key combination is blocked on that model to avoid ghosting. He replaces it with a keyboard that has N-key rollover, and the problem disappears.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think the keyboard sends ASCII letters; it sends scan codes or usage IDs, and the operating system maps them to characters. They mix up ghosting (a phantom key) with bounce (one key giving several presses). They forget that both a make and a break code are sent. Exams ask you to calculate pins needed for a matrix, explain row-by-row scanning, draw the ghosting rectangle and show where diodes go, describe software debouncing, and explain make and break codes with an example.

Recap: Keys sit in a matrix so r rows and c columns handle r x c keys with r + c pins. The controller drives one row at a time and reads the columns. Debouncing ignores the contact bounce of a few milliseconds. Ghosting appears with three keys on a rectangle and is fixed by a diode per key, which also enables N-key rollover. The keyboard sends make and break scan codes (or USB HID reports), and the operating system's layout turns key positions into characters. Next lesson, we follow your other hand to the mouse, touchpad and touch screen.
key_points: A key matrix of r rows and c columns handles r x c keys using only r + c pins.
The controller scans by driving one row at a time and reading all columns; pressed keys pull a column low.
Switch contacts bounce for a few milliseconds; debouncing in hardware (RC filter) or software (wait or sample history) removes false presses.
Ghosting is a phantom key caused by three pressed keys forming a rectangle; a diode per key fixes it.
Rollover is how many simultaneous keys are reported correctly: 2KRO, 6KRO, or N-key rollover.
Keyboards send scan codes (make on press, break on release) or USB HID reports with usage IDs, not letters.
The operating system's layout (such as English, Bijoy or Avro) maps physical keys to characters.
lessons.tip: Draw a 3 x 3 key matrix and act out a scan by hand, pressing different keys. Then press three keys on a rectangle and watch the ghost appear in your drawing. Ten minutes of this makes the topic unforgettable.
lessons.task: Open an online keyboard tester in a browser and test your own keyboard: hold down as many keys as you can and see how many register. Try combinations like W, A and Space, or Shift, Ctrl and several letters. Write down your keyboard's rollover and any blocked combinations.

quiz.q: How many pins does a 6-row by 18-column key matrix need, and how many keys can it handle?
quiz.explain: Pins = rows + columns = 24; keys = rows x columns = 108.

quiz.q: What is switch bounce?
options: A key appearing pressed that was not pressed
The keyboard bouncing on the table
Contacts rapidly opening and closing for a few milliseconds after a press
quiz.explain: Mechanical contacts bounce briefly, which can look like several presses unless debounced.

quiz.q: What is the best fix for ghosting in a key matrix?
options: A diode in series with each switch
quiz.explain: Diodes block the sneaky reverse current path, removing phantom keys and allowing N-key rollover.

quiz.q: What does a keyboard send when you release a key in PS/2 style?
quiz.explain: A make code is sent on press and a break code on release.

quiz.q: Why can the same keyboard type English or Bangla letters?
options: The operating system's layout maps the same scan codes to different characters
quiz.explain: The keyboard sends position codes; the software layout decides which character each key produces.

lessons.title: Mouse, Touchpad and Touch Screen
lessons.content:
When you slide a mouse across a desk, the pointer on screen glides with it. When you tap your phone screen, the right icon opens, even though your finger is a soft, blurry blob. Both feel like magic, but they are built from simple ideas: counting tiny movements, taking very fast photos, and measuring small changes in voltage or electric charge. This lesson explains how pointing devices know where your hand is, and why a mouse and a touch screen think about position in completely different ways.

Relative versus absolute pointing: There are two families of pointing devices. A mouse is relative: it only reports how much it moved since last time, like moved 5 steps right and 2 steps up. It has no idea where it is on the desk; you can lift it and put it down elsewhere and the pointer does not jump. A touch screen or a drawing tablet is absolute: it reports the exact position touched, like x = 300, y = 520. The screen location under your finger is the answer. Keep this difference in mind; it explains a lot about how each one is built and used.

The old ball mouse: The first popular mice had a rubber ball underneath. As the mouse moved, the ball rolled and turned two small rollers inside, one for left-right (X) and one for up-down (Y). Each roller turned a wheel with slots around its edge. On one side of the wheel was a small LED and on the other a light sensor. As the wheel turned, the slots let light through and blocked it, producing pulses. Counting pulses told how far the roller turned.

Knowing direction with two sensors: One sensor counts pulses but cannot tell left from right. So each wheel had two sensors placed slightly offset, so their pulse trains are a quarter cycle apart. This is called quadrature encoding. If sensor A changes before B, the wheel is turning one way; if B changes before A, it is turning the other way. Quadrature encoders are still used today in mouse scroll wheels, in motor speed sensors, and in the volume knobs of many car radios.

Why ball mice disappeared: The ball picked up dust and hair from the desk and spread it onto the rollers, so the pointer started jumping. Everyone who used a computer in the 1990s remembers taking the ball out to clean it. Optical mice, which have no moving parts underneath, replaced them in the 2000s.

The optical mouse: An optical mouse has an LED (often red, sometimes infrared) or a laser that lights up the desk surface at a low angle, so tiny bumps and fibres cast shadows. A small lens focuses that patch onto a tiny camera chip, an image sensor only a few dozen pixels wide. It takes pictures extremely fast, typically thousands of frames per second. A small built-in processor (a DSP, digital signal processor) compares each picture with the previous one and works out how far the pattern shifted. If the pattern moved 3 pixels left, the mouse moved right, and it reports dx and dy.

Why optical mice struggle on glass: The sensor needs texture to track. A perfectly smooth, clear or shiny surface, like glass or a polished mirror, gives the camera almost nothing to see, so the pointer stops or jumps. That is why a mouse pad, or even a sheet of paper, fixes the problem. Some special sensors are designed to work on glass, but ordinary ones are not.

DPI or CPI: Mouse sensitivity is given in DPI (dots per inch), more correctly called CPI (counts per inch). It is the number of movement counts the mouse reports when you move it one inch (2.54 centimetres). A 1,600 CPI mouse moved one inch reports 1,600 counts. If the operating system moves the pointer one pixel per count, the pointer moves 1,600 pixels, almost across a full HD screen of 1,920 pixels. A 400 CPI mouse would move it only 400 pixels for the same hand movement. Gamers often choose their CPI carefully for precise aiming.

What the mouse sends: A mouse report is small. It contains the button states (left, right, middle and maybe side buttons, one bit each), the X movement and the Y movement as signed numbers, and the wheel movement. The old PS/2 mouse sent a 3-byte packet for each report. A USB mouse sends a HID report through an interrupt endpoint, polled usually every 8 milliseconds (125 times per second), or every 1 millisecond for gaming mice.

Pointer speed and acceleration: The operating system does not have to move one pixel per count. It applies a sensitivity setting and often pointer acceleration: when you move the mouse quickly, each count moves the pointer further. That lets you cross the screen with a flick and still place it precisely with slow movements. Many gamers turn acceleration off so the same hand movement always gives the same result.

Touchpads: A laptop touchpad is a capacitive sensor, a grid of thin conductive lines under a smooth surface. Your finger, which conducts electricity and is connected to your body, changes the capacitance near the lines under it. A controller chip scans the grid many times per second and works out where the finger is. Although the touchpad knows the absolute position of your finger on the pad, it usually reports relative movement to act like a mouse. Modern touchpads detect several fingers, which lets the operating system support gestures like two-finger scrolling and pinch to zoom.

Resistive touch screens: The first common touch screens were resistive. They have two thin flexible layers, each coated with a transparent material that has resistance, separated by tiny spacer dots. When you press, the top layer bends and touches the bottom one at that point. To read X, the controller applies a voltage across one layer from left edge to right edge. The point of contact acts like the slider of a potentiometer, a voltage divider, so the other layer picks up a voltage proportional to how far across the touch is. Then the controller swaps roles to read Y.

A resistive worked example: The controller puts 3.3 volts across the X layer and measures 1.1 volts at the touch point. 1.1 divided by 3.3 is one third, so the touch is one third of the way across. With a 12-bit ADC (0 to 4095), the reading would be about 1,365. On an 800-pixel-wide screen, x is about 1,365 / 4,095 x 800, which is about 267 pixels. Real screens need calibration, because the layers are not perfectly even, which is why old resistive devices asked you to tap crosshairs in each corner.

Resistive pros and cons: Resistive screens work with anything that presses: a finger, a glove, a pen or a fingernail, and they are cheap. But they need pressure, the extra layers make the picture less clear, the top layer can wear out, and the basic 4-wire type detects only one touch at a time. You still find them in some ATM and point-of-sale machines, industrial panels and cheap devices.

Capacitive touch screens: Almost every smartphone uses projected capacitive touch. Under the glass is a grid of transparent electrodes, usually made of indium tin oxide (ITO), arranged in rows and columns. The controller sends tiny signals on one set and measures the capacitance at each crossing point. A finger near a crossing draws away some of the electric field and changes the capacitance there. By scanning every crossing, the controller builds a map of where fingers are, and can see many touches at once. Because it senses electric charge, not pressure, a light touch works, and the glass on top can be tough.

Why gloves do not work, and what does: A normal woollen glove is an insulator, so it blocks the finger's effect on the field, and the phone ignores you. Special touch-screen gloves have conductive threads in the fingertips. A cheap rubber-tipped stylus works because its tip is conductive and connected to your hand. Water drops on the screen can also cause false touches, which is why phones behave strangely in the rain.

Touch sampling and active styluses: Phones scan the touch grid many times per second, often 120 to 240 times or more in recent models, which matters for fast games and smooth scrolling. Pens that need pressure sensitivity, like those for drawing tablets and some phones, use an active method: an electromagnetic grid behind the screen detects the pen tip's position and pressure, and some pens have their own battery. This lets the screen ignore your palm resting on it while you draw.

Other touch methods: Very large touch displays, like the interactive boards in some classrooms, often use infrared frames: rows of tiny infrared LEDs along two edges and sensors along the opposite edges. A finger blocks some beams, and the blocked positions give X and Y. Some public kiosks use similar ideas.

Real-life example 1, a bank ATM in Sylhet: Some older ATMs use resistive touch screens, so they work even if you press with a fingernail or a pen, and they shrug off dust. Newer ones use capacitive screens behind thick glass, which feel smoother and are harder to damage. If a customer with dry, cracked fingers finds the capacitive screen does not respond, pressing the flat of the finger, which gives more contact area, usually helps.

Real-life example 2, a freelance designer in Dhanmondi: A graphic designer working for international clients buys a pen tablet. The tablet is absolute: the top-left corner of the tablet is the top-left of the screen. The pen also reports pressure, so pressing harder draws a thicker line in Photoshop. When she switches to her mouse for quick menu clicks, she is back to relative movement. Using both shows clearly why the two families exist.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students say a mouse reports its position; it reports only changes in position. They mix up DPI as a screen setting with mouse CPI. They think capacitive screens need pressure. Exams ask: explain how an optical mouse works, explain quadrature encoding, compare resistive and capacitive touch screens, calculate a resistive touch position from voltages, calculate pointer movement from CPI, and give examples of relative and absolute devices.

Recap: A mouse is a relative device: ball mice counted slotted-wheel pulses with quadrature to know direction, and optical mice compare thousands of tiny camera images per second. CPI tells how many counts per inch the mouse reports. Touchpads and capacitive screens sense a finger's effect on a grid of electrodes and can track many touches; resistive screens use a pressed voltage divider to read X and Y. Next lesson, we switch from input to output and learn the basics of displays: pixels, colour and frame buffers.
key_points: A mouse is a relative device reporting movement (dx, dy); touch screens and tablets are absolute, reporting exact positions.
Ball mice counted pulses from slotted wheels; two offset sensors (quadrature) tell the direction.
An optical mouse lights the surface and compares thousands of tiny camera images per second to compute movement.
CPI (DPI) is the number of counts reported per inch of movement.
Resistive touch screens work by pressure; the contact point forms a voltage divider that gives X and Y.
Projected capacitive screens sense changes in capacitance at a grid of transparent electrodes and support multi-touch.
Capacitive screens need a conductive touch, so ordinary gloves fail but conductive styluses work.
lessons.tip: For every pointing device, ask two questions: is it relative or absolute, and what physical change does it sense (light pattern, pressure, capacitance)? These two answers organise this whole topic.
lessons.task: Find your mouse's CPI (search the model, or check its software). Measure how far the pointer moves when you move the mouse exactly 5 cm (about 2 inches) with acceleration off if possible. Then try your phone's screen with a woollen glove, a fingernail, and the back of a metal spoon held in your hand, and write down which ones work and why.

quiz.q: Which of these is an absolute pointing device?
quiz.explain: A touch screen reports the exact position touched; mice only report movement.

quiz.q: How does an optical mouse detect movement?
options: It compares rapidly taken images of the surface
It measures the Earth's magnetic field
It counts the rotation of a rubber ball
quiz.explain: A tiny image sensor takes thousands of pictures per second and a DSP computes how the pattern shifted.

quiz.q: A 1,600 CPI mouse is moved 1.5 inches with one pixel per count. How far does the pointer move?
quiz.explain: 1,600 counts per inch x 1.5 inches = 2,400 counts, so 2,400 pixels.

quiz.q: In a 4-wire resistive screen, 3.3 V is across the X layer and 1.65 V is measured. Where is the touch?
quiz.explain: 1.65 / 3.3 = 0.5, so the contact point is halfway across, like a potentiometer at its middle.

quiz.q: Why does an ordinary woollen glove not work on a phone's capacitive screen?
options: The glove is the wrong colour
Wool is an insulator, so the finger cannot change the electric field
quiz.explain: Capacitive sensing needs a conductive touch; insulating wool blocks the finger's effect.

lessons.title: Display Fundamentals: Pixels, Colour and Frame Buffers
lessons.content:
Look very closely at a big billboard on the Mohakhali flyover, or at your phone screen through a magnifying glass or a drop of water. The picture breaks into tiny coloured dots, each one red, green or blue, glowing at different brightness. From a normal distance, your eyes blend them into faces, letters and cricket matches. Every screen, from a giant stadium display to a smartwatch, works on this idea. In this lesson we learn the language of displays: pixels, resolution, colour depth, refresh rate and the frame buffer, the piece of memory that holds the picture.

Pixels: A pixel (short for picture element) is the smallest dot of a digital image that can be set to its own colour. A screen is a rectangular grid of pixels. The computer decides the colour of every pixel, many times per second, and the screen shows them. Draw a letter, a photo or a game character, and in the end it is just the right colours in the right pixels.

Subpixels and additive colour: On most colour screens, each pixel is really three tiny lights side by side: a red subpixel, a green subpixel and a blue subpixel. By mixing their brightness, the pixel can show many colours. This is additive colour mixing, used for light: red plus green gives yellow, green plus blue gives cyan, red plus blue gives magenta, and all three at full gives white. All off gives black. Printing on paper uses the opposite, subtractive mixing with inks, which we will see in the printer lesson.

Resolution: Resolution is the number of pixels across and down, written width x height. Common ones are 1366 x 768 on cheap laptops, 1920 x 1080 called Full HD, 2560 x 1440 called QHD, and 3840 x 2160 called 4K UHD. Full HD has 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, about 2 million. 4K UHD has 3840 x 2160 = 8,294,400 pixels, exactly four times as many, because both width and height doubled.

The p in 720p and 1080p: Video sizes are often named only by their height. 720p means 1280 x 720, which is 921,600 pixels, often called HD. 1080p means 1920 x 1080. When YouTube lets you choose 360p, 720p or 1080p on mobile data, you are choosing how many pixels each frame has, and so how much data must be downloaded. Picking 480p instead of 1080p can save a lot of your mobile data pack.

Aspect ratio: Aspect ratio is width divided by height, written as a simple ratio. 1920 x 1080 reduces to 16:9, the shape of most TVs and laptops. Old monitors and many projectors used 4:3, like 1024 x 768. Phones are often taller, around 20:9. When a video's aspect ratio does not match the screen, you get black bars at the sides or top and bottom, or the picture is stretched.

Pixel density: Pixel density, measured in PPI (pixels per inch), tells how sharp a screen looks. Screen sizes are measured diagonally, so we first find the number of pixels along the diagonal using Pythagoras. For a 15.6-inch Full HD laptop: diagonal pixels = square root of (1920 squared + 1080 squared) = about 2,203. Divide by 15.6 and you get about 141 PPI. A 6.1-inch phone with 2400 x 1080 pixels has about 2,632 pixels on the diagonal, so about 431 PPI. That is why phone text looks so crisp even close up.

Colour depth: Colour depth (bits per pixel) tells how many different colours each pixel can show. With 8 bits for each of red, green and blue, that is 24 bits per pixel, and 2 to the power 24 = 16,777,216 colours, often called true colour or about 16.7 million colours. Each channel goes from 0 (off) to 255 (full). Pure red is (255, 0, 0), white is (255, 255, 255), and orange might be (255, 136, 0), written in web code as #FF8800. Newer HDR screens use 10 bits per channel, 30 bits per pixel, over a billion colours, giving smoother skies and sunsets with no visible bands.

Indexed colour: Old computers with very little memory used indexed colour. Each pixel stored just 8 bits, a number from 0 to 255, and a separate table called a palette said which actual 24-bit colour each number meant. So the screen could show 256 different colours at once, chosen from millions. The famous VGA game mode was 320 x 200 with 256 colours. GIF images still use a palette of up to 256 colours today.

The frame buffer: The frame buffer is a block of memory that holds the colour of every pixel on screen. The display hardware reads it again and again and sends the pixels to the screen. To change what you see, software writes new values into the frame buffer. In a PC this memory is usually on the graphics card (video memory) or, for laptops with built-in graphics, part of main RAM.

Frame buffer size worked out: For a Full HD screen with 24-bit colour, each pixel needs 3 bytes. 2,073,600 pixels x 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6.2 megabytes. Many systems store 4 bytes per pixel (the extra byte is for alignment or transparency, called alpha), which gives 8,294,400 bytes, about 8.3 megabytes. For 4K with 4 bytes per pixel, it is four times that: about 33 megabytes. And since we often keep two frame buffers (see lesson 15), double it.

Finding one pixel in memory: Pixels are usually stored row by row, from the top-left corner. The address of pixel (x, y) is: address = base + (y x width + x) x bytes_per_pixel. For example, on a 1920-wide screen with 4 bytes per pixel, pixel (100, 50) is at offset (50 x 1920 + 100) x 4 = (96,000 + 100) x 4 = 384,400 bytes from the start. Drawing a line or a letter is just a loop that writes colours into such addresses.

Refresh rate: The refresh rate is how many times per second the screen redraws the whole image from the frame buffer, measured in hertz (Hz). Most screens run at 60 Hz, meaning 60 full pictures per second. Gaming monitors and many phones run at 90, 120, 144 Hz or more, which makes scrolling and motion look smoother. Frame rate is a different thing: it is how many new pictures per second the software actually produces. A game running at 40 frames per second on a 60 Hz screen will show some frames twice.

How much data flows: Every refresh, the entire frame must be sent to the screen. Full HD at 24 bits and 60 Hz is 2,073,600 x 24 x 60 = about 2.99 billion bits per second, nearly 3 gigabits per second, just for the visible pixels. 4K at 60 Hz is four times as much, about 12 gigabits per second. This is why video cables have to be so fast, as we will see when we look at HDMI and DisplayPort.

The CRT and raster scan: Before flat screens, monitors and TVs used a CRT (cathode ray tube), a big glass vacuum tube. At the back, an electron gun shot a beam of electrons at the front glass, which was coated with phosphor dots that glow when hit.
