Magnetic coils around the neck bent the beam so it swept across the screen in lines, left to right, then jumped back and moved down a little, like reading a book. This pattern is called a raster scan. A colour CRT had three beams for red, green and blue phosphors, and a metal sheet with holes (a shadow mask) made sure each beam hit only its own colour.

Blanking and retrace: When the beam reached the right edge, it had to fly back to the left to start the next line. This is horizontal retrace, and during it the beam was switched off, a period called horizontal blanking. At the bottom of the screen, the beam returned to the top: vertical retrace, during vertical blanking. Even though flat screens have no beam, video signals still include blanking periods and sync signals, as a leftover from CRT days and because they are useful for timing.

Interlaced and progressive: To save bandwidth, old TV systems drew odd lines in one pass and even lines in the next, called interlaced scanning. Each pass is a field, and two fields make a frame. Bangladesh's old PAL analogue TV used 625 lines and 50 fields per second. Modern displays use progressive scanning, drawing every line in order each time. That is the difference between 1080i (interlaced) and 1080p (progressive).

Raster versus vector: Almost all screens are raster displays, built from a grid of pixels. Some very early displays, such as old radar and arcade screens like Asteroids, were vector displays: the beam drew lines directly from point to point instead of scanning the whole screen. They gave very sharp lines but could not fill areas easily. Today vector only survives as a way of describing images (like SVG files or fonts) that are later turned into pixels.

Real-life example 1, a cricket match on a big screen: At Sher-e-Bangla stadium, the giant screen is made of LED panels. It may have far fewer pixels than you expect, maybe only a few hundred pixels across per panel, because viewers sit far away. From the stands, the low pixel density does not matter. But walk close and you can see each glowing dot. Pixel density only has to be high enough for the viewing distance.

Real-life example 2, choosing a laptop in BCS Computer City: A student compares two 15.6-inch laptops, one with 1366 x 768 and one with 1920 x 1080. The first has about 100 PPI, the second about 141. The Full HD one shows more text at once and looks sharper for coding. The shop also offers a 144 Hz model, which helps for gaming but does little for writing assignments. Knowing these numbers lets her spend money where it matters.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up resolution with screen size, refresh rate with frame rate, and bits with bytes when calculating frame buffer size. They forget that colour depth is bits per pixel, not number of colours. Exams ask: calculate frame buffer size for a given resolution and colour depth, find the address of a pixel, calculate the number of colours from bits, calculate data rate, compute PPI, explain raster scan and blanking, and compare interlaced and progressive.

Recap: A screen is a grid of pixels, each made of red, green and blue subpixels mixed additively. Resolution counts pixels, PPI measures sharpness, and colour depth sets how many colours are possible: 24 bits give 16.7 million. The frame buffer holds every pixel's colour; its size is width x height x bytes per pixel, and a pixel's address is base + (y x width + x) x bytes per pixel. Refresh rate is how often the screen redraws. CRTs drew pictures by raster scan with blanking, ideas still used in video signals. Next lesson, we look inside today's flat screens: LCD, LED-backlit and OLED.
key_points: A pixel is the smallest settable dot; colour screens build each pixel from red, green and blue subpixels using additive mixing.
Resolution is width x height in pixels; 4K UHD (3840 x 2160) has four times the pixels of Full HD (1920 x 1080).
PPI = diagonal pixels (by Pythagoras) / diagonal size in inches.
24-bit colour gives 8 bits per channel and 16,777,216 colours.
Frame buffer size = width x height x bytes per pixel; pixel address = base + (y x width + x) x bytes per pixel.
Refresh rate is how often the screen redraws; frame rate is how often software makes a new image.
CRTs used raster scan with horizontal and vertical retrace (blanking); interlaced draws odd and even lines in separate fields.
lessons.tip: Keep one set of numbers in your head: Full HD is about 2 million pixels, 24-bit colour is 3 bytes per pixel, so one frame is about 6 MB and 60 frames per second is about 3 gigabits per second. Most display calculations start from here.
lessons.task: Find your phone's or laptop's screen size and resolution. Calculate its PPI, its frame buffer size at 4 bytes per pixel, and the raw data rate at its refresh rate. Then look at the screen through a drop of water on a clear plastic sheet to see the subpixels.

quiz.q: How many colours can 24-bit colour depth show?
quiz.explain: 2 to the power 24 = 16,777,216, from 8 bits each for red, green and blue.

quiz.q: What is the frame buffer size of a 1920 x 1080 screen at 3 bytes per pixel?
quiz.explain: 1920 x 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels; x 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6.2 MB.

quiz.q: With 4 bytes per pixel and width 800, what is the offset of pixel (10, 2)?
Adding full red and full green light gives:
quiz.explain: In additive (light) mixing, red plus green makes yellow.

quiz.q: During horizontal retrace in a CRT:
options: The beam is switched off while it returns to the left edge
The beam draws the next pixel brighter
quiz.explain: The beam flies back to start the next line and is blanked so it does not draw a stray line.

lessons.title: Display Technologies: LCD, LED, OLED and E-Paper
lessons.content:
Go into a TV showroom in Bashundhara City and you will see labels like LED TV, QLED, OLED and Mini-LED. A salesman may tell you an LED TV is completely different from an LCD TV. Here is a secret: most LED TVs are LCD TVs. The words are marketing, but underneath there are only a few real ideas. Some screens make their own light in every pixel. Others have one big lamp behind, and every pixel acts like a tiny window shutter. Once you understand those two families, every label in the showroom makes sense.

Two families: emissive and transmissive: An emissive display makes light directly in each pixel. CRTs did this with glowing phosphor, and OLED and LED billboards do it today. A transmissive display does not make light in the pixels. Instead, a light source behind the screen (the backlight) shines through, and each pixel controls how much light gets through. The LCD is transmissive. A third family, reflective displays, uses outside light bouncing off the screen; e-paper and simple calculator screens are reflective.

Polarised light, the key to LCD: Light waves can wiggle in many directions. A polariser is a filter that lets through only light wiggling in one direction, like a fence with vertical slots that lets through only up-and-down waves. If you put two polarisers on top of each other at right angles, almost no light gets through. This is easy to test: look at an LCD screen through polarised sunglasses and tilt your head; at some angle the screen goes dark.

Liquid crystals: A liquid crystal is a strange material that flows like a liquid but whose rod-shaped molecules line up in order like a crystal. In a classic LCD cell, the molecules are arranged in a twisted spiral between two glass plates. Light passing through follows the twist and its polarisation rotates by 90 degrees. When a voltage is applied across the cell, the molecules straighten out along the electric field and the twist disappears, so the light's polarisation is no longer rotated.

How one LCD subpixel works: Stack, from back to front: the backlight, a rear polariser, the liquid crystal cell, a colour filter (red, green or blue), and a front polariser at right angles to the rear one. With no voltage, the twisted crystal rotates the light by 90 degrees, so it passes the front polariser: the subpixel is bright. With full voltage, the crystal untwists, the light is not rotated, and the crossed front polariser blocks it: the subpixel is dark. A voltage in between gives a shade of grey. Put a colour filter on each subpixel and you get coloured pixels. This classic arrangement is called twisted nematic (TN).

Active matrix and TFT: A Full HD screen has over 6 million subpixels. You cannot run a wire to each one. They are arranged in a grid of rows and columns, like a key matrix. In an active matrix LCD, each subpixel has its own tiny transistor, a thin-film transistor (TFT), built on the glass, plus a small capacitor. The driver selects one row at a time by switching on its transistors, puts the right voltages on all the column wires, and those voltages are stored in the capacitors. The transistor then turns off and the capacitor holds the voltage until the next refresh, so the pixel stays steady. Older passive matrix LCDs, like those in old calculators and cheap phones, had no transistor per pixel and were slow and blurry for moving pictures.

TN, IPS and VA panels: Different ways of arranging the liquid crystals give different trade-offs. TN (twisted nematic) panels are cheap and fast, but colours shift when viewed from the side or from below. IPS (in-plane switching) panels rotate the crystals sideways in the plane of the screen, giving accurate colours and wide viewing angles, which is why designers and most good laptops and phones with LCDs use them. VA (vertical alignment) panels block light very well when off, giving deeper blacks and higher contrast, but can be slower in some colour changes.

The LCD's weakness, black is not truly black: Because an LCD works by blocking a backlight that is always on, some light always leaks through, so black looks dark grey, especially in a dark room. Contrast ratio, the brightness of white divided by the brightness of black, is around 1,000 to 1 for many IPS panels and a few thousand to 1 for VA panels.

Backlights and LED TVs: Early LCDs used thin fluorescent tubes (CCFL) as the backlight. Then makers switched to white LEDs, which are thinner, use less power and contain no mercury. These sets were sold as LED TVs, but they are LCDs with LED backlights. In edge-lit screens, LEDs sit along the edges and a light guide spreads the light. In full-array screens, LEDs sit in a grid behind the panel. If the TV can dim the LEDs behind dark parts of the picture, that is called local dimming, and it improves blacks. Mini-LED screens use thousands of tiny backlight LEDs to make many small dimming zones. QLED screens add a layer of quantum dots, tiny particles that convert blue backlight into very pure red and green light, giving richer colours. They are still LCDs.

OLED: OLED stands for organic light-emitting diode. Each subpixel is a tiny sandwich of special organic (carbon-based) layers that glow when current flows through them. There is no backlight and no liquid crystal. To show black, the pixel simply switches off completely, so black is truly black and contrast is effectively infinite. OLED screens can be very thin, can be made flexible (folding phones use them), have wide viewing angles, and respond extremely fast, in well under a millisecond. Phones usually use AMOLED, meaning active-matrix OLED, with a transistor circuit for each subpixel, just as in TFT LCDs.

OLED weaknesses: Organic materials age as they are used. If a fixed image, like a TV channel logo or a phone's status bar, stays in one place for thousands of hours, those pixels age more than the rest and a faint ghost image may remain; this is called burn-in. Blue OLED materials tend to age fastest. OLED panels are also more expensive to make in large sizes, and some may not reach the very high full-screen brightness of the best LCDs. Makers use tricks like slowly shifting static elements by a pixel or two to reduce burn-in.

Dark mode and battery life: On an OLED phone, a black pixel uses almost no power, so dark mode with lots of true black really can save battery. On an LCD phone, the backlight is on anyway, so dark mode saves very little. This is a neat example of how the hardware decides whether a software feature helps.

Response time and motion: Response time is how long a pixel takes to change from one shade to another, often measured grey to grey in milliseconds. If it is slow, fast motion leaves smears or ghost trails. Fast LCD gaming monitors claim around 1 millisecond, typical IPS panels a few milliseconds, and OLED much less. High refresh rate and fast response time together give smooth, sharp motion in games.

Brightness: Brightness is measured in nits (candela per square metre). Indoor monitors are often 250 to 400 nits. Phones need much more to be readable in bright sunlight, so modern phones can boost to over 1,000 nits outdoors. HDR content uses very bright highlights, which needs high peak brightness.

E-paper: The screen on an e-book reader such as a Kindle uses electrophoretic e-paper (often called E Ink). Each tiny cell or microcapsule contains white particles with one electric charge and black particles with the opposite charge, floating in clear fluid. Apply a voltage one way and the white particles move to the top, so you see white; reverse it and the black ones come up. It is reflective: you read it with room light or sunlight, like real paper, and it is easy on the eyes outdoors. Best of all, it is bistable: once the image is set, it stays with no power at all. Power is used only to change the page. The downsides are slow refresh, so no video, and limited or no colour.

Where e-paper shines: Because it uses power only when changing, e-paper is perfect for things that change rarely: e-book readers, electronic shelf labels in supermarkets (one coin battery can last years), some bus stop signs and smartwatches. Simple segment LCDs, like those in calculators and digital clocks, are also reflective and need tiny power, which is why a solar calculator runs from a small solar cell.

MicroLED and the future: MicroLED screens use millions of microscopic inorganic LEDs, one per subpixel, combining OLED-like perfect blacks with long life and high brightness. Giant LED walls in stadiums are a large version of the same idea. Making tiny microLED screens cheaply is still hard, so they are rare in consumer products today.

Real-life example 1, buying a TV for the World Cup: A family in Mirpur wants a TV to watch football with friends in a bright living room. An LCD with a strong LED backlight gets very bright and is cheaper, so it handles daylight well. An OLED would look stunning at night with deep blacks, but costs more and could, after years of the same news channel logo, show slight burn-in. Knowing the technology lets them choose for their real use, not the label.

Real-life example 2, reading under the sun in a village: A university student going home to a village in Kurigram reads lecture PDFs on her e-reader on the train and under a tree. The e-paper is perfectly readable in sunlight, and the battery lasts weeks because power is used only to turn pages. On her phone's LCD the same sunlight washes the screen out, and the backlight drains the battery in hours.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think LED TVs are a different technology from LCD; most are LCDs with LED backlights. They think LCD pixels make light; they only block or pass the backlight. They forget that OLED blacks are off pixels, so dark mode saves power only on OLED. Exams ask: draw and explain the layers of an LCD, explain the role of polarisers and liquid crystal, explain active matrix TFT, compare TN, IPS and VA, compare LCD and OLED, and explain how e-paper works and why it is bistable.

Recap: Displays are emissive (OLED, LED walls, CRT), transmissive (LCD with backlight) or reflective (e-paper, calculator LCD). An LCD subpixel uses crossed polarisers and a voltage-controlled liquid crystal to pass or block backlight, with a thin-film transistor per subpixel in an active matrix. IPS gives good colour and angles, VA gives better contrast, TN is cheap and fast. OLED pixels make their own light, give perfect black and fast response, but can burn in. E-paper moves charged particles, holds its image with no power, and suits slow-changing content. Next lesson, we follow the picture out of the computer through VGA, HDMI and DisplayPort.
key_points: Displays are emissive (make light per pixel), transmissive (LCD with a backlight) or reflective (use outside light).
An LCD subpixel uses crossed polarisers and a liquid crystal whose twist is controlled by voltage to pass or block backlight.
Active matrix (TFT) LCDs have a transistor and capacitor per subpixel to hold its voltage between refreshes.
TN is cheap and fast with poor angles; IPS gives accurate colour and wide angles; VA gives deeper blacks and higher contrast.
Most LED TVs are LCDs with LED backlights; local dimming, mini-LED and quantum dots improve them.
OLED pixels emit their own light, giving true black, very fast response and flexibility, but they can burn in.
E-paper moves charged black and white particles, is reflective and bistable, using power only when the image changes.
lessons.tip: For any screen label in a shop, ask: where does the light come from? A backlight means it is an LCD of some kind; light from each pixel means OLED or LED/microLED; outside light means reflective. That one question decodes most marketing names.
lessons.task: Look at a laptop or desktop LCD through polarised sunglasses and slowly tilt your head 90 degrees; note what happens. Then, if you have an OLED phone (check its specs), compare battery drain over 30 minutes in light mode and dark mode at the same brightness.

quiz.q: What does a liquid crystal do in an LCD subpixel?
options: It rotates the polarisation of light, controlled by voltage
quiz.explain: The twisted crystal rotates polarised light; voltage untwists it, changing how much passes the front polariser.

quiz.q: Why are blacks on an LCD usually dark grey rather than true black?
options: The backlight is always on and some light leaks through
LCDs cannot show black at all
quiz.explain: LCDs block an always-on backlight, and the blocking is never perfect.

quiz.q: Which panel type is known for wide viewing angles and accurate colours?
quiz.explain: In-plane switching keeps colours steady from wide angles, which is why designers prefer it.

quiz.q: What is burn-in on an OLED screen?
options: A faint permanent ghost image from pixels aging unevenly
quiz.explain: Static elements shown for very long times age their pixels more, leaving a faint image.

quiz.q: Why can an e-reader show a page for days without using power?
options: E-paper is bistable: particles stay in place until moved
quiz.explain: Charged particles stay where they were put, so power is needed only to change the image.

lessons.title: Display Interfaces and the GPU: VGA, HDMI, DisplayPort
lessons.content:
Every university teacher in Bangladesh knows the moment: the projector is on, the laptop is ready, but the cable does not fit. The projector has a blue 15-pin VGA socket, the laptop has only HDMI or USB-C, and someone runs to find an adapter. Behind that small drama is a long story of how pictures travel from a computer to a screen. In this lesson we follow the picture from where it is made, the GPU, through the frame buffer, and out over the cables: VGA, DVI, HDMI and DisplayPort.

The GPU in one paragraph: The GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor built for drawing. A CPU has a few powerful cores; a GPU has hundreds or thousands of simpler cores that do the same kind of calculation on many pixels at once. Drawing a 3D game scene means computing the colour of millions of pixels, each mostly independent, which suits this design perfectly. The GPU writes the finished picture into the frame buffer. GPUs are now also used for AI and science because many of those jobs are also huge numbers of similar calculations.

Integrated and dedicated GPUs: An integrated GPU is built into the CPU chip and uses part of the main RAM as video memory. It is cheap and power-saving, fine for office work, video and light games. A dedicated (discrete) GPU is a separate chip, usually on its own graphics card in a PCI Express x16 slot, with its own fast video memory such as GDDR6. It is much more powerful, uses much more power and makes more heat. Many laptops have both and switch between them.

The display controller: Inside the GPU is a part called the display controller (or scan-out engine). Its job is boring but vital: many times per second, it reads the frame buffer pixel by pixel, row by row, adds the timing signals the screen expects, and sends everything out through the video port. It does this regardless of whether the picture changed. This is the hardware that the refresh rate describes.

Tearing and double buffering: If the GPU writes a new picture into the same frame buffer while the display controller is halfway through reading it, the top of the screen shows the old frame and the bottom shows the new one. In a fast game, you see a horizontal break called tearing. The fix is double buffering: keep two frame buffers. The front buffer is being shown; the GPU draws the next frame into the back buffer. When it is done, the two are swapped, ideally during the vertical blanking gap, so each refresh shows one complete picture. Waiting for that gap is called vsync.

Vsync, triple buffering and variable refresh: Vsync removes tearing, but if the GPU finishes a frame just after the gap, it must wait for the next one, which can add delay and make motion stutter. Triple buffering adds a third buffer so the GPU can keep working. Newer screens support variable refresh rate (sold as FreeSync, G-SYNC or simply VRR): instead of refreshing at a fixed 60 or 144 times per second, the screen waits for the GPU and refreshes as soon as each new frame is ready, within a range. This gives smooth motion without tearing.

Video timing and blanking: A video signal does not only carry visible pixels. As we saw with CRTs, each line has a horizontal blanking period and each frame a vertical blanking period, plus sync pulses that mark the start of lines and frames. For the classic 640 x 480 at 60 Hz VGA mode, each line is 800 pixel times long (640 visible plus 160 blanking) and each frame is 525 lines (480 visible plus 45 blanking). So the pixel clock is 800 x 525 x about 60 = about 25.175 million pixels per second, and the line rate is about 31.5 kHz.

VGA: VGA (Video Graphics Array) arrived with IBM PCs in 1987. Its connector is the 15-pin D-shaped socket, often blue. VGA is analog: the red, green and blue values are sent as three voltages that vary from 0 to about 0.7 volts, plus separate horizontal sync and vertical sync wires. The monitor must turn those voltages back into pixel values, which means the picture can be slightly soft or shimmer, especially at high resolutions or with long cables. VGA was later used far beyond 640 x 480, up to Full HD and higher, but quality suffers.

EDID, the monitor's ID card: How does the computer know which resolutions a monitor supports? VGA connectors (from the late 1990s) and all later interfaces include a small data channel called DDC. It is actually an I2C bus, just like in lesson 10. Through it the computer reads a small table stored in the monitor, the EDID (Extended Display Identification Data), which lists the maker, the model, the native resolution and the supported timings. That is why Windows automatically picks the right resolution when you plug in a new monitor.

DVI: DVI (Digital Visual Interface), from 1999, brought digital video to PC monitors. Instead of analog voltages, pixel values are sent as bits over high-speed differential pairs using a method called TMDS (transition-minimised differential signalling), which encodes every 8 bits as 10 bits. There are three data pairs (one each for red, green and blue) and a clock pair. DVI-D is digital only, DVI-A analog only, and DVI-I carries both. Single-link DVI handles up to a 165 MHz pixel clock, enough for 1920 x 1200 at 60 Hz with reduced blanking. Dual-link doubles the data pairs for higher resolutions.

HDMI: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface), first released in 2002, is built on the same TMDS signalling as DVI, so a simple passive adapter connects HDMI to DVI-D. HDMI adds digital audio in the same cable, a smaller connector, HDCP copy protection used by streaming services and Blu-ray players, and CEC, which lets one remote control the TV and set-top box together. Versions keep raising the speed: HDMI 1.4 carries up to 10.2 gigabits per second, HDMI 2.0 up to 18 gigabits per second, enough for 4K at 60 Hz, and HDMI 2.1 up to 48 gigabits per second using a new packet method, enough for 4K at 120 Hz and 8K at 60 Hz with compression. HDMI is the standard on TVs, set-top boxes and game consoles.

DisplayPort: DisplayPort, from VESA (a display industry group) in 2006, was designed for computers. It sends data as packets over up to four lanes, a bit like PCI Express, rather than one pair per colour. It supports high resolutions and refresh rates, carries audio, and can drive several monitors from one port by daisy chaining them, called Multi-Stream Transport (MST). DisplayPort 1.4 carries up to 32.4 gigabits per second raw, and DisplayPort 2.0 and 2.1 go up to 80. Laptops use an internal version called eDP (embedded DisplayPort) to connect the motherboard to their own screen.

USB-C carrying video: Many laptops and phones output video through USB-C. They use DisplayPort Alternate Mode: some of the high-speed wire pairs in the USB-C cable are switched to carry DisplayPort signals instead of USB data. Thunderbolt and USB4 can also carry DisplayPort. A USB-C to HDMI adapter contains a small chip that converts DisplayPort into HDMI. This is why one USB-C port on a laptop can charge, transfer data and drive a monitor at the same time, if the laptop supports it.

Bandwidth worked example, Full HD: Standard 1080p at 60 Hz uses a total frame of 2200 x 1125 pixel times including blanking. Pixel clock = 2200 x 1125 x 60 = 148.5 million pixels per second. At 24 bits per pixel that is 148.5 million x 24 = about 3.56 gigabits per second of pixel data. TMDS sends 10 bits for every 8, so on the wire it is about 4.46 gigabits per second, spread over three data pairs, about 1.49 gigabits per second each. That fits easily in old HDMI.

Bandwidth worked example, 4K: 4K at 60 Hz uses a total of 4400 x 2250 pixel times. 4400 x 2250 x 60 = 594 million pixels per second. x 24 bits = about 14.3 gigabits per second, and with TMDS encoding about 17.8 gigabits per second. That is why 4K at 60 Hz needs HDMI 2.0 (18 gigabits per second) and why an old HDMI 1.4 cable or port can only manage 4K at 30 Hz. The maths explains the label.

Real-life example 1, the classroom projector: A teacher in a college in Bogura has a modern laptop with only HDMI and USB-C, but the room's projector has VGA. She uses an HDMI to VGA adapter. Because HDMI is digital and VGA is analog, the adapter contains a small chip, a digital-to-analog converter, powered from the HDMI port. It reads the EDID of the projector through the I2C lines so the laptop picks a resolution the projector supports, like 1024 x 768. Without the EDID, the laptop might send a resolution the projector cannot show, and the screen stays blank.

Real-life example 2, a video editor's two monitors: A video editor in a Dhaka production house connects two 4K monitors to his PC. The graphics card has DisplayPort and HDMI outputs. He uses DisplayPort for the 4K 60 Hz monitor because it has plenty of bandwidth, and a modern HDMI 2.0 cable for the second. When he first used an old HDMI cable, the second screen was stuck at 30 Hz and the mouse felt laggy. After reading the cable's label, he bought a certified high-speed cable and the problem went away.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget blanking when calculating pixel clock or bandwidth. They think VGA is digital; it is analog RGB with separate sync. They think HDMI and DVI are completely unrelated; HDMI uses the same TMDS signalling and can be adapted passively to DVI-D. They confuse tearing (two frames in one refresh) with stutter (frames shown unevenly). Exams ask: calculate the pixel clock and data rate for a given mode, compare VGA, DVI, HDMI and DisplayPort, explain EDID and DDC, explain double buffering and vsync, and describe the job of the display controller.

Recap: The GPU draws frames into a frame buffer, and its display controller scans it out many times per second with blanking and sync. Double buffering and vsync prevent tearing; variable refresh rate matches the screen to the GPU. VGA sends analog RGB with separate sync on a 15-pin connector. DVI and HDMI send digital pixels with TMDS encoding (8 bits as 10), HDMI adding audio, HDCP and CEC. DisplayPort sends packets over lanes and can daisy chain monitors, and USB-C can carry it. EDID over the I2C-based DDC tells the computer what the monitor supports. Next lesson, we build tiny displays ourselves: LEDs, 7-segment displays and character LCDs on a microcontroller.
key_points: The GPU draws frames into the frame buffer; the display controller scans it out at the refresh rate with blanking and sync.
Double buffering (front and back buffers) swapped during vertical blanking (vsync) prevents tearing; VRR lets the screen wait for each frame.
Pixel clock = total width x total height (including blanking) x refresh rate.
VGA is analog RGB with separate H and V sync on a 15-pin connector.
DVI and HDMI send digital pixels using TMDS (8 bits sent as 10); HDMI adds audio, HDCP and CEC.
DisplayPort sends packets over up to four lanes, supports daisy chaining (MST), and can run through USB-C Alternate Mode.
EDID, read over the I2C-based DDC lines, tells the computer the monitor's supported resolutions.
lessons.tip: When you see a resolution and refresh rate, always ask: what is the total frame including blanking? Using visible pixels only gives an answer about 15 to 30 percent too low.
lessons.task: Check what video ports your laptop or desktop has and what your monitor, TV or a nearby projector accepts. Then calculate the pixel data rate (visible pixels only) for your screen's resolution at 24 bits and its refresh rate, and decide which of HDMI 1.4 (10.2 Gbps) or HDMI 2.0 (18 Gbps) would be needed.

quiz.q: What causes screen tearing?
options: The frame buffer changing while it is being scanned out
quiz.explain: If a new frame is written mid-scan, part of the screen shows the old frame and part the new one.

quiz.q: VGA sends colour information as:
options: Three analog voltages for red, green and blue
quiz.explain: VGA is analog RGB, with separate horizontal and vertical sync wires.

quiz.q: A video mode has a total frame of 2200 x 1125 at 60 Hz. What is the pixel clock?
quiz.explain: 2200 x 1125 x 60 = 148,500,000 pixels per second.

quiz.q: How does a computer learn which resolutions a monitor supports?
options: By reading the monitor's EDID over the DDC (I2C) lines
quiz.explain: The monitor stores EDID data, which the computer reads over the I2C-based DDC channel.

quiz.q: Which interface can daisy chain several monitors from one port using MST?
quiz.explain: DisplayPort's Multi-Stream Transport carries several video streams through a chain of monitors.

lessons.title: Small Displays on a Microcontroller: LEDs, 7-Segment and Character LCDs
lessons.content:
Look at the token display in a bank, the digital scale at a mudi shop, the timer on a microwave oven, or the price board at a petrol pump. None of them has a big colour screen. They use simple LEDs, glowing number segments or small text LCDs, driven by a tiny microcontroller. These are often the first displays an engineering student builds in a lab, and they teach real interfacing skills: calculating resistors, saving pins with multiplexing, and following a device's exact timing rules.

The humble LED: An LED (light-emitting diode) lights up when current flows through it in the forward direction, from the anode (longer leg) to the cathode (shorter leg, flat side). It has a forward voltage, the voltage dropped across it when lit: about 1.8 to 2.2 volts for red, yellow and some green LEDs, and about 3 volts for blue and white. A typical small indicator LED is happy at 5 to 20 milliamps. Too much current and it burns out in an instant.

Why the resistor is not optional: An LED does not limit its own current. Connect it straight to a 5 volt pin and the current shoots up until something is damaged, the LED or the microcontroller pin. So we add a series resistor. Using Ohm's law: R = (Vsupply - Vforward) / I. For a red LED (2 volts) on a 5 volt pin at 15 milliamps: R = (5 - 2) / 0.015 = 200 ohms. Resistors come in standard values, so we pick the next one up, 220 ohms, which gives about 13.6 milliamps. For the same LED on a 3.3 volt board at 10 milliamps: R = (3.3 - 2) / 0.010 = 130 ohms, so choose 150 ohms.

Respect the pin limits: A microcontroller pin can only supply or absorb a limited current. Many common chips are comfortable with about 20 milliamps per pin, and there is also a limit for the whole chip together. Always check the datasheet. If you need more current, for a bright LED strip or many LEDs, use a transistor as a switch, which we will see in lesson 23.

Sourcing and sinking: There are two ways to wire an LED to a pin. In current sourcing, the pin goes to the resistor and LED, and the LED's cathode goes to ground; writing 1 (high) turns it on. In current sinking, the LED's anode goes to the supply through the resistor, and its cathode goes to the pin; writing 0 (low) turns it on. Both work. Many chips can sink current a little better than they can source it, which is why active-low LEDs are common.

The 7-segment display: A 7-segment display has seven bar-shaped LEDs labelled a to g, arranged like the number 8, plus often a dot (dp). Segment a is the top bar, then b and c go clockwise down the right side, d is the bottom, e and f go up the left side, and g is the middle bar. Lighting the right combination shows any digit from 0 to 9 and some letters like A, b, C, d, E and F, which is handy for hexadecimal.

Common cathode and common anode: To save pins, all seven LEDs share one connection. In a common cathode display, all cathodes are joined and go to ground; you light a segment by driving its pin high. In a common anode display, all anodes are joined to the supply; you light a segment by driving its pin low. Using the wrong type gives an inverted, garbled display, so always check which you have.

Segment codes: Put segments into one byte in the order dp, g, f, e, d, c, b, a (bit 7 to bit 0). For a common cathode display, the digit 0 needs a, b, c, d, e and f on and g off, which is 0011 1111 = 3F hex. Digit 1 needs only b and c: 0000 0110 = 06 hex. Digit 8 needs all seven: 0111 1111 = 7F hex. Digit 7 is a, b, c: 07 hex. For a common anode display, invert every bit: 0 becomes C0 hex. A program usually keeps a small lookup table of the ten codes and indexes it with the digit.

BCD decoder chips: If you do not want to store a table, a decoder chip can do it in hardware. You feed it a 4-bit BCD number on four pins, and it lights the right segments. The 7447 is a classic decoder for common anode displays, with active-low outputs, and the CD4511 is a common one for common cathode displays. This saves microcontroller pins too: 4 inputs instead of 7.

Multiplexing several digits: A 4-digit display wired separately would need 4 x 8 = 32 segment pins. Instead, multiplexing connects the same segment of all four digits together, so there are just 8 shared segment lines, plus one common line per digit, 12 pins in total. The trick is to turn on only one digit at a time. The microcontroller puts the pattern for digit 1 on the segment lines and switches digit 1 on, waits a couple of milliseconds, switches it off, puts the pattern for digit 2 on the lines, switches digit 2 on, and so on, round and round.

Persistence of vision: Your eyes keep seeing a light for a short moment after it turns off. If the whole display is cycled fast enough, at least about 50 to 100 times per second, all four digits seem to glow steadily at the same time, even though only one is ever lit. With 4 digits and 3 milliseconds each, one full cycle takes 12 milliseconds, about 83 times per second, which looks steady. Because each digit is on only a quarter of the time, it is dimmer, so designers often use a little more current, within the LED's pulse limits. Each digit's common line usually goes through a transistor, because a whole digit with all segments lit can draw more current than a pin can handle.

Doing it in code: In pseudo-code, a timer interrupt every 3 milliseconds runs: turn off current digit; current = (current + 1) mod 4; set segment lines = table[value[current]]; turn on digit current. The main program only changes the value array, for example to show a new score or price. Moving the refresh into a timer interrupt keeps the display steady even while the main program is busy.

LED matrices: The same idea scales to an 8 x 8 dot matrix, which has 64 LEDs but only 16 lines (8 rows and 8 columns). You light one row at a time with the right column pattern and scan quickly. Scrolling message boards in shops and buses are built from many such matrices. Special driver chips handle the scanning and talk to the microcontroller over a simple serial interface, so the main chip does not have to refresh every LED itself.

The 16x2 character LCD: For text, the classic choice is a character LCD with 2 lines of 16 characters, controlled by the HD44780 chip or a compatible one. It has 16 pins: 1 ground, 2 supply (5 volts), 3 contrast (V0, usually from a potentiometer), 4 RS (register select), 5 R/W (read or write), 6 E (enable), 7 to 14 the data lines D0 to D7, and 15 and 16 for the backlight LED (anode and cathode). The controller has a built-in character ROM, so you send the ASCII code 65 and it draws an A. You do not handle individual pixels.

Commands and data: The RS pin chooses what you are sending. RS = 0 means a command, RS = 1 means a character to display. You put the byte on the data lines, then pulse E from high to low; the LCD reads the byte on that falling edge. Common commands are 01 hex (clear display), 0C hex (display on, cursor off), 06 hex (move the cursor right after each character), 38 hex (8-bit mode, 2 lines, 5 x 8 dots) and 80 hex plus an address to move the cursor. The first line starts at address 00 and the second line at 40 hex, so command C0 hex jumps to the start of line 2. Some commands, like clear, take over a millisecond, so the program must wait before sending the next one.

4-bit mode: To save pins, the HD44780 can run in 4-bit mode using only D4 to D7. Each byte is sent as two halves: first the high nibble, then the low nibble, each with its own E pulse. With RS, E and four data lines, and R/W tied to ground for write-only use, the LCD needs just 6 microcontroller pins. Many students also use a small I2C adapter board on the back of the LCD, which brings it down to just the two I2C wires.

Custom characters: The HD44780 has a small RAM where you can design up to 8 of your own characters, each 5 dots wide and 8 rows tall. This is how hobbyists show a battery icon, a degree symbol, or even a few simple Bangla letters on an LCD that only knows English characters in its ROM.

Real-life example 1, a bank token display: At a bank branch in Narayanganj, the token number above each counter is a 3-digit 7-segment display. A microcontroller multiplexes the three digits from a timer interrupt and receives the next token number from the counter's button or the queue software. Large digits need more current than a pin can give, so each segment line and digit line goes through a transistor driver. The design is simple, cheap and readable from across the hall.

Real-life example 2, a student's digital thermometer: A first-year project in Rajshahi University uses a temperature sensor, a microcontroller and a 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode. Line 1 shows Temp: 31.5 with a custom degree symbol, and line 2 shows the highest and lowest readings of the day. The students first see nothing but black boxes, then learn that the contrast potentiometer on pin 3 needs adjusting, the most famous 16x2 beginner problem.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the current-limiting resistor, mixing up common anode and common cathode, and forgetting that a multiplexed digit is only on part of the time, so brightness drops. With the LCD, beginners forget to wait after slow commands, forget the contrast adjustment, or leave RS in the wrong state. Exams ask: calculate an LED resistor, give the 7-segment code for a digit for either type, explain multiplexing and persistence of vision with a pin count, describe the HD44780 pins, and explain 4-bit mode.

Recap: An LED needs a series resistor: R = (Vsupply - Vforward) / I, and must stay within pin current limits. A 7-segment display lights segments a to g; common cathode needs high to light, common anode needs low, and codes like 3F hex for 0 come from a lookup table or a BCD decoder. Multiplexing shares segment lines and lights one digit at a time fast enough for persistence of vision. The HD44780 16x2 LCD takes commands (RS = 0) and characters (RS = 1) latched on the E falling edge, and 4-bit mode saves pins. Next lesson, we move from screens to paper: printers.
key_points: An LED needs a series resistor: R = (Vsupply - Vforward) / I, choosing the next standard value up.
Microcontroller pins have current limits (often around 20 mA); larger loads need a transistor.
7-segment displays are common cathode (drive segment high to light) or common anode (drive low to light).
With bit order dp g f e d c b a, common cathode codes are 3F hex for 0, 06 for 1 and 7F for 8.
Multiplexing shares segment lines and lights one digit at a time, cycling at roughly 50 to 100 Hz or more for persistence of vision.
The HD44780 16x2 LCD uses RS to choose command or data and latches each byte on the falling edge of E.
4-bit mode sends each byte as two nibbles on D4 to D7, cutting the LCD to about 6 pins.
lessons.tip: Before wiring any LED or display, write down three numbers: supply voltage, LED forward voltage and the current you want. Do the resistor calculation on paper first. It takes a minute and saves components.
lessons.task: Calculate the resistor for a white LED (3.0 V) at 12 mA on a 5 V supply and on a 3.3 V supply, and pick standard values. Then write the common cathode and common anode segment codes for the digits 2, 5 and 9 using bit order dp g f e d c b a.

quiz.q: What resistor is needed for a red LED (2 V) at 15 mA on a 5 V supply?
quiz.explain: R = (5 - 2) / 0.015 = 200 ohms; in practice the next standard value, 220 ohms, is used.

quiz.q: In a common anode 7-segment display, a segment lights when its pin is:
quiz.explain: All anodes are tied to the supply, so pulling a segment's cathode low lets current flow.

quiz.q: With bit order dp g f e d c b a, what is the common cathode code for digit 1?
quiz.explain: Digit 1 lights only b and c: 0000 0110 = 06 hex.

quiz.q: How many pins does a multiplexed 4-digit 7-segment display (with dots) need?
quiz.explain: 8 shared segment lines plus 4 digit commons = 12.

quiz.q: On an HD44780 LCD, RS = 1 means the byte on the data lines is:
quiz.explain: RS = 0 selects the command register; RS = 1 selects the data register for characters.

lessons.title: Printers: Dot Matrix, Inkjet, Laser and Thermal
lessons.content:
Walk past any photocopy shop near a university gate in Bangladesh during exam season and you will hear the hum of laser printers working nonstop. At the bank counter, a noisy dot matrix printer still stamps your passbook. At the supershop, a tiny printer spits out a receipt in a second with no ink at all. These are four very different machines solving the same problem: putting marks on paper exactly where the computer wants them. In this lesson we open each one up and also see how the computer describes a page to a printer.

The printer's basic job: A printer is an output peripheral that turns a digital page into marks on paper. The computer sends a description of the page, and the printer must place tiny dots at the right spots, line by line or page by page. Two numbers describe how well it does this: resolution in DPI (dots per inch), meaning how many dots fit along one inch, and speed in PPM (pages per minute). A typical office laser printer offers 600 DPI or more and 20 to 40 pages per minute.

Impact and non-impact: Printers split into two families. Impact printers hit an ink ribbon against the paper, like an old typewriter. The dot matrix printer is the main survivor of this family. Non-impact printers put marks on paper without striking it: inkjet, laser and thermal printers. Non-impact printers are much quieter and give better quality, but impact printers have one trick they cannot match.

Dot matrix printers: A dot matrix printer has a print head with a vertical column of tiny pins, typically 9 or 24. Each pin is pushed by a small electromagnet. The head moves across the paper, and at each position the printer fires the right pins, which strike an inked ribbon against the paper and leave dots. A letter is made from a small grid of dots. More pins give finer characters. They are noisy and slow compared with modern printers and poor at pictures.

Why dot matrix printers survive: Because they physically strike the paper, they can print through several layers at once, making carbon copies or multi-part forms in one pass. Banks, courier offices, government offices and some shops still use them for passbooks, invoices and multi-copy receipts. They are also very cheap to run, since a ribbon lasts a long time, and they handle continuous fan-fold paper with holes on the sides.

Inkjet printers: An inkjet printer sprays tiny droplets of liquid ink through hundreds or thousands of microscopic nozzles in the print head as it moves across the page. Each droplet is incredibly small, measured in picolitres (a millionth of a millionth of a litre). Colour inkjets usually use four inks: cyan, magenta, yellow and black, called CMYK, and some photo printers add extra light colours.

Thermal versus piezo inkjet: There are two ways to fire a droplet. In thermal inkjet (also called bubble jet), a tiny resistor behind each nozzle heats the ink in a few microseconds, a vapour bubble forms and pushes a droplet out; when the bubble collapses, fresh ink is drawn in. In piezoelectric inkjet, a piezo crystal behind each nozzle bends when a voltage is applied, squeezing out a droplet like a tiny pump, with no heat. Different makers use different methods; piezo heads can handle a wider range of inks.

Subtractive colour, CMYK: Paper reflects light, and ink works by absorbing (subtracting) some colours. Cyan ink absorbs red, magenta absorbs green and yellow absorbs blue. Mixing cyan and yellow leaves only green reflected. Mixing all three in theory gives black, but in practice it gives a muddy brown and wastes ink, so a separate black ink (the K, from key) is used. This is the opposite of the additive RGB mixing used by screens, which is why a picture can look different on screen and on paper.

Halftoning: An inkjet or laser dot is either there or not. So how does a printer show light grey or a soft pink? It uses halftoning (or dithering): placing dots in patterns with different spacing. Dense dots look dark, sparse dots look light, and from normal distance the eye blends them. Newspapers use the same trick, which you can see with a magnifying glass on a printed photo.

Ink tank printers: Traditional inkjet printers use small cartridges that can be costly per page. Ink tank printers have large refillable bottles feeding the head through tubes, which brings the cost per page down sharply. They are very popular in Bangladesh for homes, students and small offices that print a lot of colour pages.

Laser printers, the big idea: A laser printer uses static electricity and powder. At its heart is a drum coated with a photoconductive material, which holds an electric charge in the dark but loses it where light hits it. A laser draws the page onto the drum as a pattern of charge, powdered toner sticks to that pattern, and the toner is transferred to paper and melted on. It is the same basic process used in photocopiers.

Laser printing step by step: Step 1, charging: a charge roller or corona wire gives the whole drum surface an even negative charge. Step 2, writing (exposing): a laser beam, swept across the drum by a fast-spinning mirror, switches on and off to hit the spots that should be printed, removing charge there. Step 3, developing: toner particles, which are also given a charge, stick only to the spots the laser touched. Step 4, transferring: the paper is given a charge that pulls the toner off the drum onto the paper. Step 5, fusing: the paper passes between hot rollers (around 200 degrees Celsius) that melt the toner into the paper fibres; this is why fresh laser prints are warm. Step 6, cleaning: a blade wipes leftover toner off the drum and the charge is cleared, ready for the next turn.

Laser printer facts: Laser printers are fast, sharp (600 to 1200 DPI is common), and have a low cost per page for text, which is why photocopy shops love them. Because the drum must be written for the whole page, a laser printer needs enough memory to hold a page image. Some printers use a row of LEDs instead of a laser and mirror to light the drum; they are called LED printers but work the same way. Colour laser printers repeat the process with four toners, cyan, magenta, yellow and black.

Thermal printers: A thermal printer has a print head that is a long row of tiny heating elements. In direct thermal printing, special heat-sensitive paper turns dark wherever the head heats it. There is no ink, toner or ribbon, so these printers are small, quiet and almost maintenance-free. They are used for shop receipts, ATM slips, ticket machines and card payment terminals. The downside: the print fades with time, heat and sunlight, which is why old receipts become blank. Thermal transfer printers instead melt ink from a ribbon onto normal labels, giving long-lasting barcodes for shipping labels.

How big is a page: Imagine a black and white A4 page at 600 DPI. A4 is about 8.27 x 11.69 inches, so the page is about 4,962 x 7,014 dots, about 34.8 million dots. At 1 bit per dot, that is about 4.35 million bytes, roughly 4.35 MB. A CMYK colour page needs four such planes, around 17 MB. That is why sending raw dots would be slow, and why computers usually send a compact description of the page instead.

Printer drivers and page description languages: When you click Print, the application hands the page to the operating system, which uses the printer driver to convert it into something the printer understands. Some printers accept a page description language, a small programming language that describes text, fonts, lines and pictures. The two famous ones are PostScript, created by Adobe in the 1980s, and PCL (Printer Command Language), created by HP. The printer's own processor then rasterises the page into dots. Cheaper printers leave that work to the computer and receive ready-made dot data. PDF files grew out of the PostScript idea.

Spooling: Printers are slow compared with computers, and several people may print at once. So the operating system uses a print spooler: each print job is first saved to disk in a queue, and the spooler feeds jobs to the printer one by one in the background. That is why you can close Word right after clicking Print, and why a stuck job at the top of the queue blocks everyone else's prints.

Connecting printers: Older printers used the parallel port. Today most use USB, Ethernet or Wi-Fi. Network printers have their own IP address and can be shared by a whole office. Phones can print over Wi-Fi using standard protocols, so the phone does not need a driver for each model.

3D printers, a new kind of printer: A 3D printer builds solid objects layer by layer. The most common type, FDM (fused deposition modelling), pushes a plastic filament such as PLA through a hot nozzle and lays down thin lines, one layer on top of another. Stepper motors move the nozzle and the bed with high precision, following commands in a text format called G-code. Universities and makers in Bangladesh use them for prototypes, robot parts and models.

Real-life example 1, the exam-season photocopy shop: A shop next to Dhaka University prints and photocopies thousands of pages of notes every day during exams. It uses heavy-duty laser printers because the cost per page is low and speed is high. The owner keeps spare toner cartridges and drums. When pages come out with a repeating smudge at the same spot, he knows the drum is scratched, because the drum turns several times per page and repeats the mark at regular intervals.

Real-life example 2, a mobile financial service agent: A bKash or Nagad agent shop may use a small thermal printer for transaction slips. It needs no ink, fits on a small counter, and prints in a second. The agent advises customers to photograph important slips, because thermal paper fades if kept in a hot pocket or in the sun.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix up the order of the laser printing steps, think thermal printers use ink, or confuse CMYK (subtractive, for print) with RGB (additive, for screens). They also forget that dot matrix printers survive because of multi-part forms. Exams ask: classify printers as impact or non-impact, explain thermal versus piezo inkjet, list and explain the laser printing steps in order, compare printers in a table (quality, speed, cost, noise), explain halftoning, calculate page bitmap size, and explain spooling and page description languages.

Recap: Dot matrix printers strike a ribbon with pins, are noisy and slow but can print multi-part forms. Inkjets spray picolitre droplets using heat (bubble) or a piezo crystal, and mix CMYK inks with halftoning. Laser printers charge a photoconductive drum, write it with a laser, develop it with toner, transfer it to paper and fuse it with heat. Thermal printers darken heat-sensitive paper with no ink. Drivers, page description languages like PostScript and PCL, and spoolers connect the computer to the printer. Next lesson, we look at devices that go the other way, turning paper and the world into data: scanners and cameras.
key_points: Print quality is measured in DPI and speed in PPM; printers are impact (dot matrix) or non-impact (inkjet, laser, thermal).
Dot matrix printers fire pins against an ink ribbon and can print multi-part carbon copies.
Inkjets fire picolitre droplets using a heated bubble (thermal) or a flexing piezo crystal.
Print uses subtractive CMYK colour; halftoning makes shades from patterns of dots.
Laser printing steps: charge the drum, write with the laser, develop with toner, transfer to paper, fuse with heat, clean.
Direct thermal printers darken heat-sensitive paper with no ink; prints fade over time.
Drivers, page description languages (PostScript, PCL) and the print spooler connect applications to printers.
lessons.tip: Learn the laser steps with a short memory chain: Charge, Write, Develop, Transfer, Fuse, Clean. Say it while imagining the drum turning once.
lessons.task: Find an old shop receipt and a laser-printed page. Gently warm a corner of the receipt with a hair dryer or a warm cup (not a flame) and watch it darken, proving it is direct thermal paper. Then look at a printed colour photo with a magnifying glass or phone camera zoom and identify the cyan, magenta, yellow and black dots.

quiz.q: Which printer can print carbon copies on multi-part forms in one pass?
quiz.explain: Only impact printers physically strike through several layers of paper.

quiz.q: In thermal (bubble jet) inkjet printing, a droplet is pushed out by:
options: A vapour bubble formed by heating the ink
quiz.explain: A tiny resistor heats the ink, forming a bubble that pushes a droplet out of the nozzle.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the main laser printing steps?
quiz.explain: The drum is charged, written by the laser, developed with toner, the toner is transferred to paper, then fused by heat.

quiz.q: Why do printers use CMYK instead of RGB?
options: Ink absorbs (subtracts) light, so print uses subtractive colours
RGB is only for black and white
quiz.explain: Screens add light (RGB); inks on paper subtract light, so cyan, magenta, yellow and black are used.

quiz.q: Why do old ATM and shop receipts often become blank?
options: Direct thermal paper fades with time, heat and light
quiz.explain: Direct thermal prints are a heat-triggered colour change in the paper, which fades over time.

lessons.title: Scanners, Cameras and Other Input Devices
lessons.content:
When you bought a SIM card in Bangladesh, the shop put your finger on a small glowing pad and checked it against your national ID record. When you pay at a shop, a scanner reads a QR code. When you submit a form at a government office, a clerk may scan it into a PDF. When you join a video class, a tiny camera above your screen turns your face into numbers. All of these devices do the opposite of a printer or a screen: they take light, patterns or sound from the real world and turn them into data. This lesson looks at how.

The common idea, sensing light: Most of these devices start with a light sensor called a photodiode. When light hits it, it produces a small electric charge or current, and more light gives more charge. Put millions of tiny photodiodes in a grid and you have an image sensor; put one row of them and you have the eye of a scanner. Everything else is about focusing light onto them, reading the charges out, and turning them into numbers.

The flatbed scanner: A flatbed scanner has a glass plate on which you place the page face down. Under the glass, a bar carrying a light source and a sensor moves slowly from one end to the other, driven by a stepper motor. At each small step, the sensor captures one thin line across the page. Line by line, the whole page is built up as an image, a bit like a raster scan in reverse.

CCD and CIS scanners: There are two common sensor designs. In a CCD scanner, light reflected from the page travels through a set of mirrors and a lens onto a small CCD sensor. This gives good depth of field, so slightly raised objects like a thick book spine stay in focus. In a CIS (contact image sensor) scanner, a row of sensors as wide as the page sits right under the glass, lit by LEDs, with no mirrors. CIS scanners are thinner, cheaper and use less power, which is why most low-cost and portable scanners use them, but anything not flat against the glass looks blurry.

Scanner resolution and file size: Scanner resolution is given in DPI, often as two numbers like 600 x 1200. The first comes from the number of sensor elements across the page; the second from how finely the motor steps. Be careful of very large interpolated DPI numbers in adverts: those are made by software guessing extra pixels, not by the hardware. To see file size, scan an A4 page (8.27 x 11.69 inches) at 300 DPI in 24-bit colour: about 2,481 x 3,507 pixels, roughly 8.7 million pixels, x 3 bytes is about 26 MB before compression. That is why scanned documents are usually saved as compressed JPEG or PDF, and why 200 to 300 DPI is enough for text documents.

Scanner drivers and feeders: Scanners talk to the computer usually over USB or the network, and applications reach them through a standard driver interface, such as TWAIN on Windows, so any program can request a scan. Office scanners and photocopiers often have an automatic document feeder (ADF) that pulls pages through one by one, and some scan both sides in one pass.

Image sensors, CCD versus CMOS: Cameras use a 2D grid of photodiodes. In a CCD (charge-coupled device) sensor, after exposure, the charges are shifted from pixel to pixel along the rows, like buckets of water passed down a line of people, to a single output amplifier at the corner, where they are measured one by one. CCDs gave excellent image quality and were used in early digital cameras and in scientific instruments. In a CMOS sensor (also called an active pixel sensor), each pixel has its own small amplifier, and pixels are read out by selecting rows and columns, much like reading memory. CMOS sensors use far less power, are faster, and can include the analog-to-digital converter and processing on the same chip, so almost every phone and webcam today uses CMOS.

Rolling shutter: Many CMOS sensors read the image row by row from top to bottom, which takes a short time. If something moves fast during that time, like a ceiling fan blade or a train passing, it can look bent or slanted in the photo. This is the rolling shutter effect. Sensors with a global shutter capture all rows at the same instant, which is important for machine vision and some video uses.

How a sensor sees colour, the Bayer filter: A photodiode measures only brightness, not colour. To capture colour, a tiny colour filter is placed over each pixel. The most common pattern, the Bayer filter, uses repeating 2 x 2 blocks with one red, two green and one blue filter. Green gets twice as many pixels because human eyes are most sensitive to green, which carries most of the detail we notice. Each pixel therefore knows only one colour, and the camera's processor estimates the other two colours for every pixel from its neighbours, a step called demosaicing.

Megapixels: A 12-megapixel camera has about 12 million pixels, for example 4,000 x 3,000. More megapixels allow larger prints and more cropping, but image quality also depends heavily on the size of each pixel, the lens and the processing. A small phone sensor crammed with tiny pixels can produce noisier pictures in dim light than a larger sensor with fewer, bigger pixels.

Webcams and phone cameras as peripherals: A USB webcam usually follows the USB Video Class (the Video class from lesson 9), so it works without a special driver, and streams using isochronous transfers. Inside a phone, the camera sensor connects to the main chip using a fast serial interface designed for cameras, and a dedicated image signal processor does demosaicing, noise reduction and colour correction before the photo even reaches the app.

OCR, turning pictures of text into text: A scanned page is just a picture. Optical character recognition (OCR) software turns it into real, editable text. The basic steps are: clean the image (convert to black and white, straighten a tilted scan), find lines, words and characters, recognise each character (modern systems use trained neural networks), and finally use dictionaries and language rules to fix likely mistakes. Bangla OCR is harder than English because of joined conjunct letters, vowel signs placed before, after, above or below a letter, and the headline (matra) that connects letters in a word, so it needs specially trained models.

Barcode scanners: A 1D barcode stores a number in the widths of black bars and white spaces. A laser barcode scanner sweeps a red laser line across the code, and a photodiode measures how much light reflects back: little from black bars, lots from white spaces. The timing of these changes gives the bar widths, which decode into digits. Many modern scanners are image-based instead: a small camera takes a picture of the code and software decodes it, which also lets them read 2D codes.

The EAN-13 check digit: Products in shops usually carry an EAN-13 barcode with 13 digits. The last digit is a check digit that catches most reading errors. Example: for 590123412345, add the digits in odd positions (5 + 0 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 4 = 17), add the digits in even positions (9 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 5 = 22) and multiply that by 3 (66). The total is 83. The check digit is the number that brings it up to the next multiple of 10: 90 - 83 = 7. So the full barcode is 5901234123457. If a scanner misreads one digit, the check fails and it beeps an error instead of charging the wrong product.

QR codes: A QR code is a 2D barcode, a square grid of black and white modules, invented in Japan in 1994. Three big squares in the corners, called finder patterns, let a camera find the code and work out its angle from any direction. QR codes include error correction, so even if part of the code is dirty or covered, the data can still be recovered: up to about 7, 15, 25 or 30 percent damage depending on the chosen level. In Bangladesh, payment QR codes, including the shared Bangla QR standard, let customers pay from different apps by scanning one code.

Fingerprint readers: A fingerprint has ridges and valleys, and their unique details (where ridges end or split, called minutiae) identify a person. Optical readers photograph the finger pressed on a glass prism. Capacitive readers use a grid of tiny capacitor plates; ridges touching the surface change the capacitance more than valleys, giving a map of the print. Some phones use ultrasonic readers under the screen that bounce sound off the finger. The reader does not usually store a photo; it extracts a template of minutiae and compares it with a stored template.

Microphones: A microphone turns sound, which is tiny changes in air pressure, into a changing voltage. A dynamic microphone moves a coil in a magnet's field. A condenser microphone has a thin diaphragm that forms one plate of a capacitor; as sound moves it, the capacitance and so the voltage changes. Phones use tiny MEMS microphones, which are condenser microphones built on a silicon chip. The output is analog and must be sampled by an analog-to-digital converter, which is exactly the topic of lesson 21.

Real-life example 1, SIM registration: When a customer in Cumilla buys a new SIM, the retailer uses a small fingerprint scanner connected to a phone or computer. The scanner captures the print, the software extracts a template, and it is checked against the national ID database. Only if it matches is the SIM activated. The whole chain uses an input peripheral, USB or Bluetooth interfacing, and secure network communication.

Real-life example 2, digitising old land records: A government project scans old paper land records so citizens can look them up online. Operators use scanners with automatic feeders at 300 DPI, save the pages as compressed PDFs to keep file sizes small, and run OCR so the records can be searched by name or plot number. Pages with faded ink or handwritten Bangla are the hardest, and still need people to check them.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students confuse optical DPI with interpolated DPI, think every camera pixel sees full colour (Bayer filter pixels see only one), and mix up CCD and CMOS readout. They also forget that a barcode's last digit is a check digit, not part of the product code. Exams ask: explain how a flatbed scanner works and compare CCD and CIS, compare CCD and CMOS image sensors, explain the Bayer filter and why there are two greens, compute a scan's file size, outline OCR steps, compute an EAN-13 check digit, and explain how QR codes survive damage.

Recap: Scanners and cameras convert light into charge with photodiodes. Flatbed scanners build a page line by line using CCD (with mirrors) or CIS (contact) sensors. CMOS sensors read each pixel with its own amplifier and now dominate cameras; CCDs shift charges to one output. A Bayer filter gives each pixel one colour, and demosaicing fills in the rest. OCR turns text images into text, barcodes and QR codes encode numbers with checks and error correction, fingerprint readers compare minutiae, and microphones turn sound into voltage. Next lesson, we look at where all this data is stored: the magnetic hard disk.
key_points: Photodiodes turn light into charge; image sensors are grids of them, scanners use a row.
Flatbed scanners use CCD sensors with mirrors and a lens (good depth of field) or CIS sensors right under the glass (thin and cheap).
CCD sensors shift charges to one output amplifier; CMOS sensors have an amplifier per pixel and dominate phones and webcams.
A Bayer filter gives each pixel one colour in RGGB blocks (two greens), and demosaicing estimates the rest.
OCR cleans the image, segments characters and recognises them; Bangla OCR is harder because of conjuncts and the matra line.
EAN-13 barcodes end with a check digit; QR codes have finder patterns and error correction up to about 30 percent.
Fingerprint readers (optical, capacitive, ultrasonic) compare minutiae templates; microphones turn sound pressure into voltage.
lessons.tip: For every input device, trace three steps: what physical thing it senses, what converts it to an electrical signal, and how that becomes numbers. This simple chain helps you explain any device in an exam.
lessons.task: Pick any product with a 13-digit barcode at home. Using its first 12 digits, calculate the check digit by hand (odd positions x 1, even positions x 3) and confirm it matches the 13th digit. Then cover a small corner of a QR code with your finger and see whether your phone can still read it.

quiz.q: Why does a Bayer filter have two green filters in each 2 x 2 block?
options: Human eyes are most sensitive to green
Green light is brighter than the sun
quiz.explain: Our eyes are most sensitive to green, which carries much of the detail we see, so more pixels sample it.

quiz.q: Which image sensor has an amplifier in every pixel and is used in almost all phones?
quiz.explain: CMOS active pixel sensors read each pixel with its own amplifier, using less power and allowing on-chip processing.

quiz.q: An A4 page scanned at 300 DPI in 24-bit colour is about how large before compression?
quiz.explain: About 2,481 x 3,507 pixels = 8.7 million pixels, x 3 bytes = about 26 MB.

quiz.q: The first 12 digits of an EAN-13 code give odd-position sum 20 and even-position sum 15. What is the check digit?
quiz.explain: 20 + 15 x 3 = 65; the next multiple of 10 is 70, so the check digit is 70 - 65 = 5.

quiz.q: Why can a QR code still be read when part of it is dirty?
options: It contains error correction data that can rebuild damaged parts
quiz.explain: QR codes include error correction that can recover roughly 7 to 30 percent damage depending on the level.

lessons.title: The Magnetic Hard Disk
lessons.content:
Picture an old record player, but spinning more than a hundred times every second, with a needle that never touches the record and floats on a cushion of air thinner than a speck of dust. Now imagine that needle can jump to any groove in a few thousandths of a second and read or write tiny magnetic patterns. That is a hard disk drive (HDD). SSDs have taken over laptops, but hard disks still store a huge share of the world's data in data centres, CCTV recorders and backup drives, because they give lots of space for little money. Understanding how they work also explains why they are slow at some jobs and fast at others.

The parts of a hard disk: Inside the sealed metal case are one or more platters, rigid discs made of aluminium or glass, coated with a thin magnetic layer on both sides. They are stacked on a spindle turned by a motor at a constant speed. For each surface there is a read/write head at the end of a thin arm. All arms are joined together and moved by an actuator, a voice coil motor that swings them across the platters like a fast, precise windscreen wiper. A small circuit board underneath holds the controller, a cache memory and the interface to the computer.

How bits are stored: The magnetic coating is made of tiny grains that can be magnetised in one direction or the other. The write head is a tiny electromagnet that sets the direction of a small region as the platter passes underneath. The read head senses changes in the magnetic field as regions pass by. Modern read heads use a magnetoresistive effect, whose electrical resistance changes with the magnetic field, which makes them extremely sensitive. Since about the mid-2000s, drives have used perpendicular recording, with the magnetic regions standing up and down instead of lying flat, which packs bits more tightly.

The flying head: The head does not touch the platter. As the platter spins, it drags a thin layer of air (or helium, in some high-capacity drives) along with it, and the head's slider rides on this cushion just a few nanometres above the surface. This is why hard disks hate shocks. A strong knock while running can make the head touch the surface, a head crash, which scratches the coating and destroys data. When the drive stops, the heads are parked on a ramp off the platters or on a special landing zone.

Protecting the heads: Many laptops with hard disks contain a small motion sensor, an accelerometer. If it feels the laptop falling, it tells the drive to park its heads within a fraction of a second, before the laptop hits the floor. Portable external hard disks are still fragile, though. Dropping one while it is running, or moving a desktop PC while its disk is busy, is a common reason data recovery shops in Bangladesh get so much work.

Tracks, sectors and cylinders: Each surface is divided into concentric circles called tracks, like the rings of a tree, but there are hundreds of thousands of them. Each track is divided into sectors, the smallest unit the drive reads or writes. For decades a sector held 512 bytes of data; modern drives use 4,096-byte sectors, called Advanced Format. A cylinder is the set of tracks at the same position on all surfaces; because all heads move together, the drive can read a whole cylinder without moving the arm.

Zoned bit recording: An outer track is much longer than an inner one. Old drives put the same number of sectors on every track, wasting space on the outside. Modern drives use zoned bit recording: the surface is divided into zones, and outer zones have more sectors per track. Since the platter spins at a constant speed, more sectors pass under the head per second on the outer tracks, so data transfer is faster at the start of the disk (outer edge) than at the end (inner edge).

RPM and rotational speed: Drives spin at fixed speeds, given in RPM (revolutions per minute). Common speeds are 5,400 RPM for laptop and low-power drives, 7,200 RPM for desktop drives, and 10,000 or 15,000 RPM for older enterprise drives. Faster spinning means less waiting for the right sector, but more heat, noise and power.

The three parts of access time: To read a random sector, the drive must do three things. First, seek: move the arm to the right track. Average seek time is a few milliseconds, typically around 8 to 12 for desktop drives. Second, rotational latency: wait for the right sector to spin round under the head. On average this is half a revolution. Third, transfer: actually read the bits as they pass under the head. Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time, plus a small controller overhead.

Rotational latency worked: A 7,200 RPM drive turns 7,200 / 60 = 120 times per second, so one revolution takes 1 / 120 second = 8.33 milliseconds. Average rotational latency is half of that: about 4.17 milliseconds. For 5,400 RPM: 90 revolutions per second, 11.1 milliseconds per revolution, average latency about 5.56 milliseconds. For 15,000 RPM: 250 per second, 4 milliseconds per revolution, average latency 2 milliseconds.

Full access time example: A 7,200 RPM drive has an average seek time of 9 milliseconds and a transfer rate of 150 MB per second. How long to read one random 4 KB block? Seek is 9 milliseconds. Rotational latency is 4.17 milliseconds. Transfer time is 4,096 bytes / 150,000,000 bytes per second = about 0.027 milliseconds. Total: about 13.2 milliseconds. Notice the transfer itself is tiny; almost all the time is mechanical waiting. So the drive can do only about 1,000 / 13.2 = about 75 random reads per second.

Sequential versus random: If instead you read a big file whose sectors lie one after another on the same tracks, the drive seeks once and then streams data at full speed, perhaps 150 to 250 MB per second for a modern drive. That is why hard disks are fine for copying big videos or backups, but feel very slow when booting an operating system or opening many small files scattered around the disk. This single fact explains most of the speed difference people notice between HDD and SSD computers.

Capacity calculation: Capacity = number of surfaces x tracks per surface x sectors per track x bytes per sector. Example: 4 platters give 8 surfaces. With 100,000 tracks per surface, an average of 1,000 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector: 8 x 100,000 x 1,000 x 512 = 409,600,000,000 bytes, about 409.6 GB. Real drives today reach many terabytes using very high densities and up to around ten platters in a helium-filled case.

GB versus GiB, the missing space mystery: Drive makers count in powers of ten: 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Windows traditionally reports sizes in powers of two: 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes, but labels it GB. So a 1 TB drive shows as about 1,000,000,000,000 / 1,073,741,824 = about 931 GB in Windows. Nothing is missing; the units are different.

CHS and LBA addressing: Early PCs addressed a sector by its Cylinder, Head and Sector numbers (CHS), with sectors numbered from 1. This exposed the disk's geometry and ran into limits as drives grew. Modern systems use LBA (logical block addressing): sectors are simply numbered 0, 1, 2 and so on, and the drive's controller works out where each one physically lives. The conversion is LBA = (C x heads + H) x sectors_per_track + (S - 1). For example, with 16 heads and 63 sectors per track, C = 2, H = 3, S = 4 gives (2 x 16 + 3) x 63 + 3 = 2,208.

Partitions, MBR and GPT: The first sector of a disk traditionally held the Master Boot Record (MBR), with a small partition table. MBR uses 32-bit sector numbers, so with 512-byte sectors it can address at most 2 to the power 32 x 512 bytes = 2 TiB. Larger disks use the newer GUID Partition Table (GPT), which uses 64-bit addresses and is required for booting with modern UEFI firmware.

Drive cache and scheduling: The drive's circuit board has a cache, often tens to a few hundred megabytes, which holds recently read data and data waiting to be written, and reads ahead in case you want the next sectors. Drives and operating systems also reorder pending requests to reduce arm movement; you may meet algorithms like shortest seek time first and the elevator algorithm in the Operating Systems course.

Fragmentation: When files are created and deleted for months, a file's pieces may end up scattered across the disk. Reading it then needs many seeks. Defragmentation moves pieces together so files are stored in order. This helps hard disks noticeably. It is pointless for SSDs, which have no moving parts, as we will see next lesson.

Real-life example 1, CCTV in a shopping mall: A shopping mall in Chattogram records 32 CCTV cameras around the clock. Its recorder uses several large hard disks, because storing weeks of video on SSDs would cost far more. Video is written in long, steady streams, which suits a hard disk's strong sequential speed. Special surveillance drives are designed for this nonstop writing.

Real-life example 2, the slow office computer: A government office computer with a 5,400 RPM hard disk takes three minutes to start and freezes when opening files.
