Booting reads thousands of small files scattered across the disk, and each random read costs over 10 milliseconds of seeking and waiting. A technician from Nilkhet replaces it with a small SSD for the operating system and keeps the old disk for archives. The computer now starts in under a minute, though the CPU and RAM are unchanged.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget to divide RPM by 60, forget that average rotational latency is half a revolution, or mix up milliseconds and microseconds in transfer time. They also confuse tracks with cylinders and think the head touches the platter. Exams ask: label the parts of an HDD, define track, sector and cylinder, calculate rotational latency and access time, calculate capacity, convert CHS to LBA, explain why random access is slow, and explain GB versus GiB.

Recap: A hard disk stores bits as magnetised regions on spinning platters, read and written by heads flying nanometres above the surface. Surfaces are divided into tracks and sectors, and a cylinder is the same track on every surface. Access time = seek time + rotational latency (half a revolution on average) + transfer time, and random access is dominated by mechanical waiting. Capacity = surfaces x tracks x sectors x bytes per sector. LBA numbers sectors simply, MBR is limited to 2 TiB, and GPT handles larger disks. Next lesson, we look at the interfaces that connect storage and at the SSD, which has no moving parts at all.
key_points: An HDD has spinning magnetic platters and read/write heads on an actuator arm that fly nanometres above the surface.
Surfaces are divided into tracks and sectors (512 or 4,096 bytes); a cylinder is the same track on all surfaces.
Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time; random reads are dominated by mechanical delay.
Average rotational latency = half a revolution = 0.5 x 60 / RPM seconds (about 4.17 ms at 7,200 RPM).
Capacity = surfaces x tracks per surface x sectors per track x bytes per sector.
LBA numbers sectors from 0; CHS to LBA: (C x heads + H) x sectors per track + (S - 1).
A 1 TB drive shows about 931 GB in Windows because makers use powers of ten and Windows uses powers of two.
lessons.tip: For every disk timing question, write three lines: seek, rotation (half a turn), transfer. Fill each in milliseconds and add. Most mistakes disappear when you keep units in milliseconds throughout.
lessons.task: Find the RPM and capacity of a hard disk you have or one sold online. Calculate its average rotational latency, and assuming 10 ms average seek and 160 MB/s transfer, calculate the time to read one random 4 KB block and one 1 GB file stored sequentially. Then work out how many GB Windows would show for its capacity.

quiz.q: What is the average rotational latency of a 7,200 RPM disk?
quiz.explain: 7,200 / 60 = 120 revolutions per second, so one turn is 8.33 ms; the average wait is half a turn, about 4.17 ms.

quiz.q: What is a cylinder in a hard disk?
options: The set of tracks at the same position on all surfaces
The motor that spins the platters
quiz.explain: All heads move together, so a cylinder is the group of tracks that can be read without moving the arm.

quiz.q: Why are random small reads slow on a hard disk?
options: Most of the time is spent seeking and waiting for rotation
quiz.explain: Transfer of a small block takes microseconds, but seek and rotation take milliseconds.

quiz.q: 8 surfaces, 50,000 tracks per surface, 500 sectors per track, 512 bytes per sector. What is the capacity?
Why does a new 1 TB disk show about 931 GB in Windows?
options: The partition table uses the missing space
Makers count in powers of ten, Windows in powers of two

lessons.title: Storage Interfaces, SSDs, Flash Cards, Optical Discs and RAID
lessons.content:
Ten years ago, a typical laptop took a minute or two to start. Today many start in a few seconds. The CPU got faster, but the biggest change was storage: the spinning hard disk was replaced by an SSD, which has no moving parts at all. At the same time, the cables changed from wide grey ribbons to thin SATA cables to no cable at all, with the drive plugged straight into a PCI Express slot. In this lesson we follow both stories: the interfaces that connect storage, and the flash memory inside SSDs, pen drives and memory cards. We finish with optical discs and RAID.

PATA, the old ribbon: From the late 1980s, PC hard disks and CD drives connected using ATA, later called Parallel ATA (PATA) or IDE. A wide 40-pin flat ribbon cable carried 16 data bits in parallel. Each cable could hold two devices, set as master and slave using small jumpers. The fastest version reached 133 MB per second. The wide cables blocked airflow inside the case, and parallel signals hit the skew limits we studied in lesson 6.

SATA: Serial ATA (SATA), introduced in 2003, replaced the ribbon with a thin 7-pin cable carrying two differential pairs, one in each direction, plus a separate power connector. Each drive gets its own link to the controller, so there is no master and slave. Speeds went from 1.5 to 3 to 6 gigabits per second. SATA uses 8b/10b encoding, so 6 gigabits per second gives at most 600 MB per second of data. SATA supports hot plugging and Native Command Queuing (NCQ), which lets the drive receive up to 32 commands and reorder them to reduce head movement.

AHCI, the software side: Under SATA sits a standard controller interface called AHCI, which the operating system uses to talk to SATA controllers. It was designed with spinning disks in mind: one command queue with up to 32 commands. That was plenty for a disk that can do around a hundred random operations per second, but it became a bottleneck for SSDs.

SAS for servers: Servers often use SAS (Serial Attached SCSI). It looks similar to SATA but is built for heavy work: higher speeds such as 12 gigabits per second, two ports per drive so it can stay reachable if one path fails, and support for long cables and many drives. SAS controllers can usually also run SATA drives, but not the other way round.

NVMe: When SSDs got fast, SATA's 600 MB per second and AHCI's single queue became the limit. NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is a protocol designed for flash memory that runs directly over PCI Express. It supports up to about 65,000 queues, each with up to about 65,000 commands, so many CPU cores can send requests in parallel without waiting on each other. An NVMe SSD on PCIe 3.0 x4 reaches about 3,500 MB per second, and PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 drives go much higher.

M.2 is a shape, not a speed: Most laptop SSDs today are small M.2 sticks, often 22 mm wide and 80 mm long, called 2280. But M.2 is only the physical shape. An M.2 drive can use SATA (up to about 600 MB per second) or NVMe over PCIe (thousands of MB per second). The notches on the connector, called keys, and the laptop's manual tell you which it supports. This is the same lesson as USB-C: the connector does not tell you the speed.

Inside an SSD, NAND flash: An SSD stores data in NAND flash memory chips. Each cell is a transistor that can trap electrons in an insulated layer. Trapped charge changes the voltage at which the transistor turns on, and the controller reads that threshold to decide what the cell stores. No power is needed to keep the charge, so data stays when the computer is off. A controller chip, often with its own DRAM cache, manages everything and speaks NVMe or SATA to the computer.

SLC, MLC, TLC and QLC: A cell can store more than one bit by using several charge levels. SLC stores 1 bit (2 levels), MLC 2 bits (4 levels), TLC 3 bits (8 levels) and QLC 4 bits (16 levels). More bits per cell means more capacity per chip and lower cost, but the levels are closer together, so reading and writing take more care, writes are slower, and cells wear out sooner. Most consumer SSDs use TLC or QLC, often with part of the flash working in faster SLC mode as a write cache.

Pages and blocks, the big flash rule: Flash is read and written in pages, often a few to sixteen kilobytes. But it can only be erased in much larger blocks, each containing hundreds of pages. And a page cannot be overwritten directly; it must be erased first. So when you change a small part of a file, the SSD writes the new data into a fresh empty page and marks the old page as invalid. Later, a background task called garbage collection copies the still-valid pages out of a mostly-invalid block, then erases the whole block to make it fresh again.

The flash translation layer: Because data keeps moving, the logical block address that the operating system uses (LBA, from last lesson) no longer matches a fixed physical place. The SSD controller keeps a mapping table, the flash translation layer (FTL), that records where each logical block currently lives. To the computer, the SSD looks like a simple numbered list of blocks, just like a hard disk.

Wear levelling and endurance: Each flash block can only be erased a limited number of times before it wears out, typically in the thousands for common consumer types. If one block were rewritten constantly, it would die early. Wear levelling spreads writes evenly over all blocks. SSDs also keep spare hidden space, called over-provisioning, to replace worn blocks and help garbage collection. Makers state endurance as TBW (terabytes written), for example 600 TBW for a 1 TB drive, which is more than most home users write in many years.

TRIM: When you delete a file, the operating system normally only marks the space as free in its own records; the SSD does not know those pages are now useless and would keep copying them during garbage collection. The TRIM command (called deallocate in NVMe) lets the operating system tell the SSD exactly which blocks are no longer needed, so it can erase them in advance. This keeps write speed high and reduces wear. Defragmenting an SSD is unnecessary and only adds wear, because there is no seek time to save.

SSD versus HDD numbers: A hard disk needs around 10 milliseconds for a random read; an SSD needs well under a tenth of a millisecond, often tens of microseconds. A hard disk manages about a hundred random reads per second; a good NVMe SSD can manage hundreds of thousands. SSDs are silent, light, shock-resistant and use less power. Hard disks still win on price per terabyte, which is why they remain in bulk storage and backups.

Pen drives and memory cards: USB flash drives and SD and microSD cards use the same NAND flash with a simpler, cheaper controller, usually with less wear levelling and no DRAM cache, so they are slower and less durable than SSDs. SD cards carry speed marks: Class 10 and U1 guarantee at least 10 MB per second sequential writing, U3 and V30 at least 30 MB per second, important for recording video in phones and cameras. Many are formatted with FAT32, which cannot store a single file larger than 4 GB, which is why copying a big movie may fail until the drive is reformatted as exFAT or NTFS.

Optical discs: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs store data as tiny pits and flat areas called lands along a single spiral track. A laser shines on the track and a sensor measures the reflection; changes between pit and land mark the bits. Shorter laser wavelengths make a smaller spot, so data can be packed more tightly. A CD uses a 780 nanometre infrared laser and holds about 700 MB; a DVD uses a 650 nanometre red laser and holds 4.7 GB per layer; a Blu-ray disc uses a 405 nanometre blue-violet laser and holds 25 GB per layer. Writable discs use a dye layer that the laser darkens, and rewritable ones use a phase-change material. Optical drives are rare in new PCs but discs are still used for some archives and software.

RAID: RAID (redundant array of independent disks) combines several drives for speed, safety or both. RAID 0 (striping) splits data across drives for speed, but if any one drive fails, everything is lost. RAID 1 (mirroring) writes the same data to two drives, so either can fail safely, but you get only half the total space. RAID 5 stripes data and spreads parity across at least three drives; it survives one drive failure and gives the space of n - 1 drives. For example, four 2 TB drives in RAID 5 give 6 TB usable. RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping. Remember: RAID protects against a drive failing, not against deleting a file, a virus or a fire. It is not a backup.

Real-life example 1, upgrading a student laptop: A student in Khulna has a slow laptop with a 1 TB 5,400 RPM hard disk. A shop at the local computer market checks the manual and finds an empty M.2 slot that supports NVMe. They install a 512 GB NVMe SSD, move Windows onto it, and keep the hard disk for movies and backups. Boot time drops from two minutes to about fifteen seconds. If the slot had been SATA only, a SATA M.2 SSD would still help hugely, though with lower peak speed.

Real-life example 2, a small office file server: An accounting firm in Motijheel keeps client files on a small network storage box with four hard disks in RAID 5. One morning a drive fails; the box beeps but keeps working, and the files stay available. The technician replaces the drive and the array rebuilds. But the firm also keeps a weekly backup on a separate drive at the owner's home, because a fire, theft or a ransomware attack would destroy all four disks at once.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students think M.2 always means NVMe, that RAID is a backup, or that SSDs can overwrite a page in place. They forget SATA's 8b/10b encoding when converting 6 gigabits per second to MB per second. Exams ask: compare PATA, SATA, SAS and NVMe, explain why NVMe is faster than AHCI, explain pages and blocks, garbage collection, wear levelling and TRIM, compare SLC to QLC, compare SSD and HDD, compute RAID capacities, and explain how laser wavelength affects optical disc capacity.

Recap: Storage moved from parallel PATA ribbons to serial SATA links (up to 600 MB per second), SAS in servers, and NVMe over PCI Express with many deep queues. M.2 is a shape that may carry SATA or NVMe. SSDs store charge in NAND cells (SLC to QLC), read and write pages but erase whole blocks, and use an FTL, garbage collection, wear levelling and TRIM to stay fast and last long. Pen drives and SD cards use simpler flash controllers. Optical discs store pits on a spiral read by lasers of shorter and shorter wavelength. RAID combines drives for speed or redundancy but is not a backup. Next lesson, we cross from the digital world to the analog one: ADCs and DACs.
key_points: PATA used wide parallel ribbons (up to 133 MB/s); SATA uses thin serial links up to 6 Gbit/s, about 600 MB/s after 8b/10b.
NVMe runs over PCI Express with up to about 65,000 deep queues, unlike AHCI's single 32-command queue.
M.2 is a physical shape that can carry either SATA or NVMe.
NAND flash cells store 1 (SLC) to 4 (QLC) bits; more bits mean cheaper but slower and less durable.
Flash reads and writes pages but erases whole blocks; garbage collection and the FTL manage moved data.
Wear levelling spreads writes; TRIM tells the SSD which blocks are free; defragmenting SSDs is unnecessary.
RAID 0 stripes, RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 gives n - 1 drives of space and survives one failure; RAID is not a backup.
lessons.tip: Separate three ideas whenever you see a storage product: the shape (2.5 inch, M.2), the link (SATA, PCIe) and the protocol (AHCI, NVMe). Most confusion comes from mixing these up.
lessons.task: On your computer, find out whether your drive is HDD or SSD and which interface it uses (Windows: Task Manager, Performance, Disk; or Device Manager; Mac: System Information, Storage). Then calculate usable space for five 4 TB drives in RAID 0, RAID 1 (as two mirrored pairs, ignoring the fifth) and RAID 5.

quiz.q: What is the maximum data rate of SATA III (6 Gbit/s) after 8b/10b encoding?
quiz.explain: Only 8 of every 10 bits are data: 6,000 Mbit/s x 0.8 / 8 = 600 MB/s.

quiz.q: Why can't an SSD simply overwrite a page in place?
options: Flash pages must be erased first, and erasing works only on whole blocks
quiz.explain: Flash cells must be erased before rewriting, and erase happens at block level, so new data goes to a fresh page.

quiz.q: What does the TRIM command do?
options: Tells the SSD which blocks no longer hold useful data
quiz.explain: TRIM lets the SSD erase unneeded blocks in advance, keeping writes fast and reducing wear.

quiz.q: Four 2 TB drives are set up as RAID 5. How much usable space is there?
quiz.explain: RAID 5 uses one drive's worth of space for parity: (4 - 1) x 2 TB = 6 TB.

quiz.q: Why does a Blu-ray disc hold more data than a DVD?
options: Its shorter wavelength laser makes a smaller spot, so data can be packed tighter
quiz.explain: Blu-ray uses a 405 nm laser versus 650 nm for DVD, allowing smaller pits and tighter tracks.

lessons.title: ADC and DAC: Crossing Between Analog and Digital
lessons.content:
The real world is smooth. Temperature in Dhaka rises gradually through the morning, not in jumps. Your voice is a smooth wave of air pressure. The weight of rice on a scale can be any amount. But a computer only understands numbers, in fixed steps. Every time a phone records your voice, a digital scale weighs fish at Karwan Bazar, or a thermometer shows 31.4 degrees, a chip called an ADC (analog-to-digital converter) is turning the smooth world into numbers. And every time music plays from your earphones, a DAC (digital-to-analog converter) turns numbers back into a smooth signal. This lesson explains both.

Analog and digital signals: An analog signal can take any value in a range and changes smoothly, like the voltage from a microphone that might be 0.312 volts, then 0.318 volts, then 0.325 volts. A digital signal has only a fixed set of values, and is usually stored as binary numbers. To bring an analog signal into a computer, we must do two things: sample it (measure it only at certain moments) and quantise it (round each measurement to one of a fixed set of levels).

Sampling: Sampling means measuring the signal at regular intervals. The sampling rate, in samples per second (hertz), says how often. If you sample a temperature once per second, you get 60 numbers per minute. Between samples, you know nothing. So how often is often enough? It depends on how fast the signal changes.

The Nyquist rule: The key rule, called the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, says: to capture a signal correctly, the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal. Human hearing goes up to about 20,000 hertz, so music needs a sampling rate above 40,000 per second. That is why audio CDs use 44,100 samples per second. Ordinary telephone calls only carry voice frequencies up to about 3,400 hertz, so the classic digital phone system samples at 8,000 per second.

Aliasing: If you sample too slowly, high frequencies do not just disappear; they pretend to be lower frequencies that were never there. This is aliasing. You have seen it in videos where a car's wheels or a fan's blades seem to spin slowly backwards: the camera's frame rate is sampling the rotation too slowly. To prevent aliasing, an anti-aliasing filter, a low-pass filter, removes frequencies above half the sampling rate before the ADC sees the signal.

Resolution and levels: Quantisation rounds each sample to the nearest of a fixed number of levels. An n-bit ADC has 2 to the power n levels. An 8-bit ADC has 256 levels, a 10-bit ADC has 1,024, a 12-bit ADC 4,096, and 16-bit audio has 65,536. More bits mean finer steps and a more accurate picture of the signal.

Step size: The ADC compares the input to a reference voltage, Vref, which sets the full range. The step size, also called 1 LSB (least significant bit), is Vref / 2 to the power n. For a 10-bit ADC with a 5 volt reference: 5 / 1,024 = about 4.88 millivolts per step. For a 12-bit ADC with 3.3 volts: 3.3 / 4,096 = about 0.81 millivolts. A change smaller than one step is invisible to the ADC.

Converting voltage to a number: The digital output is roughly D = Vin / Vref x 2 to the power n, rounded down, and capped at 2 to the power n minus 1. Example: a 10-bit ADC with a 5 volt reference reads 2.0 volts. D = 2.0 / 5 x 1,024 = 409.6, so the output is 409. Going back: 409 x 4.88 millivolts = about 1.997 volts. Many microcontrollers have exactly this kind of 10-bit or 12-bit ADC built in, giving numbers like 0 to 1,023 or 0 to 4,095.

Quantisation error: Because of rounding, the number never matches the true voltage exactly. The difference is the quantisation error, at most half a step when the ADC rounds to the nearest level (or up to one step when it simply truncates). This error sounds like a faint hiss in audio. Each extra bit halves the step size and improves the signal-to-noise ratio by about 6 decibels, which is why 16-bit audio sounds clean and 8-bit audio sounds rough.

Sample and hold: A real input may change while the ADC is still working on it. So most ADCs have a sample-and-hold circuit in front: a switch and a small capacitor. At the sampling moment the switch closes briefly, the capacitor charges to the input voltage, then the switch opens and the capacitor holds that voltage steady while the ADC converts it.

The DAC: A DAC does the reverse: it takes a binary number and produces a matching voltage. The ideal output is Vout = Vref x D / 2 to the power n. For an 8-bit DAC with a 5 volt reference, D = 128 gives 5 x 128 / 256 = 2.5 volts, and D = 200 gives about 3.91 volts. The output comes in small steps like a staircase, so a smoothing low-pass filter after the DAC rounds off the steps to recreate a smooth wave.

The binary-weighted resistor DAC: The simplest idea gives each bit a resistor whose value halves for each more significant bit: R for the most significant bit, 2R for the next, then 4R, 8R and so on, all feeding into an op-amp that adds their currents. The most significant bit contributes the most current, as it should. The problem: an 8-bit version needs resistors from R up to 128R, all very precise, which is hard and expensive to make accurately on a chip.

The R-2R ladder DAC: The clever fix uses only two resistor values, R and 2R, arranged in a repeating ladder. Because of the way the ladder divides current, each stage contributes exactly half as much as the stage before, giving the same binary weighting with just two values. Two values are easy to match precisely, so R-2R ladders are popular in real DAC chips and are a favourite exam topic.

The flash ADC: The fastest ADC is the flash ADC. It uses a chain of resistors to create every possible threshold voltage and one comparator for each threshold, all working at the same time. A small encoder turns the comparator outputs into a binary number. An n-bit flash ADC needs 2 to the power n minus 1 comparators: an 8-bit one needs 255. It converts in one step, so it suits very fast signals like video and radar, but it is large and power hungry at high resolutions.

The successive approximation ADC: The most common ADC inside microcontrollers is the successive approximation (SAR) ADC. It works like a binary search, deciding one bit per step, from the most significant to the least, using a DAC and one comparator. It tries setting a bit to 1, converts that guess to a voltage, and compares it with the input. If the guess is too high, it clears the bit; otherwise it keeps it. An n-bit SAR ADC needs n steps. It balances speed, accuracy and cost well.

SAR worked example: A 4-bit SAR ADC with a 16 volt reference has 1 volt steps. The input is 11.3 volts. Step 1: try 1000 (8 volts); 8 is below 11.3, keep it. Step 2: try 1100 (12 volts); 12 is above 11.3, clear it, giving 1000. Step 3: try 1010 (10 volts); below, keep it. Step 4: try 1011 (11 volts); below, keep it. The result is 1011, which is 11. Four bits, four steps.

Other ADC types: A dual-slope (integrating) ADC charges a capacitor from the input for a fixed time, then discharges it with a known reference and measures how long that takes. It is slow but very accurate and naturally ignores mains hum, so it is used in digital multimeters. A sigma-delta ADC samples very fast with just 1 bit and uses digital filtering to produce high-resolution results; it is common in audio and precision weighing scales.

PWM, a cheap DAC: Many microcontrollers have no real DAC. Instead they use PWM (pulse width modulation): the pin switches rapidly between 0 and the supply voltage, and the fraction of time it is high, the duty cycle, sets the average voltage. On a 5 volt pin, a 25 percent duty cycle gives an average of 1.25 volts. For an LED, your eye averages the flicker into a dimmer glow; for a motor, its inertia averages it into a slower speed. Add a resistor and capacitor low-pass filter, and you get a fairly smooth analog voltage. On Arduino boards, analogWrite with a value from 0 to 255 sets an 8-bit PWM duty cycle, while analogRead returns a 10-bit ADC reading from 0 to 1,023.

Data rate of digital audio: Sampling rate x bits per sample x channels gives the raw bit rate. CD audio: 44,100 x 16 x 2 = 1,411,200 bits per second, about 1.4 megabits per second. A classic digital phone call: 8,000 x 8 x 1 = 64,000 bits per second. Formats like MP3 and the codecs used by WhatsApp calls compress this much further.

Real-life example 1, the digital scale in a fish market: At a fish market in Chandpur, the seller's digital scale has a load cell, a metal piece whose resistance changes very slightly under weight. A small amplifier boosts the tiny voltage, and a high-resolution ADC, often sigma-delta, converts it into a number. A microcontroller subtracts the tray weight and shows 1.25 kg on a 7-segment display. If the ADC had too few bits, the scale could only show steps of, say, 50 grams, and buyers would complain.

Real-life example 2, a mobile phone call from Barishal to Dhaka: When you speak, the phone's microphone produces an analog voltage. An ADC samples it thousands of times per second, a codec compresses the numbers, and they travel as digital data across the network. At the other end, a DAC turns the numbers back into a voltage that drives the earpiece speaker. Your voice made two trips across the analog-digital border in a fraction of a second.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students mix 2 to the power n and 2 to the power n minus 1 when finding step size, forget that Nyquist needs more than twice the highest frequency, or forget that a flash ADC needs 2 to the power n minus 1 comparators. Exams ask: calculate step size and digital output, apply Nyquist and explain aliasing, compute quantisation error, compare flash, SAR and dual-slope ADCs, trace a SAR conversion, explain the R-2R ladder, compute DAC output, and calculate audio bit rates.

Recap: Converting analog to digital means sampling (more than twice the highest frequency, by Nyquist, with an anti-aliasing filter) and quantising into 2 to the power n levels with step size Vref / 2 to the power n. Quantisation error is at most half a step. DACs produce Vref x D / 2 to the power n, often with an R-2R ladder, followed by smoothing. Flash ADCs are fastest, SAR ADCs do a binary search in n steps, dual-slope ADCs are accurate and slow, sigma-delta suits audio, and PWM gives a cheap average voltage. Next lesson, we use ADCs to read real sensors.
key_points: Converting analog to digital involves sampling (measuring at intervals) and quantising (rounding to fixed levels).
Nyquist: sample at more than twice the highest frequency; otherwise aliasing creates false low frequencies.
An n-bit converter has 2^n levels; step size (1 LSB) = Vref / 2^n; output D is about Vin / Vref x 2^n.
Quantisation error is at most half a step with rounding; each extra bit adds about 6 dB of signal-to-noise ratio.
DAC output = Vref x D / 2^n; the R-2R ladder needs only two resistor values.
Flash ADCs need 2^n - 1 comparators and are fastest; SAR ADCs use n binary-search steps; dual-slope ADCs are slow but accurate.
PWM varies duty cycle to give an average voltage, a cheap substitute for a DAC.
lessons.tip: Write the two core formulas on one card: step = Vref / 2^n and D = Vin / step. Almost every ADC and DAC question is these two lines plus careful rounding.
lessons.task: A 12-bit ADC uses a 3.3 V reference. Calculate its step size, the digital output for 1.65 V and for 2.5 V, and the voltage that a reading of 3,000 represents. Then trace by hand a 4-bit SAR conversion of 6.7 V with a 16 V reference.

quiz.q: What is the minimum sampling rate needed for a signal whose highest frequency is 5 kHz?
quiz.explain: Nyquist requires a sampling rate greater than twice the highest frequency: more than 10 kHz.

quiz.q: What is the step size of a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference?
quiz.explain: 5 / 1,024 = about 0.00488 V, which is 4.88 mV.

quiz.q: How many comparators does an 8-bit flash ADC need?
quiz.explain: A flash ADC needs 2^n - 1 comparators: 2^8 - 1 = 255.

quiz.q: An 8-bit DAC with a 5 V reference receives D = 64. What is the output?
A 5 V PWM pin runs at 40 percent duty cycle. What is the average voltage?
quiz.explain: Average = duty cycle x high voltage = 0.4 x 5 = 2 V.

lessons.title: Sensors and Signal Conditioning
lessons.content:
A computer by itself is blind, deaf and numb. It cannot feel heat, see light or notice a person walking past. Sensors are its senses. A sensor turns something physical, like temperature, light, distance, motion or gas, into an electrical signal, usually a voltage, resistance or digital value. Last lesson we learned how an ADC turns a voltage into a number. This lesson fills the gap before the ADC: the sensors themselves, and the small circuits, called signal conditioning, that make a sensor's signal clean and the right size for the ADC.

What a sensor is: A sensor (or transducer) converts one kind of energy or quantity into an electrical signal. Some are analog: their output voltage or resistance varies smoothly, and we read them with an ADC. Others are digital: they contain their own ADC and processor and send numbers over I2C, SPI or a single data pin, as we saw in lesson 10. Some are simple on-off switches, like a door sensor or a float switch in a water tank.

Important sensor words: Range is the span of values the sensor can measure, for example minus 55 to 150 degrees Celsius. Sensitivity is how much the output changes per unit of input, for example 10 millivolts per degree. Resolution is the smallest change it can detect. Accuracy is how close the reading is to the true value; precision is how repeatable readings are. A sensor can be precise but inaccurate, like a scale that always reads exactly 200 grams too heavy. Response time is how fast it reacts. Calibration means comparing with a known reference and correcting the readings.

The LM35 temperature sensor: The LM35 is a classic analog temperature sensor with three pins: power, ground and output. Its output is 10 millivolts per degree Celsius, starting from 0 volts at 0 degrees. So at 25 degrees it outputs 250 millivolts, and at 35 degrees, 350 millivolts. Reading it with a 10-bit ADC at 5 volts, where each step is about 4.88 millivolts: a reading of 72 means 72 x 4.88 = 351 millivolts, which is about 35.1 degrees. Notice each ADC step is about half a degree, which is fine for weather but not for a medical thermometer.

Thermistors: A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance changes a lot with temperature. The common NTC type (negative temperature coefficient) has lower resistance when hotter. A typical one is 10 kilohms at 25 degrees. It is cheap and sensitive, but its curve is not a straight line, so software uses a formula or a lookup table to turn resistance into temperature. Thermistors are inside phone batteries, rice cookers and air conditioners.

The voltage divider, turning resistance into voltage: An ADC measures voltage, not resistance. So we put the sensor in a voltage divider: a fixed resistor and the sensor in series between the supply and ground, and we measure the voltage at the point between them. Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2), where R2 is the resistor connected to ground. Example: 5 volts, fixed resistor R1 = 10 kilohms on top, thermistor R2 below. At 25 degrees R2 = 10 kilohms, so Vout = 5 x 10 / 20 = 2.5 volts. When it gets hotter and R2 drops to 5 kilohms, Vout = 5 x 5 / 15 = about 1.67 volts.

The LDR, sensing light: A light dependent resistor (LDR) has high resistance in the dark, often around a megohm, and low resistance in bright light, perhaps a few hundred ohms to a few kilohms. Put it in a voltage divider and the ADC reading rises or falls with light. This is how simple automatic street lights and garden lamps switch on at dusk. Phones use more accurate photodiode-based ambient light sensors to adjust screen brightness.

The ultrasonic distance sensor: The popular HC-SR04 module measures distance like a bat. When you send a short pulse to its trigger pin, it emits a burst of 40 kilohertz ultrasound, too high for humans to hear. The sound bounces off an object and returns. The module sets its echo pin high for the time the sound took for the round trip. Distance = speed of sound x time / 2, divided by two because the sound went there and back. Sound travels about 343 metres per second in air at 20 degrees, which is 0.0343 centimetres per microsecond.

Ultrasonic worked example: The echo pulse lasts 1,166 microseconds. Distance = 0.0343 x 1,166 / 2 = about 20 centimetres. If the echo lasts 5,830 microseconds, the object is about 100 centimetres away. On a hot 35 degree day in Bangladesh, sound travels a little faster, about 352 metres per second, so careful projects correct for temperature. The module works up to about 4 metres and struggles with soft materials like cloth that absorb sound.

PIR motion sensors: A PIR (passive infrared) sensor detects the heat radiation given off by people and animals. It does not send anything out; it watches. A special lens, often a white plastic dome with ridges, divides its view into zones. When a warm body moves from one zone to the next, the sensor notices the change and sets its output pin high. It detects movement, not presence: a person sitting perfectly still may not trigger it. PIR sensors switch on corridor lights in many offices and apartment buildings.

Gas sensors: The MQ series of low-cost gas sensors use a heated metal oxide layer whose resistance falls when certain gases are present. The MQ-2 responds to smoke and flammable gases like LPG and methane; the MQ-135 to several air pollutants. They need a heater that draws noticeable current, a warm-up time, and calibration in clean air. They are good for alarms that say gas is present, but not for precise measurements. A kitchen gas leak alarm is a common student project in Bangladesh, where LPG cylinders are widely used.

Accelerometers and other MEMS sensors: Phones contain tiny MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) sensors. An accelerometer has a microscopic mass on springs; when the phone tilts or moves, the mass shifts and changes a capacitance. It measures acceleration, including gravity, so it can tell which way is down. That is how the screen rotates and how step counters work. A gyroscope measures rotation speed, and a magnetometer senses the Earth's magnetic field as a compass. These usually talk over I2C or SPI.

Signal conditioning, why it is needed: The raw signal from a sensor is rarely ready for the ADC. It may be too small (a load cell gives only a few millivolts), too large (a 12 volt signal would destroy a 3.3 volt microcontroller pin), noisy (picking up interference from motors and mains wiring), or offset (not starting from zero). Signal conditioning is everything we do between the sensor and the ADC to fix this: amplifying, attenuating, filtering, shifting and protecting.

Amplification: An op-amp (operational amplifier) circuit can multiply a small voltage by a set gain. A non-inverting amplifier has gain = 1 + Rf / Rg, set by two resistors. Example: the LM35 gives at most about 0.5 volts at 50 degrees. With Rf = 9 kilohms and Rg = 1 kilohm, gain = 1 + 9 = 10, so 0.5 volts becomes 5 volts, using the ADC's full range and giving ten times finer temperature steps. Very tiny signals like a load cell's need a precise instrumentation amplifier, such as the common HX711 module used with weighing scales.

Attenuation and level shifting: If a signal is too big, a simple voltage divider scales it down. To read a 12 volt battery with a 5 volt ADC, use R1 = 20 kilohms and R2 = 10 kilohms: 12 x 10 / 30 = 4 volts at the pin. Software then multiplies the reading by 3 to show the battery voltage. If a signal swings negative, like audio, a level shifting circuit adds an offset, for example lifting it to sit around 2.5 volts so it stays between 0 and 5 volts.

Filtering: Noise is unwanted variation. A simple RC low-pass filter, a resistor followed by a capacitor to ground, lets slow changes pass and blocks fast spikes. Its cutoff frequency is 1 / (2 x pi x R x C). With R = 10 kilohms and C = 1 microfarad, the cutoff is about 16 hertz, good for a temperature sensor that changes slowly. Software can filter too: averaging the last 10 readings, or taking the median of 5 to throw away single wild values.

Protection: Sensor wires can pick up voltage spikes, and a mistake can connect too high a voltage. A series resistor limits current, clamp diodes or a Zener diode stop the voltage going above the safe limit, and a small capacitor absorbs fast spikes. A few cents of protection can save a whole board, which matters a lot in projects placed outdoors on farms or rooftops.

Real-life example 1, a flood warning sensor on a river: An NGO places an ultrasonic sensor on a bridge above a river in Sunamganj, pointing down at the water. A microcontroller measures the distance every minute, averages several readings to remove ripples, corrects for air temperature, and calculates the water level. If the level rises faster than a set rate, it sends an SMS warning to nearby villages through a GSM module. The whole system is a sensor, conditioning in software and a communication link.

Real-life example 2, a poultry farm controller: A broiler farm in Gazipur must keep chicks warm. A digital temperature and humidity sensor reads the shed every few seconds, a gas sensor watches for ammonia build-up, and an LDR checks daylight. A small controller switches heaters, fans and lights accordingly. The analog sensors pass through dividers and RC filters because long wires in the shed pick up noise from the fan motors.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students forget to divide by 2 in the ultrasonic formula, mix up which resistor is R2 in the divider formula, or connect a 5 volt sensor output directly to a 3.3 volt pin. They also confuse accuracy with precision. Exams ask: define sensor characteristics, compute LM35 temperature from an ADC reading, design a voltage divider, calculate ultrasonic distance, explain how PIR works, explain why signal conditioning is needed, compute op-amp gain, and calculate an RC cutoff frequency.

Recap: Sensors convert physical quantities into electrical signals, analog or digital. Know range, sensitivity, resolution, accuracy, precision and calibration. The LM35 gives 10 millivolts per degree; thermistors and LDRs change resistance and are read through a voltage divider. Ultrasonic sensors time an echo and halve it; PIR sensors detect moving warmth; MQ gas sensors and MEMS accelerometers cover other senses. Signal conditioning amplifies, attenuates, shifts, filters and protects so the ADC gets a clean, correctly sized signal. Next lesson, we go the other way: making things move with actuators.
key_points: Sensors turn physical quantities into electrical signals; analog ones are read with an ADC, digital ones send numbers over I2C, SPI or a data pin.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability; calibration corrects readings against a reference.
The LM35 outputs 10 mV per degree Celsius; thermistors and LDRs change resistance.
A voltage divider turns resistance into voltage: Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2).
Ultrasonic distance = speed of sound x echo time / 2 (about 0.0343 cm per microsecond).
PIR sensors detect moving body heat; MQ gas sensors and MEMS accelerometers sense gas and motion.
Signal conditioning amplifies (gain = 1 + Rf / Rg), attenuates, shifts, filters (cutoff = 1 / 2piRC) and protects.
lessons.tip: For any sensor question, draw a chain: physical quantity, sensor output, conditioning, ADC, number, software conversion. Write the unit at each arrow and the calculation becomes obvious.
lessons.task: Design on paper a light-activated night lamp: choose a fixed resistor for an LDR that is 1 kilohm in daylight and 100 kilohms at night, calculate the divider voltage in both cases with a 5 V supply, and decide what ADC reading (10-bit) should switch the lamp on.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC at 5 V reads 61 from an LM35. What is the temperature, roughly?
quiz.explain: 61 x 4.88 mV = about 298 mV; at 10 mV per degree that is about 29.8 degrees.

quiz.q: An ultrasonic echo lasts 2,332 microseconds. How far is the object?
In a divider with 5 V, R1 = 10 kilohms on top and R2 = 40 kilohms to ground, what is Vout?
What does a PIR sensor actually detect?
options: Changes in infrared heat as a warm body moves
quiz.explain: PIR sensors passively watch infrared radiation and trigger when a warm body moves between zones.

quiz.q: A non-inverting op-amp has Rf = 47 kilohms and Rg = 1 kilohm. What is its gain?

lessons.title: Actuators and Driving Loads
lessons.content:
Sensors let a computer feel the world; actuators let it act on the world. An actuator turns an electrical signal into something physical: light, sound, heat or movement. A motor spinning a fan, a relay switching a water pump, a buzzer beeping, a servo turning a robot's arm, a solenoid unlocking a door. The challenge is that a microcontroller pin is weak. It can supply only a few milliamps to a few tens of milliamps, at 3.3 or 5 volts. A water pump may need several amps at 12 volts or even mains 220 volts. This lesson is about bridging that gap safely: driving loads.

The pin's limits: A typical microcontroller output pin can safely supply around 20 milliamps, and the whole chip has a total limit too, often in the low hundreds of milliamps. Some modern chips allow even less per pin. An LED with a resistor is fine. A small buzzer may be fine. But a motor, relay coil, long LED strip or heater is far beyond what a pin can give. Connecting one directly can damage the pin, reset the chip because the supply voltage drops, or destroy the microcontroller completely.

LEDs and current-limiting resistors: An LED needs a resistor in series to limit current. R = (Vsupply - Vled) / I. For a red LED (about 2 volts) on a 5 volt pin at 15 milliamps: (5 - 2) / 0.015 = 200 ohms; the nearest common value, 220 ohms, gives about 13.6 milliamps. For a blue or white LED, around 3 volts, the resistor is smaller. Without the resistor the LED would try to draw far too much current and burn out, possibly taking the pin with it.

The transistor as a switch: The basic trick is to let the weak pin control a transistor, and let the transistor switch the big current from a separate supply. With an NPN bipolar transistor, the load connects between the positive supply and the collector, the emitter goes to ground, and the pin drives the base through a resistor. When the pin is high, a small base current flows and the transistor turns fully on, letting a much larger collector current flow through the load. When the pin is low, it turns off. This is called low-side switching because the transistor sits between the load and ground.

Base resistor worked example: A small motor needs 200 milliamps, and the transistor has a current gain of about 100. The base needs at least 200 / 100 = 2 milliamps; to be sure it is fully switched on, designers give several times more, say 10 milliamps. With a 5 volt pin and about 0.7 volts across the base-emitter junction: R = (5 - 0.7) / 0.01 = 430 ohms, so a 470 ohm resistor is a good choice. The pin supplies just 10 milliamps while the motor gets its 200 milliamps.

MOSFETs, the modern switch: For bigger currents, a MOSFET is usually better. It is controlled by voltage at its gate rather than current, so it draws almost no steady current from the pin, and when fully on it has a very small resistance, so it wastes little power as heat. The key is to choose a logic-level MOSFET, which turns fully on with only 3.3 or 5 volts at the gate. A standard MOSFET may need about 10 volts to turn fully on and will stay half-on and get hot if driven from a microcontroller pin. A resistor of around 10 kilohms from gate to ground keeps it off while the microcontroller starts up.

The flyback diode, protecting against coils: Motors, relays and solenoids contain coils of wire, which are inductors. A coil resists sudden changes in current. When the transistor switches off, the coil's magnetic field collapses and produces a sudden high voltage spike, which can be tens or hundreds of volts, in the reverse direction. This spike can destroy the transistor. The fix is a flyback diode placed across the coil, pointing so it normally does not conduct (its stripe towards the positive supply). When the spike comes, the diode gives the current a safe loop to die away. Forgetting this diode is one of the most common reasons student projects suddenly stop working.

Relays, switching big and mains loads: A relay is an electrically operated switch. A small coil, driven through a transistor, pulls a metal contact that closes or opens a separate circuit. The coil side and the contact side are electrically separate, so a 5 volt circuit can switch a 220 volt pump or light. Relay contacts are labelled COM (common), NO (normally open, connected only when the coil is on) and NC (normally closed, connected when the coil is off). Common relay modules sold for hobby use include the transistor, flyback diode and an indicator LED on one small board. Relays are slow, click audibly and their contacts wear out over many cycles. A solid state relay uses semiconductors instead, with no moving parts and no click.

Mains safety: 220 volt mains in Bangladesh can kill. Work on mains wiring only with an adult who is trained, keep it inside a closed box, never touch the board when it is plugged in, use proper wire and fuses, and keep low-voltage and high-voltage parts well apart on the board.

Optocouplers, electrical isolation: An optocoupler contains an LED and a light sensor, such as a phototransistor, sealed in one small package. The microcontroller turns on the LED; the light switches the phototransistor on the other side. There is no electrical connection between the two sides, only light. This isolation protects the sensitive microcontroller from spikes and different ground voltages in noisy or high-voltage circuits. Many relay modules and industrial controllers use optocouplers.

DC motors and speed control: A brushed DC motor spins when current flows; reversing the current reverses the direction. Its speed depends on the voltage. To control speed with a microcontroller, we use PWM through a transistor or MOSFET. At 75 percent duty cycle from a 12 volt supply, the motor behaves roughly as if it received 9 volts on average and runs slower than full speed. A PWM frequency of several kilohertz or higher avoids an audible whine from the motor.

The H-bridge, forward and reverse: To run a DC motor both ways, we use an H-bridge: four switches arranged in the shape of the letter H with the motor in the middle bar. Turning on the top-left and bottom-right switches sends current one way; the top-right and bottom-left send it the other way. Turning on both switches on the same side at once would short the supply directly to ground, called shoot-through, which can destroy the circuit, so driver chips include protection and dead time. Ready-made H-bridge chips such as the L298N and the more efficient TB6612FNG are common in robot car kits, each driving two motors with direction pins and a PWM speed pin.

Servo motors: A hobby servo, such as the SG90, contains a small motor, gears, a position sensor and a control circuit. You tell it what angle to go to using a pulse, repeated every 20 milliseconds (50 times per second). A pulse of about 1 millisecond means one end, about 1.5 milliseconds means the middle, and about 2 milliseconds means the other end, typically covering 0 to 180 degrees. The exact pulse lengths vary slightly between servo models. The servo holds that angle until told otherwise. Servos move robot arms, steering on model cars and the flaps of small automatic doors.

Stepper motors: A stepper motor moves in fixed steps instead of spinning freely. A very common type takes 200 steps per revolution, which is 1.8 degrees per step. The controller energises its coils in a sequence; each change in the pattern moves the shaft one step. Because you count steps, you know the position without a sensor, as long as the motor does not miss steps because of too much load. Example: to turn 90 degrees with 1.8 degree steps, send 90 / 1.8 = 50 steps. With a lead screw that moves 8 millimetres per revolution, one step moves 8 / 200 = 0.04 millimetres. Drivers such as the A4988 also support microstepping, splitting each step into smaller parts for smoother motion. Steppers drive 3D printers, scanners and CNC machines.

Buzzers, speakers and solenoids: An active buzzer has its own oscillator and beeps when given a steady voltage. A passive buzzer or a small speaker needs a square wave at the desired frequency, which the microcontroller generates, so it can play different tones. A solenoid is a coil that pulls a metal plunger, used in electric door locks and some water valves; like relays and motors, it needs a transistor and a flyback diode.

Separate power supplies and common ground: Motors draw big bursts of current, causing voltage dips and electrical noise. Good practice is to power motors from a separate supply or at least separate wiring, add a large capacitor near the motor driver, and connect the grounds of the microcontroller and the motor supply together so the control signals have a shared reference. Forgetting the common ground is a classic reason a motor driver does not respond at all.

Real-life example 1, an automatic water pump: Many houses in Dhaka have a rooftop tank filled by a pump from an underground reservoir. A controller reads two float switches in the tank. When the water drops below the low switch, the microcontroller turns on a transistor, which energises a relay coil, and the relay's contacts switch on the 220 volt pump. When water reaches the high switch, it switches off. A flyback diode protects the transistor, and the relay keeps the mains completely separate from the logic.

Real-life example 2, a student robot car at a university fest: A team in Rajshahi builds a line-following car. Two infrared sensors watch a black line on the floor. A microcontroller sends PWM and direction signals to an H-bridge driver that runs two DC motors from a battery pack. When the left sensor sees the line, it slows the left motor to turn. A servo at the front sweeps an ultrasonic sensor to detect obstacles. The first version kept resetting until they added a separate supply for the motors and a capacitor across the battery.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students drive a motor or relay directly from a pin, forget the flyback diode, use a non-logic-level MOSFET, forget the common ground, or confuse NO and NC contacts. Exams ask: calculate an LED resistor, calculate a base resistor, explain why a flyback diode is needed, explain relays and optocouplers, draw and explain an H-bridge, describe PWM speed control, explain servo pulse timing, and calculate stepper steps for a given angle or distance.

Recap: Microcontroller pins give only milliamps, so loads are driven through transistors or logic-level MOSFETs. LEDs need series resistors. Coils need flyback diodes. Relays switch large or mains loads with isolation, and optocouplers isolate with light. DC motors use PWM for speed and H-bridges for direction; servos take 1 to 2 millisecond pulses every 20 milliseconds; steppers move in fixed steps such as 1.8 degrees. Separate motor power, add capacitors and share ground. Next lesson, we bring everything together in microcontroller-based interfacing.
key_points: A microcontroller pin supplies only around 20 mA, so bigger loads need a transistor, MOSFET or driver chip.
LED resistor: R = (Vsupply - Vled) / I; base resistor: R = (Vpin - 0.7) / Ibase.
Use logic-level MOSFETs that turn fully on at 3.3 or 5 V gate voltage.
Coils (motors, relays, solenoids) need a flyback diode to absorb the voltage spike at switch-off.
Relays (COM, NO, NC) and optocouplers isolate low-voltage logic from high-voltage or noisy circuits.
DC motors use PWM for speed and an H-bridge for direction; servos use 1 to 2 ms pulses every 20 ms.
A 1.8 degree stepper has 200 steps per revolution; steps = angle / step angle.
lessons.tip: Before connecting anything to a pin, ask two questions: how much current does it need, and does it contain a coil? If more than a few milliamps, add a transistor. If it has a coil, add a flyback diode.
lessons.task: Design on paper a circuit where a 5 V microcontroller switches a 12 V, 300 mA DC fan: choose NPN transistor or logic-level MOSFET, calculate the base resistor if using a transistor with gain 100 (aim for 10 times the minimum base current), show the flyback diode direction, and add PWM speed control at 60 percent. What average voltage does the fan see?

quiz.q: Why is a flyback diode placed across a relay coil?
options: To make the relay click louder
To absorb the voltage spike when the coil is switched off
To make the relay switch faster on
quiz.explain: The collapsing magnetic field produces a reverse spike; the diode gives that current a safe path so the transistor is not damaged.

quiz.q: What series resistor does a 2 V red LED need on a 5 V pin for 10 mA?
A stepper motor has 1.8 degree steps. How many steps for 180 degrees?
What pulse width usually puts a hobby servo in its middle position?
quiz.explain: About 1 ms is one end, 1.5 ms the middle and 2 ms the other end, repeated every 20 ms.

quiz.q: What does an H-bridge allow you to do with a DC motor?
quiz.explain: By turning on diagonal pairs of switches, an H-bridge sends current through the motor either way.

lessons.title: Microcontroller-Based Interfacing: Putting It Together
lessons.content:
Over the last few lessons we met ADCs, sensors, transistors, relays and motors one at a time. Real projects use all of them together, connected to a small brain: a microcontroller. A microcontroller is a whole tiny computer on one chip, with a CPU, flash memory for the program, RAM, and lots of built-in peripherals: digital pins, ADCs, timers, PWM, UART, SPI and I2C. It costs from under a hundred taka to a few hundred, runs on very little power, and sits inside washing machines, microwave ovens, remote controls, digital meters and toys. This lesson shows how to plan and build an interfacing project around one.

Microcontroller versus microprocessor: A microprocessor, like the 8086 or the CPU in your laptop, is only the processing core; memory and I/O chips sit outside it on the board. A microcontroller puts the CPU, memory and I/O on one chip, so a working system needs very few extra parts. Microcontrollers are slower and have much less memory, often a few kilobytes to a few megabytes, but they start instantly, use little power and have pins that connect directly to the outside world. Popular families include AVR (used in the classic Arduino Uno's ATmega328P), ARM Cortex-M chips such as STM32, and the ESP32, which adds Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

GPIO, general purpose input and output: Most pins are GPIO pins. In software, you set each one as input or output. As an output, writing 1 makes the pin high (close to the supply voltage) and 0 makes it low (close to ground). As an input, reading tells you whether the voltage on it is above or below certain thresholds. Inside, each GPIO port is controlled by registers, just like the I/O ports of lesson 2: a direction register, an output register and an input register. Libraries such as Arduino's hide these behind friendly functions.

Floating inputs and pull-up resistors: An input pin connected to nothing is floating: it picks up stray electrical noise and may read randomly as 0 or 1. A push button connected from a pin to ground only pulls the pin low when pressed; when released, the pin floats. The fix is a pull-up resistor, often 10 kilohms, from the pin to the supply, so the pin reads 1 when the button is released and 0 when pressed. A pull-down resistor to ground does the opposite. Most microcontrollers have built-in pull-ups you can turn on in software, so you often need no external resistor at all.

Switch bounce: When a mechanical button is pressed, its metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, making the pin flicker between 0 and 1 many times. A program counting presses may count 5 instead of 1. Debouncing fixes this: in hardware, with a small capacitor, or in software, by accepting a change only after the pin has stayed steady for about 20 to 50 milliseconds.

Voltage levels, 5 volts versus 3.3 volts: The Arduino Uno runs at 5 volts; the ESP32, STM32 and Raspberry Pi run at 3.3 volts, and their pins are generally not 5 volt tolerant. Connecting a 5 volt output, such as an HC-SR04's echo pin, straight into a 3.3 volt input can damage it over time. Solutions: a voltage divider (for example 1 kilohm and 2 kilohms gives 5 x 2 / 3 = 3.33 volts), or a level shifter module, which also works in both directions for buses like I2C. Going the other way, a 3.3 volt output is usually high enough to count as logic 1 for many 5 volt inputs, but check the datasheet.

Reading analog values: The microcontroller's built-in ADC is used through a simple function, such as analogRead on Arduino. The Uno returns 0 to 1,023; the ESP32 returns 0 to 4,095. Its ADC is known to be somewhat non-linear near the ends of its range, which is a good reminder to calibrate against known values instead of trusting the formula blindly.

Reading the datasheet: The datasheet is the official manual for a chip or module. It lists the supply voltage range, absolute maximum ratings (values that must never be exceeded), current limits, timing diagrams, pin descriptions and registers. Learning to look up just the part you need, such as the pinout and the electrical characteristics table, is one of the most valuable skills in interfacing.

Timers: A microcontroller timer is a hardware counter that ticks with the clock, divided by a prescaler. It can measure time, create delays, generate PWM and trigger interrupts at precise intervals. Example: a 16 megahertz clock with a prescaler of 64 ticks 16,000,000 / 64 = 250,000 times per second, so each tick is 4 microseconds. To get an interrupt every 1 millisecond, the timer counts 250 ticks. Hardware PWM is just a timer that switches a pin when its count reaches a compare value.

Interrupts on a microcontroller: Pins can trigger interrupts on a rising edge, a falling edge or any change. Timers, the ADC finishing a conversion and the UART receiving a byte can trigger interrupts too. This is the same idea as the interrupts in lesson 3, now on a tiny chip. An interrupt service routine should be short: set a flag or save a value and return, and let the main loop do the slow work. A variable shared between an ISR and the main code should be marked volatile in C so the compiler always reads its latest value.

The program structure, setup and loop: Most microcontroller programs have two parts. Setup runs once at power-on: configure pins, start serial communication, initialise sensors. Loop then runs forever: read inputs, decide, write outputs, repeat. A simple Arduino style example in words: in setup, set pin 13 as output and pin 2 as input with pull-up. In loop, if digitalRead of pin 2 is LOW (button pressed), digitalWrite pin 13 HIGH to turn on the LED; otherwise write LOW. There is no operating system, just your loop running thousands of times per second.

Avoiding blocking delays: Beginners often use delay(1000) to wait a second. During that time the microcontroller does nothing else and misses button presses. A better pattern compares the current time from millis() with the time an action last happened, and acts only when enough time has passed. This lets one microcontroller blink an LED, read a sensor and watch a button at once, a simple form of cooperative multitasking.

Serial monitor and debugging: The UART connects the microcontroller to a computer through a USB-to-serial chip (lesson 7). Printing sensor values with Serial.println lets you watch what is happening on a serial monitor, the simplest and most useful debugging tool. A multimeter checks voltages and continuity, and a logic analyser or oscilloscope shows timing on I2C, SPI or PWM lines when things go wrong.

Power for projects: Many boards take power from USB (5 volts), a 9 to 12 volt adapter through a regulator, or batteries. A linear regulator such as the 7805 drops excess voltage as heat: from 12 volts to 5 volts at 0.5 amps, it wastes (12 - 5) x 0.5 = 3.5 watts and gets hot. A switching buck converter does the same job with much less waste. For battery projects, sleep modes matter: an ESP32 may use around 100 milliamps or more with Wi-Fi active but only microamps in deep sleep, so waking briefly every few minutes can make a battery last weeks or months.

A complete project, smart irrigation: Let us design a soil-moisture-based irrigation controller for a rooftop garden in Dhaka. Inputs: a capacitive soil moisture sensor (analog output) and a digital temperature and humidity sensor. Output: a 12 volt DC water pump, driven by a logic-level MOSFET with a flyback diode, and a small LCD showing readings. Brain: an ESP32, so the owner can check the garden on a phone over Wi-Fi.

Irrigation step by step: Step 1, calibrate the moisture sensor: read the ADC in dry air and in a glass of water; suppose the ESP32's 12-bit ADC gives 3,000 dry and 1,300 wet (capacitive sensors read lower when wet). Step 2, convert a reading to percent: moisture = (3,000 - reading) / (3,000 - 1,300) x 100. A reading of 2,150 gives 850 / 1,700 x 100 = 50 percent. Step 3, decide: if moisture falls below 30 percent, turn the pump on; turn it off above 60 percent. Using two different thresholds, called hysteresis, stops the pump from switching on and off rapidly around one value. Step 4, safety: never run the pump more than 5 minutes at a time, in case the sensor fails or the tank is empty. Step 5, every 10 minutes, send readings over Wi-Fi and go back to sleep.

Why capacitive and not resistive moisture sensors: Cheap resistive moisture probes pass a current through the soil between two metal prongs; this slowly corrodes them, often within weeks. Capacitive probes measure the soil's effect on a capacitor through a protective coating, with no exposed metal, so they last much longer outdoors. A small design choice like this decides whether a project survives the monsoon.

Testing and reliability: Test each part separately before combining: blink an LED, read the sensor and print it, run the pump from a test pin. Then combine step by step. Add a watchdog timer, a hardware timer that resets the microcontroller if the program freezes and stops resetting the watchdog. Protect outdoor circuits from water, use proper connectors instead of loose jumper wires, and think about what happens on power cuts: the system should restart in a safe state with the pump off.

Real-life example, a school science fair in Mymensingh: A group of class 9 students builds an automatic hand sanitiser dispenser. An infrared proximity sensor detects a hand, an Arduino turns on a small pump through a transistor for half a second, and a counter on a 7-segment display shows how many people used it. Their first version kept pumping because of electrical noise from the pump motor on the sensor line. A flyback diode, a capacitor and a separate pump supply fixed it, the same lessons professionals learn.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students leave inputs floating, forget debouncing, connect 5 volt signals to 3.3 volt pins, use delay everywhere, write long interrupt routines, forget volatile, and power motors from the board's 5 volt pin. Exams ask: compare microcontroller and microprocessor, explain GPIO and pull-up resistors, explain debouncing, calculate timer ticks and prescaler settings, explain interrupt use, design a level shifter, calculate regulator power loss, and design a complete system block diagram with sensors, conditioning, microcontroller, drivers and actuators.

Recap: A microcontroller combines CPU, memory and peripherals on one chip. GPIO pins need pull-ups for buttons and debouncing; voltage levels must match, using dividers or level shifters. Timers create delays, PWM and periodic interrupts; ISRs stay short and shared variables are volatile. Programs run setup once and loop forever, using millis-style timing instead of blocking delays. Plan power and sleep, calibrate sensors, use hysteresis and safety limits, and test parts one by one. Next and final lesson: networking peripherals, wireless links, power supplies and a wrap-up of the whole course.
key_points: A microcontroller has CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals (GPIO, ADC, timers, PWM, UART, SPI, I2C) on one chip.
Floating inputs read randomly; use pull-up or pull-down resistors, often built in.
Debounce buttons in hardware or by waiting 20 to 50 ms for a stable reading.
3.3 V pins are usually not 5 V tolerant; use a voltage divider or level shifter.
Timer tick = prescaler / clock; e.g. 16 MHz / 64 gives 4 microsecond ticks, 250 ticks per millisecond.
Keep ISRs short, mark shared variables volatile, and use millis-style timing instead of blocking delays.
Real projects need calibration, hysteresis, safety limits, watchdog timers and careful power design.
lessons.tip: Build every project in layers: first make one LED blink, then read one sensor and print it, then drive one actuator, and only then combine them. When something breaks, you will know exactly which layer to check.
lessons.task: Draw a block diagram for an automatic fish pond aerator: a dissolved oxygen or temperature sensor, signal conditioning, a microcontroller, a relay driving a 220 V aerator pump, an LCD and an SMS alert. Label voltage levels on each connection, mark where flyback diodes and pull-ups go, and choose on and off thresholds with hysteresis.

quiz.q: Why does a push button input usually need a pull-up resistor?
options: To make the button last longer
To increase the pin's output current
So the pin has a defined level instead of floating when the button is released
quiz.explain: Without a pull-up or pull-down, a released button leaves the pin floating and it reads randomly.

quiz.q: A 16 MHz clock with a prescaler of 64. How long is one timer tick?
quiz.explain: 16,000,000 / 64 = 250,000 ticks per second, so each tick is 4 microseconds.

quiz.q: Why use two thresholds (hysteresis) for switching a pump?
options: To make the sensor more accurate
To stop the pump switching on and off rapidly around one value
quiz.explain: Separate on and off thresholds give a gap so small fluctuations do not toggle the pump repeatedly.

quiz.q: A 7805 regulator drops 12 V to 5 V at 0.4 A. How much power is wasted as heat?
What does a watchdog timer do?
options: Resets the microcontroller if the program freezes
quiz.explain: If the program stops resetting the watchdog in time, the watchdog assumes a hang and resets the chip.

lessons.title: Network and Wireless Peripherals, Power, and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
A computer today is rarely alone. Your laptop talks to the internet over Wi-Fi, your phone to earbuds over Bluetooth, a shop's card machine to a tap-to-pay card over NFC, and an office PC to the server over an Ethernet cable. All of these are peripherals too: network interfaces that move data between this computer and others. And every peripheral, from keyboard to hard disk, needs clean, steady power, which is a big challenge in a country with load shedding and voltage swings. In this final lesson we cover network and wireless interfaces, power supplies and protection, and then tie the whole course together.

The network interface card: A network interface card (NIC), today usually a chip on the motherboard, connects a computer to a network. It turns frames of data from the computer into electrical, light or radio signals and back again, checks incoming frames for errors, and uses DMA to move packets directly to and from memory, raising an interrupt when packets arrive, just as we saw in lesson 3. Fast NICs sit on PCI Express. The operating system's network driver hands packets to the NIC through queues in memory called ring buffers.

MAC addresses: Every network interface has a MAC address, a 48-bit identifier written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits, like 3C:52:82:1A:9F:07. The first half usually identifies the manufacturer. On a local network, devices use MAC addresses to deliver frames to the right machine. Your laptop's Wi-Fi and Ethernet ports each have their own MAC address. Modern phones often use a random MAC address for each Wi-Fi network for privacy.

Ethernet: Wired Ethernet is the most common local network. Common speeds are 100 megabits per second (Fast Ethernet), 1 gigabit per second (Gigabit Ethernet) and higher in servers. It usually uses twisted-pair copper cable with RJ45 plugs, such as Cat5e or Cat6, up to 100 metres per run. Twisting each pair cancels interference, the same differential idea we met in SATA and USB. Gigabit Ethernet uses all four pairs in both directions at once. For long distances, between buildings or across a city, optical fibre carries light instead and is not affected by electrical interference or lightning.

Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi is wireless Ethernet, defined by the IEEE 802.11 standards. It works in the 2.4 gigahertz band (longer range, more crowded, passes walls better) and the 5 gigahertz band (faster, shorter range), with Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 adding 6 gigahertz. Marketing names map to standards: Wi-Fi 4 is 802.11n, Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac, Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax. The Wi-Fi chip in a laptop is a peripheral on PCIe or USB; tiny ones like the ESP32's are built into the microcontroller. Advertised speeds are shared by all devices on a channel and drop with distance and walls, so real speed is usually much lower.

Bluetooth: Bluetooth is a short-range radio link, also in the 2.4 gigahertz band, designed for low power personal devices: earbuds, keyboards, mice, watches and fitness bands. It hops quickly between many narrow channels to avoid interference. Bluetooth Classic carries continuous streams like audio; Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) sends small bursts of data and sleeps in between, so a sensor can run for months or even years on a coin cell battery. Devices must be paired first, exchanging keys so later connections are encrypted.

NFC and RFID: RFID tags hold an ID that a reader can read by radio, often without a battery: the reader's field powers the tag. NFC (near field communication) is a short-range form working at 13.56 megahertz over a few centimetres. Tapping a metro rail card at a station gate in Dhaka, tapping a contactless bank card, or tapping a phone to pay uses NFC. The very short range is a security feature: you must deliberately bring the card close. Office ID cards that unlock doors usually use RFID.

Cellular modems: Phones and some IoT devices include a cellular modem for 4G or 5G networks. Simple projects use GSM or 4G modules controlled with text commands over UART, called AT commands, to send SMS messages or open data connections, as in the flood warning example from lesson 22. A SIM card identifies the subscriber to the mobile operator.

Choosing a link for a project: Wired Ethernet gives the most reliable, fastest local link. Wi-Fi suits devices near a router with mains power. BLE suits tiny battery devices near a phone. Cellular works where there is no Wi-Fi, for example on a farm or a river bank, but costs money per month. Long-range low-power radio systems such as LoRa can send small messages several kilometres with very little power, useful for village water level and agriculture sensors.

Wireless and security: Radio signals travel through walls and can be received by anyone nearby, so wireless peripherals must encrypt their data. Use WPA2 or WPA3 on Wi-Fi with a strong password, keep router firmware updated, and pair Bluetooth devices only when you mean to. An open café Wi-Fi network in a busy area like Dhanmondi is convenient, but anything sent over it without encryption, such as a site without HTTPS, could be read by others on the same network.

The computer's power supply: A desktop PC's power supply unit (PSU) converts 220 volt AC mains into low-voltage DC rails. A standard ATX supply provides 12 volts (for the CPU, graphics card and motors), 5 volts and 3.3 volts (for older logic, USB and drives), plus a 5 volt standby rail that stays on when the PC is off so it can wake up from a keyboard press or network signal. Modern PSUs are switch-mode supplies: they chop the mains at high frequency so a small, light transformer can do the job, wasting much less power than old heavy linear supplies. Efficiency ratings such as 80 Plus show how much of the input power reaches the computer instead of becoming heat.

Power budget: Every design needs a power budget. Add up the current of all parts at each voltage, and choose a supply with margin. Example: a project has an ESP32 at about 250 milliamps peak, an LCD backlight at 30 milliamps and sensors at 20 milliamps, all at 3.3 or 5 volts, plus a 12 volt pump at 800 milliamps. A 12 volt 2 amp adapter with a buck converter for the logic gives safe headroom. Ignoring the budget leads to brownouts: the voltage dips when the pump starts and the microcontroller resets.

UPS and IPS: Load shedding is common in Bangladesh. A UPS (uninterruptible power supply) keeps a computer running from a battery when mains fails. An offline or standby UPS switches to battery within a few milliseconds, short enough that most PC supplies keep running; a line-interactive UPS also corrects small voltage changes; an online UPS powers the load from the inverter all the time, with no switch-over gap at all, and is used for servers and medical equipment. Home IPS systems are inverters with large batteries designed to run fans and lights for hours, usually with a slower switch-over. A UPS rated in VA (volt-amperes) gives roughly 0.6 times that in watts for many small models: a 650 VA UPS can carry about 390 watts.

Voltage swings and surges: Mains voltage in some areas may drop well below 220 volts in the evening or jump higher at night, and lightning or switching of heavy loads can cause sudden spikes. Surge protectors use components such as MOVs (metal oxide varistors) to clamp spikes. Voltage stabilisers correct long-lasting high or low voltage. A proper earth connection is important, both for safety and so that surge protection has somewhere to send the extra energy.

ESD, the invisible danger: Walking across a carpet can charge your body to thousands of volts. You feel a spark at about 3,000 volts, but chips can be damaged by much smaller discharges that you never notice. When handling RAM, cards or bare boards, touch a grounded metal object first, use an antistatic wrist strap if you can, hold boards by the edges, and keep them in antistatic bags. Peripheral ports include ESD protection diodes, but bare chips do not.

Course wrap-up, the big picture: Every peripheral follows the same pattern. Something physical happens outside: a key is pressed, light hits a sensor, a platter spins. An interface carries signals across a bus or cable using an agreed protocol: UART, USB, SATA, PCIe, I2C, Ethernet. A controller with registers turns those signals into data, and a driver lets the operating system use it. The CPU learns about events by polling, interrupts or DMA. Analog signals cross into the digital world through ADCs and back through DACs, and weak logic pins control big loads through transistors, MOSFETs and relays.

How the lessons connect: Lessons 1 to 5 built the foundation: the I/O system, polling, interrupts, DMA, buses and PCI Express. Lessons 6 to 10 covered the cables and protocols: serial and parallel, UART, RS-232, USB, SPI and I2C. Lessons 11 to 18 explored human interface and media devices: keyboards, mice, touch screens, displays, GPUs, small LCDs, printers, scanners and cameras. Lessons 19 and 20 covered storage, from hard disks to NVMe SSDs and RAID. Lessons 21 to 24 crossed into embedded interfacing: ADC and DAC, sensors, actuators and microcontrollers. And this lesson connected the computer to networks and to power.

How to revise for the exam: Make a one-page sheet of formulas: polling overhead, bus bandwidth, UART frame time, USB and SATA encoding, display bandwidth and frame buffer size, disk access time and capacity, ADC step size and output, DAC output, voltage divider, ultrasonic distance, LED and base resistors, timer ticks and stepper steps. Practise each with one worked example. Then draw block diagrams from memory: an interrupt-driven I/O system, a DMA transfer, a USB tree, an HDD, an SSD, an ADC, an H-bridge and a complete microcontroller project.

Real-life example, a smart classroom in a Sylhet school: A school installs a projector over HDMI, a document camera over USB, ceiling fans controlled by relays and a temperature sensor, Wi-Fi for tablets, an Ethernet link to the office, and a UPS so the lesson continues during load shedding. Every part of this room is something you studied in this course, and a technician who understands the whole chain can fix any piece of it.

Recap: NICs move packets with DMA and interrupts and have 48-bit MAC addresses. Ethernet uses twisted pairs or fibre, Wi-Fi uses 2.4, 5 and 6 gigahertz bands, Bluetooth Low Energy saves power, and NFC works at 13.56 megahertz over a few centimetres. PSUs provide 12, 5 and 3.3 volt rails with switch-mode efficiency; power budgets prevent brownouts; UPS types differ in switch-over time; surge protection and ESD care save hardware. Above all, peripherals and interfacing are about turning the physical world into data and back, safely and reliably. You now understand how a computer meets the world.
key_points: A NIC moves frames between the computer and network using DMA and interrupts; each has a 48-bit MAC address.
Ethernet uses twisted-pair copper up to 100 m or optical fibre for long distances.
Wi-Fi uses 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands; Bluetooth Low Energy suits tiny battery devices; NFC works at 13.56 MHz over a few centimetres.
An ATX PSU gives 12 V, 5 V, 3.3 V and 5 V standby rails using efficient switch-mode conversion.
A power budget sums current at each voltage with margin, preventing brownouts.
Offline UPS switches in a few milliseconds; online UPS has no switch-over gap; IPS units run home loads for hours.
Surge protectors, stabilisers, proper earthing and ESD precautions protect peripherals and boards.
lessons.tip: For revision, make one formula sheet and one diagram sheet for the whole course. If you can explain each diagram aloud to a friend in two minutes, you are ready for any long question.
lessons.task: Check your home or school network: find your computer's MAC address and whether it uses Wi-Fi 2.4 or 5 GHz or Ethernet. Then write a power budget for a project with an ESP32 (250 mA peak at 3.3 V), two servos (500 mA each at 5 V) and a 12 V pump (1 A), and choose a suitable supply.

quiz.q: How long is a MAC address?
quiz.explain: A MAC address is 48 bits, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits.

quiz.q: Which wireless technology is used when you tap a metro rail card or contactless bank card?
quiz.explain: NFC works at 13.56 MHz over a few centimetres, used for tap cards and phone payments.

quiz.q: Which ATX rail stays on even when the PC is switched off?
quiz.explain: The 5 V standby rail lets the PC wake from a keyboard, mouse or network signal.

quiz.q: Which UPS type has no switch-over gap at all?
quiz.explain: An online UPS always powers the load from its inverter, so mains failure causes no gap.

quiz.q: Why does a PC's switch-mode supply waste less power than an old linear supply?
options: It uses no transformer at all
It switches at high frequency, so a small transformer and efficient switching replace burning off extra voltage
quiz.explain: Switch-mode supplies chop the input at high frequency, using small transformers and switches instead of dropping excess voltage as heat.
